capabilities.prediction: Accuracy ≥ 0.9 for each of m = 1, 2, 3. The baseline is a matched single layer with the same RLS/EDMD update and readout W_o K_t^T Phi[q], i.e. a readout linear in the state, as in MesaNet/DeltaNet. It reaches ≥ 0.9 at m = 1 but ≤ 0.5 at m = 2 and m = 3.
capabilities.task: Iterated rule application on unseen tokens. V_c = 64 ordinal content tokens. Context: BOS, then 16 demonstrations 'a f(a) ;' of a shift-by-s rule, with s uniform in {1..63}. Query: '@m q', where '@m' is a single marker token, m ∈ {1, 2, 3}, and q is not among the demonstrated inputs. Target: q + m s mod 64. Prediction is the argmax over all V logits at q's position. Single layer, d = 16, M = 4. 500 trials per m.

capabilities.prediction: Accuracy ≥ 0.95 for K ≤ 48. Accuracy ≤ 0.6 for K = 256 (4d). A d×d least-squares operator interpolates at most d linearly independent input lifts and averages beyond that, so this is a hard capacity limit of the core.
capabilities.task: Associative recall of K random token bindings. V_c = 1024 content tokens. Context: BOS, then K pairs 'a b ;' with distinct a's and b's drawn uniformly, then the query '@1 a' for a demonstrated a. Single layer, d = 64. 500 trials per K. A trial is correct iff the argmax of W_o y over all V tokens (content and reserved) at the position of a equals b.

capabilities.prediction: Accuracy ≥ 0.85. This follows because c_0, c_1 and c_2 are all demonstrated inputs, so (K_t^T)^3 Phi[c_0] ≈ Phi[c_3] within the 32 ≤ d capacity. If alpha is forced onto power 1 (M = 1), accuracy is ≤ 0.1, since the readout then returns c_1.
capabilities.task: Pointer chasing. V_c = 1024 content tokens. Each trial draws 8 disjoint chains of 5 distinct tokens (c_0 → c_1 → c_2 → c_3 → c_4), giving K = 32 pairs. The 32 pairs are presented as 'c_i c_{i+1} ;' in random order after BOS. The query is '@3 c_0' for a randomly chosen chain, and the target is c_3. Prediction is the argmax over all V logits. Single layer, d = 64, M = 4. 1000 trials.

capabilities.prediction: k*(V_c = 64) and k*(V_c = 256) are both ≤ 16 and differ by at most 2.
capabilities.task: Demonstration count vs vocabulary size for lift-linear rules. This is the k* protocol of claims.sample_efficiency (d = 16, query '@1 q' on undemonstrated q, argmax over all V logits, 500 trials per k, k ∈ {2, 4, ..., 32}), run at V_c = 64 and at V_c = 256.

complexity.constants_notes: The RLS updates of P_t and K_t cost about 4d^2 multiply-adds per token. The power readout costs M matrix-vector products, about M d^2 in total. M is a fixed small constant (≤ 4). V d is the usual output projection. At inference the recurrent state is two d×d matrices, independent of n. Training unrolls the same recurrence, so it has the same O(n (M d^2 + V d)) time. Without checkpointing it stores O(n d^2) activations for backpropagation. These are training activations, not inference state. For very long n, RLS in float32 can drift away from positive-definiteness. The optional periodic re-solve extension handles this and is not part of the core.

sample_efficiency.mechanism: Identifying a lift-linear rule needs as many demonstrations as the rank of the lift (d), not as many as the vocabulary size (V). Once the demonstrated lifts span R^d with sigma_min^2 ≥ lambda, the least-squares solution is within eps ≤ lambda||K*||/(lambda + sigma_min^2) + ||E||/sigma_min of K*. That solution applies to all V content tokens and to all iterates.

prediction.metric: k*, measured by this protocol. Single layer, d = 16. Ordinal alphabet of V_c = 256 content tokens. For each k in {2, 4, 6, ..., 32}, run 500 trials. Each trial draws a shift s uniformly from {1, ..., V_c - 1}. It draws k distinct demonstrated inputs a_i uniformly without replacement and presents 'a_i (a_i + s mod V_c) ;' in random order after BOS. It then presents '@1 q', with q drawn uniformly from the content tokens not among the a_i. k* is the smallest k whose mean accuracy is ≥ 0.9, where a trial is correct if the argmax over all V logits at q's position equals q + s mod V_c.
prediction.statement: k* ≤ 16 = d for V_c = 256, and k* stays the same within ±2 when V_c changes from 64 to 256. An in-context memory based on counting or lookup has to see each input it is queried on, so its accuracy on undemonstrated queries stays near chance at every k < V_c.

card.core_idea: Treat the context as trajectory data of an unknown map, estimate that map's Koopman operator on a learned dictionary of token observables by online least squares (EDMD), and answer each query by applying a token-selected power of the operator, so that a rule seen on d linearly independent examples transfers to unseen tokens and to its own iterates through the Koopman semigroup law U_{f^m} = (U_f)^m.

extensions.description: Following the history-discretization construction for delay systems, lift a window of the last L tokens so that rules depending on more than one previous token become linear on the lifted space. The state grows to (Ld)×(Ld).

equations.plain: u = concat(Phi[x[t-1]], ..., Phi[x[t-L]])  # positions before 0 padded with BOS

extensions.name: Delay (history) lift

extensions.description: Replace integer powers by exp(tau L_t), where L_t = log K_t is the in-context generator (the neural-ODE flow view) and tau ≥ 0 is a learned clock. This allows interpolated or continuous-time iteration. Each eigendecomposition costs O(d^3), so the readout is applied only at query positions.
extensions.name: Generator readout with fractional time

extensions.description: Multiply the Gram and cross statistics by gamma < 1 per token, i.e. use standard exponentially weighted RLS, so that the operator tracks rule changes within a long context.
extensions.name: Forgetting factor

extensions.description: As a numerical safeguard for very long n in low precision, keep running sums G_t and C_t and recompute P_t = G_t^{-1} and K_t = P_t C_t every r tokens. The amortized cost is O(d^3 / r) per token.
extensions.name: Periodic re-solve

extensions.description: Add Gaussian noise to Phi[x] during training, following the neural SDE regularization view. The learned lift then keeps the Gram matrices well conditioned (larger sigma_min in the error bound), so the operator powers do not amplify errors.
extensions.name: Noise-injected lift during pretraining

extensions.description: Feed the y_t of one layer as the lift input of the next. This is for natural-language modeling, where single-layer bigram-like dynamics are insufficient.
extensions.name: Stacked layers

falsifiers: On the iterated-rule task (V_c = 64, d = 16, 16 demonstrations, unseen query tokens, argmax over all V logits), the single-layer model fails to beat a matched single layer with a degree-1 readout (same RLS update, alpha forced onto power 1) by at least 0.3 absolute accuracy at m = 2. That result would mean the power readout adds nothing.

Under the k* protocol (d = 16, 500 trials per k, undemonstrated queries), k* grows roughly in proportion to V_c, for example from ≤ 16 at V_c = 64 to ≥ 50 at V_c = 256. That result would refute the argument that a Koopman-invariant lift identifies the rule.

Single-layer associative recall with d = 64 stays ≥ 0.9 at K = 4d = 256 pairs. That result would mean something other than the d×d least-squares operator stores the bindings, and the capacity analysis of the core is wrong.

EDMD residual test. Predicted mean relative residual ≤ 0.2; the theory is falsified if the mean exceeds 0.5. Setup: after pretraining, evaluate 500 held-out sequences with V_c = 64 and d = 16. Each sequence has a shift s drawn uniformly from {1..63} and 16 demonstrations 'a (a+s mod 64) ;' with a drawn without replacement (context length 49 tokens including BOS). Each sequence also has one query token q drawn uniformly from the undemonstrated content tokens. Compute ||Phi[q+s mod 64] − K_t^T Phi[q]||^2 / ||Phi[q+s mod 64]||^2 with K_t taken after the last demonstration, and average over the 500 sequences. A mean above 0.5 would mean pretraining did not produce an approximately Koopman-invariant lift, so the few-shot mechanism would not be what drives any observed accuracy.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: The novelty is confined to the readout. y = sum_m alpha_m (K_t^T)^m Phi[x_t] is a polynomial of degree up to M in the state, and the token-selected powers implement rule iterates through the Koopman semigroup law. The relative layers read out q^T S, which has degree 1, so a single layer can return only f(q) and not f^m(q) for an unseen q.
known_relatives.name: Recursive least squares / Kalman filter; DeltaNet and MesaNet-style in-context least-squares layers
known_relatives.relation: The update is exactly weighted RLS. As a recurrence, K_t = (I - beta_t P_t u_t u_t^T) K_{t-1} + beta_t P_t u_t v_t^T, which has the form S_t = A_t S_{t-1} + B_t x_t. The update alone is therefore an SSM/linear-attention-family recurrence (a preconditioned delta rule). MesaNet-style layers already compute the same (G + lambda I)^{-1} C solution.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: Linear attention has no inverse Gram, so it cannot identify a rule from d non-orthogonal demonstrations, and it has no operator powers. The unseen-token claim needs the inverse Gram, and the iterate claim needs the powers.
known_relatives.name: Linear attention (Transformers are RNNs)
known_relatives.relation: C_t = sum beta u v^T is the linear-attention key-value state. Its keys are the lifts of the previous tokens and its values are the lifts of the current tokens.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: In those models the transitions are diagonal maps or decays chosen to summarize history. Here the state is a least-squares operator estimate with a closed-form meaning: the EDMD Koopman matrix of the context's rule. The readout applies that state to itself repeatedly as a dynamical operator.
known_relatives.name: Mamba / S4 / RetNet / RWKV
known_relatives.relation: Linear-time recurrent state with an input-dependent transition.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: TTT reads out the inner model once per token. Here the inner model is treated as a Koopman operator and composed with itself m times on demand.
known_relatives.name: Test-time training layers (Learning to learn at test time)
known_relatives.relation: With a linear inner model and an exact least-squares inner solve, TTT reduces to the same K_t.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: Those methods fit one global operator offline for one system. Here the dictionary is shared across sequences and the operator is re-estimated in context for each sequence, so each context is itself the system to identify.
known_relatives.name: Deep Koopman autoencoders / EDMD with learned dictionaries
known_relatives.relation: A learned lift with a linear operator in the lifted space.

learning.description: Pretraining learns Phi, W_o, w_beta and A by minimizing next-token cross-entropy and backpropagating through the in-context EDMD estimate and its powers. The training corpus mixes text with synthetic rule-induction sequences built from vocabulary tokens. Demonstrations have the form 'a f(a) ;'. Queries have the form '@m q', where '@m' is one marker token and the target is f^m(q). Chain data use the same pair format. Training unrolls the same recurrent RLS form used at inference (backpropagation through time), with the same update-then-readout order at each position. The parallel identity below is the closed form that the recurrence computes, and it can be used to check the recurrence. No parameter is updated at inference. All in-context learning happens in P_t and K_t, which are closed-form least-squares statistics.

equations.latex: K_t = \Big(\lambda I + \sum_{s=1}^{t} \beta_s u_s u_s^\top\Big)^{-1} \sum_{s=1}^{t} \beta_s u_s v_s^\top
equations.name: closed form computed by the recurrence
equations.plain: G = lambda*I + sum_{s<=t} beta_s*outer(u_s,u_s); C = sum_{s<=t} beta_s*outer(u_s,v_s); K_t = solve(G, C)

equations.latex: \mathcal{L}(\Phi, W_o, w_\beta, A) = -\sum_{t=1}^{n-1} \log p(x_{t+1} \mid x_{\le t})
equations.name: pretraining loss
equations.plain: loss = -sum_t log p_t[x[t+1]]; gradients flow through the RLS recursion and the powers of K_t

learning.few_shot_argument:
The argument combines Koopman invariance with the semigroup law and gives an explicit error bound.

Setup. Stack the gated pairs seen up to t as rows: U in R^{k×d} with rows sqrt(beta_s) u_s, and Y in R^{k×d} with rows sqrt(beta_s) v_s. Then K_t = (lambda I + U^T U)^{-1} U^T Y. Approximate invariance of the lift for a rule f means Y = U K* + E for some d×d K*. E holds the residuals: E = 0 under exact invariance, and pairs leaking through the gate with small beta also enter E. Let sigma_min be the smallest singular value of U. This requires k ≥ d demonstrations whose lifts span R^d. Assume sigma_min^2 ≥ lambda.

Operator bound. K_t − K* = −lambda (lambda I + U^T U)^{-1} K* + (lambda I + U^T U)^{-1} U^T E. Hence
eps := ||K_t − K*||_2 ≤ lambda ||K*||_2 / (lambda + sigma_min^2) + ||E||_2 / sigma_min.
The second term uses max_sigma sigma/(lambda + sigma^2) ≤ 1/sigma_min for sigma ≥ sqrt(lambda).

Unseen tokens. For any query q, including tokens never shown, ||K_t^T Phi[q] − Phi[f(q)]|| ≤ eps ||Phi[q]|| + r_q, where r_q = ||K*^T Phi[q] − Phi[f(q)]|| is the invariance residual at q (0 under exact invariance). Generalization goes through linearity in the lift, not lookup.

Iterates. Let rho = max(||K_t||_2, ||K*||_2). With E = 0, ||K_t||_2 ≤ ||K*||_2 because K_t = (I − lambda(lambda I + U^T U)^{-1}) K* and the first factor has norm ≤ 1. Telescoping gives ||(K_t^T)^m − (K*^T)^m||_2 ≤ m rho^{m−1} eps. The Koopman semigroup law U_{f∘g} = U_g U_f gives (K*^T)^m Phi[q] = Phi[f^m(q)] under exact invariance. The marker '@m' concentrates alpha on power m, so the readout evaluates f^m although f^m was never demonstrated.

Decision. The argmax decode is correct whenever 2 max_j ||W_o[j]|| · m rho^{m−1} eps ||Phi[q]|| is smaller than the logit margin gamma = (W_o Phi[f^m(q)])_{f^m(q)} − max_{j ≠ f^m(q)} (W_o Phi[f^m(q)])_j.

Toy check. In the toy example U^T U = I, so sigma_min = 1, E = 0 and eps = lambda/(1 + lambda) ≈ 1e-3. This is exactly K = K*/1.001.

Bindings. For rules that are not linear on the lift, such as arbitrary bindings, the same bound holds on the span of the demonstrated lifts. This allows up to d bindings with linearly independent lifts, which is the capacity limit stated in the claims.

Role of pretraining. Pretraining only has to make ||E|| and r_q small for common rule families (shifts, permutations of structured alphabets, successor relations).

readout.latex: \alpha_t = \mathrm{softmax}(A[x_{t-1}]),\quad y_t = \sum_{m=0}^{M} \alpha_{t,m} \,(K_t^\top)^m \,\Phi[x_t]
readout.name: operator power polynomial (computed after the position-t update)
readout.plain:
# order per position t: (1) update P, K with pair (x[t-1], x[t]); (2) read out with this K = K_t
alpha = softmax(A[x[t-1]]); h = Phi[x[t]]; y = alpha[0]*h; for m in 1..M: h = K.T @ h; y += alpha[m]*h

readout.latex: p(x_{t+1} = j \mid x_{\le t}) = \mathrm{softmax}(W_o y_t)_j,\qquad \hat{x}_{t+1} = \arg\max_{j \in \{1..V\}} (W_o y_t)_j
readout.name: token distribution and decision rule
readout.plain: p = softmax(W_o @ y); prediction for every accuracy claim = argmax over all V logits (no restriction to content tokens)

state.meaning: Lift. Row Phi[x] is the d-dimensional vector of observables of token x, where d is the lift dimension. V is the vocabulary size. The vocabulary contains the content tokens plus the reserved tokens BOS (start of sequence, prepended as x_0 to every sequence), ';' (separator) and the M marker tokens '@1', ..., '@M'. Each marker is one vocabulary token. Pretraining shapes Phi so that frequent rule families act linearly on it, i.e. its span is approximately Koopman-invariant for those rules.
state.name: Phi

state.meaning: Decoder that maps a predicted lift vector y in R^d to V logits. It may be tied to Phi, as in the toy example.
state.name: W_o

state.meaning: Pair-gate weights. beta_t = sigmoid(w_beta^T [u_t; v_t]) decides whether the adjacent pair (x_{t-1}, x_t) is a transition of the rule and should enter the operator fit. It is near 0 for pairs that involve BOS, ';' or a marker '@m'. In particular the query pairs (';', '@m') and ('@m', q) get beta ≈ 0.
state.name: w_beta

state.meaning: Iteration-coefficient table. This is the only object named A in the card; the EDMD cross statistic is called C. Row A[x] is passed through a softmax to give alpha in R^{M+1}, the weights on operator powers 0..M. M is a small fixed maximum iteration count, M = 4 in experiments. The previous token selects the row. In the query '@m q', the token '@m' precedes q, so A['@m'] sets the weights used when q is read out. Because x_0 = BOS, the row A[BOS] is used at t = 1.
state.name: A

state.meaning: Inverse regularized Gram matrix (lambda I + sum_{1<=s<=t} beta_s u_s u_s^T)^{-1} of the gated input lifts. It is initialized to P_0 = I/lambda, where lambda > 0 is the ridge constant (1e-3 by default).
state.name: P_t

state.meaning: In-context Koopman (EDMD) operator estimate K_t = P_t C_t, where C_t = sum_{1<=s<=t} beta_s u_s v_s^T is the gated cross statistic (not stored separately). K_0 = 0. K_t already includes the pair (x_{t-1}, x_t). K_t^T maps the lift of a token to the predicted lift of its successor under the rule shown in the context.
state.name: K_t

update.name: lift and gate
update.plain: x[0] = BOS; for t in 1..n: u = Phi[x[t-1]]; v = Phi[x[t]]; beta = sigmoid(dot(w_beta, concat(u, v)))

update.latex: P_t = P_{t-1} - \frac{\beta_t P_{t-1} u_t u_t^\top P_{t-1}}{1 + \beta_t u_t^\top P_{t-1} u_t}
update.name: inverse Gram (RLS) update
update.plain: Pu = P @ u; P = P - beta * outer(Pu, Pu) / (1 + beta * dot(u, Pu))

update.latex: K_t = K_{t-1} + \beta_t P_t u_t \left(v_t^\top - u_t^\top K_{t-1}\right)
update.name: Koopman operator (EDMD) update
update.plain: K = K + beta * outer(P @ u, v - u @ K)   # uses the already-updated P; equals (lambda I + sum_{s<=t} beta_s u_s u_s^T)^{-1} sum_{s<=t} beta_s u_s v_s^T exactly

references.why: Source of the data-driven Koopman operator as a least-squares fit on a chosen basis of observables, and of its use as a linear model rolled forward for multi-step model-based prediction. The card uses these as the per-sequence operator and the power readout. This paper also supplies the point that the choice of basis decides what becomes linear, which becomes the learned lift Phi here.

Koopman-MPC predicts future outputs over a horizon by applying the lifted linear model repeatedly to a nonlinear (hysteretic) system. This is the source of the readout that applies powers of the operator to get m-step-ahead predictions.

Source of the finite-dimensional EDMD approximation of a Koopman operator together with a reconstruction map from lifted coordinates back to states, which corresponds to the decoder W_o. Its history-discretization construction motivates the delay-lift extension.
Its view of a neural ODE flow map composed with an embedding and a projection motivates the generator/fractional-time extension, in which the iteration count becomes a continuous flow time.
Noise injection as a regularizer of continuous-time networks motivates the noise-injected-lift extension, which keeps the in-context Gram well conditioned.

source_transplant.change: In the sources, the data come from one physical system and the operator is fitted offline. Five things change here. (1) The data matrix is the current context, and weighted RLS re-estimates the operator online for every sequence. (2) A learned gate weights each pair, so separators and markers do not contaminate the fit. (3) The dictionary is a token embedding learned across many sequences in pretraining, not a set of hand-chosen basis functions. (4) The rollout horizon m is not a fixed control horizon. The previous token selects it through learned coefficients. (5) The predicted lift is decoded to a distribution over V tokens.
source_transplant.object: The extended dynamic mode decomposition (EDMD) least-squares estimate of the Koopman operator on a dictionary of observables, K = G^{-1} C with G = sum psi(x_t) psi(x_t)^T and C = sum psi(x_t) psi(x_{t+1})^T. It comes with its multi-step predictor psi(x_{t+m}) ≈ (K^T)^m psi(x_t), which Koopman model-predictive control uses for horizon rollouts.

card.summary: Pretraining learns four things: a lift Phi that maps every vocabulary token to d observables, a decoder W_o, a pair gate, and a small table of iteration coefficients. The vocabulary holds the content tokens plus the reserved tokens BOS, ';' and the M single-token iteration markers '@1'..'@M'. Each sequence starts with x_0 = BOS. Gated adjacent token pairs feed a recursive-least-squares (RLS) estimate K_t of the Koopman operator on the lift, which is the extended dynamic mode decomposition (EDMD) solution K = (lambda I + G)^{-1} C. At each position the operator is updated with the pair (x_{t-1}, x_t) first. The readout then applies a polynomial in K_t^T to the lift of the current token. The previous token selects the polynomial's coefficients, so a marker '@m' can request f, f∘f or f∘f∘f. Suppose a rule is linear on the lift, meaning the lift spans a Koopman-invariant subspace for that rule. Then k ≥ d demonstrations identify the rule on every token, including tokens never shown, with the explicit error bound ||K_t − K*|| ≤ lambda||K*||/(lambda + sigma_min^2) + ||E||/sigma_min. The rule's iterates follow from operator powers within one layer. The update is a known recurrence (RLS, a preconditioned delta rule). The new part is the readout, which has degree M in the state and is justified by Koopman semigroup composition. The state is O(d^2) and the cost is linear in n.
card.title: Koopman Power Readout: in-context EDMD whose operator is iterated by the semigroup law

toy_example.description: Vocabulary V = 13: content tokens 0..7 on a cycle, 8 = ';', 9 = BOS, and 10, 11, 12 = the markers '@1', '@2', '@3' (M = 3). Settings: d = 2, lambda = 1e-3. A hand-fixed lift stands in for a learned one. Content tokens get Fourier features Phi[j] = (cos 2πj/8, sin 2πj/8), and reserved tokens get zero rows. A hand-set gate stands in for the learned w_beta: beta = 1 for content-content pairs and 0 otherwise. Alpha rows are set directly to one-hot vectors, the large-logit limit of the softmax. '@m' selects power m, and every other token selects power 1. W_o = Phi. The context 'BOS 0 1 ; 2 3 ;' shows two demonstrations of f(j) = j + 1 mod 8. The demonstrated lifts (1,0) and (0,1) give U^T U = I, so sigma_min = 1 and RLS gives K = K*/1.001: a 45-degree rotation shrunk by the ridge, matching the bound eps = lambda/(1+lambda). Queries are read out with the final K. This equals K_t at the query position, because the query pairs (';','@m') and ('@m', q) have beta = 0 and leave P and K unchanged. The readout gives: '@2 5' → 7, '@3 6' → 9 mod 8 = 1, '@1 4' → 5. Tokens 4, 5 and 6 never appear in the context. With a degree-1 readout ('@1 5'), the only possible answer is 6.
toy_example.python:
import json
import numpy as np
NC, d, lam, M = 8, 2, 1e-3, 3
SEP, BOS = 8, 9
AT = {1: 10, 2: 11, 3: 12}
V = 13
ang = 2 * np.pi * np.arange(NC) / NC
Phi = np.zeros((V, d))
Phi[:NC] = np.stack([np.cos(ang), np.sin(ang)], axis=1)
A = np.zeros((V, M + 1))
A[:, 1] = 1.0
for m in range(1, M + 1):
    A[AT[m]] = np.eye(M + 1)[m]
seq = [BOS, 0, 1, SEP, 2, 3, SEP]
P = np.eye(d) / lam
K = np.zeros((d, d))
pairs = 0
for t in range(1, len(seq)):
    a, b = seq[t - 1], seq[t]
    beta = 1.0 if (a < NC and b < NC) else 0.0
    u, v = Phi[a], Phi[b]
    Pu = P @ u
    P = P - beta * np.outer(Pu, Pu) / (1.0 + beta * (u @ Pu))
    K = K + beta * np.outer(P @ u, v - u @ K)
    pairs += int(beta > 0)
def readout(prev, q):
    alpha = A[prev]
    h = Phi[q]
    y = alpha[0] * h
    for m in range(1, M + 1):
        h = K.T @ h
        y = y + alpha[m] * h
    logits = Phi @ y
    return int(np.argmax(logits)), round(float(logits.max()), 4)
p52 = readout(AT[2], 5)
p63 = readout(AT[3], 6)
p41 = readout(AT[1], 4)
p51 = readout(AT[1], 5)
out = {"pairs_used": pairs, "K": [[round(float(x), 4) for x in row] for row in K], "pred_5_m2": p52[0], "logit_5_m2": p52[1], "pred_6_m3": p63[0], "logit_6_m3": p63[1], "pred_4_m1": p41[0], "one_step_pred_5": p51[0]}
print(json.dumps(out))

critic.difference_if_any: The update is MesaNet/RLS with no change. What remains is the readout. The memory matrix is applied m times to the query, and a token-indexed softmax mixes the hop depths. The same state is reused for every hop, so this is a weight-tied multi-hop read of a least-squares fast-weight memory. Iterated reads of one associative memory already exist (Fast Weight Memory multi-step reads, iterative Hopfield retrieval, looped/universal transformers with shared weights). The Koopman semigroup framing explains why the hops compose to f^m for lift-linear rules, but it adds no new operation. The learning rule is ordinary next-token backprop through the recurrence, the same as MesaNet/DeltaNet training.
critic.mapping: Key k_t := u_t = Phi[x_{t-1}] (a token-shifted key, as in RWKV token-shift or induction-style previous-token keys). Value v_t := Phi[x_t]. Write strength / gate beta_t := sigmoid(w_beta^T[k_t; v_t]), the same role as the delta-rule beta. The card's update K_t = K_{t-1} + beta_t P_t u_t (v_t^T - u_t^T K_{t-1}) with the RLS update of P_t is the preconditioned delta rule. Its closed form is K_t = (lambda I + sum beta k k^T)^{-1} sum beta k v^T. MesaNet keeps G_t = sum beta k k^T and C_t = sum beta k v^T (the linear-attention KV state) and reads out C_t^T (G_t + lambda I)^{-1} q. With q := Phi[x_t], the card's degree-1 term K_t^T Phi[x_t] = C_t^T (lambda I + G_t)^{-1} q is exactly the MesaNet / Preconditioned-DeltaNet output; it is also exact linear-inner-model TTT. As a recurrence it is S_t = A_t S_{t-1} + B_t x_t with A_t = I - beta_t P_t u_t u_t^T. The power readout sum_m alpha_m (K_t^T)^m q is the same memory read iterated with the retrieved vector fed back as the next query. This is the multi-hop read of Fast Weight Memory (Schlag, Munkhdalai, Schmidhuber 2021, n_r read steps on one fast-weight matrix). It is equivalently a weight-tied looped linear-attention layer that shares one state across M hops, with a learned softmax mixture over hop depths selected by the previous token (alpha = softmax(A[x_{t-1}]), a per-token gate on hop outputs). Output projection W_o y is the standard LM head.
critic.textbook_why: The core is textbook EDMD (K = G^{-1}C on a dictionary of observables) computed by standard weighted RLS, plus the standard Koopman multi-step predictor psi(x_{t+m}) ≈ (K^T)^m psi(x_t) used in Koopman MPC. The card substitutes the token stream (adjacent token pairs) for system snapshots, uses a learned dictionary and a learned pair weight (ordinary weighted least squares), and adds a token-selected horizon mixture and a vocabulary decoder. These are input and readout substitutions, not changes to the estimator, update or rollout law.
critic.why: The card itself concedes that the update is weighted RLS, i.e. the MesaNet / preconditioned-DeltaNet in-context least-squares layer, and the equations confirm it exactly. The claimed novelty is a degree-M polynomial readout in the state. That is the same linear-attention read applied repeatedly with its output as the next query, a known multi-hop fast-weight read and a known looped-layer construction, here mixed by a token-selected coefficient table. Renaming the key-value least-squares state 'the EDMD Koopman operator' and the multi-hop read 'the semigroup law' changes no equation. The capability predictions (d-limited capacity, multi-hop iterates on lift-linear rules) follow directly from known properties of least-squares linear memories. A researcher familiar with DeltaNet, MesaNet and Fast Weight Memory would not be surprised by the mechanism.

capabilities.prediction: Take two internally connected components of eight sites each. One correctly labeled bridge makes all 64 cross-component parity queries deterministic and correct. Before that bridge, every such query gives probability 0.5 to each answer under the stated prior.
capabilities.task: One-shot relational bridge generalization

capabilities.prediction: For d=64, after 63 noiseless spanning-tree demonstrations, all 2016 unordered pair queries remain exactly correct after 100000 additional consistent redundant demonstrations. Memory stays O(d), and there is no fading-memory loss of accuracy.
capabilities.task: Exact long-context retention at bounded capacity

capabilities.prediction: For disconnected endpoints under independent fair latent bits, the returned probability 0.5 is the exact posterior. A single wrong cycle-closing demonstration, or a self-pair demonstration DEMO(a,a,1), sets C immediately. Every later query then gets probability 0.5 until a fresh learner is constructed. This detects contradictions but does not repair noisy evidence.
capabilities.task: Uncertainty and contradiction detection

complexity.constants_notes: The bounds assume a word-RAM with O(log d)-bit words, union by size, and no path compression. Initialization costs O(d) time, so the end-to-end cost including construction is O(d + n log d). Memory is O(d log d) bits. Vocabulary tokens have an arithmetic encoding. The output distribution is returned sparsely with at most two nonzero entries; writing out all V entries would instead cost O(V) per readout. Capacity is at most d named sites and d-1 independent consistent binary relations. It is not an unbounded store of arbitrary associations.

sample_efficiency.mechanism: Exact quotient identification. Connected-component membership decides whether a pairwise answer is identifiable, and accumulated edge parity supplies that answer.

prediction.metric: Accuracy on all unobserved pairs among four sites after three path demonstrations
prediction.statement: For every noiseless assignment of four binary site values, demonstrations on edges (0,1), (1,2) and (2,3) give 100% accuracy on the three remaining unordered pairs. No pretraining or fitted readout weights are used.

card.core_idea: Store demonstrations as an exact quotient of a binary constraint graph, so that a handful of relations can determine many unseen answers without storing or replaying the sequence.
falsifiers: Any consistent four-site assignment for which the three path demonstrations give a wrong answer on a remaining pair refutes the exact sufficient-statistic claim.
If any of the 64 cross-component queries stays ambiguous or becomes incorrect after a valid bridge between two eight-site connected components, the one-shot bridge-generalization claim is false.

Each of the following refutes the claimed idempotent constraint encoding: a valid consistent cycle that changes a previously determined pairwise answer; a contradictory cycle that does not set C; or DEMO(a,a,1) failing to set C.
An implementation of the specified union-by-size operations whose storage grows with the number of redundant demonstrations would refute the stated streaming memory bound.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: This core replaces contraction with an exact discrete quotient of constraint solutions. It has no randomly initialized recurrent weights, no fitted regression readout and no decay. Sample complexity is set by connectivity rather than by numerical reservoir separation.
known_relatives.name: Graph Echo State Networks
known_relatives.relation: The source uses a fixed contractive graph reservoir and an adaptive readout.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: No novelty is claimed for union-find or binary gauge constraints. The proposed learner theory uses their exact sufficient statistic as a reservoir and makes the connectivity-dependent generalization law explicit. The contribution is a narrow sequence-learning mechanism and a testable theory, not a new general-purpose data structure.
known_relatives.name: Parity union-find, graph constraint propagation, and binary gauge synchronization
known_relatives.relation: These are the direct algorithmic and mathematical relatives. The core implementation is parity union-find.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: The update here changes a discrete component partition and its parent pointers. It is not of the form S_t=A_t S_{t-1}+B_t x_t. A finite-state one-hot encoding could represent the whole algorithm with an enormous transition system. The distinction is therefore one of efficiency and representation, not a claim that a recurrence cannot simulate it.
known_relatives.name: Mamba, RWKV, RetNet, and linear-attention recurrences
known_relatives.relation: All of these keep a context-dependent persistent state with subquadratic processing cost.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: Here evidence changes an exact constraint quotient. It does not optimize weights or write outer-product associations. Generalization follows logical entailment within a fixed binary relation class, not a learned optimizer.
known_relatives.name: Test-time training and fast-weight memory
known_relatives.relation: Both can absorb demonstrations while processing a sequence.

learning.description: There are no learned numerical parameters. Structure learning is the union operation that each demonstration induces. The model assumes independent fair latent binary values at the d sites, with noiseless observations of their pairwise XOR. For a consistent context, P and H are an exact sufficient statistic for every pairwise posterior. Each connected component keeps one unidentifiable global bit flip. The learner is specialized to this supplied relational hypothesis class. It does not discover XOR semantics from unrestricted text.
learning.few_shot_argument: The mechanism is gauge elimination through connectivity. A demonstration that connects two components removes one independent component-flip ambiguity. A spanning tree on k+1 sites therefore needs exactly k independent demonstrations to identify every pairwise relation among those sites. For example, three demonstrations along a four-site path determine all three unobserved pairs exactly. If two large components are already internally identified, one bridge demonstration determines every cross-component pair. Repeated cycles add no information, and disconnected components remain genuinely ambiguous.

readout.latex: z=h_a\mathbin{\mathrm{XOR}}h_b\in\{0,1\};\qquad q=\begin{cases}\mathbf{1}[z=1],&x_t=\operatorname{ASK}(a,b),\ r_a=r_b,\ \neg C,\\1/2,&\text{otherwise};\end{cases}\qquad p_t(y_1)=q,\ \ p_t(y_0)=1-q,\ \ p_t(y)=0\ \text{for all other }y.
readout.name: Exact relational posterior
readout.plain: After ASK(a,b), compute the bit z = h_a XOR h_b. If the endpoints share a root and C is false, the probability q is 1.0 when z = 1 and 0.0 when z = 0. In every other case q = 0.5. These other cases are disconnected endpoints, an inconsistent context, and any non-ASK position, which is not claimed to give a useful prediction. Output probability q on y_1 (bit 1) and 1 - q on y_0 (bit 0), and probability zero on every other token. The distribution is stored sparsely as these two entries. ASK(a,a) therefore gives probability 1 on y_0 in a consistent context.

state.meaning:
Protocol. There are d >= 2 named sites, indexed 0 through d-1. The context has length n. The fixed vocabulary has V = 3*d*d + 2 tokens: DEMO(a,b,s) for site indices a,b and parity s in {0,1}; ASK(a,b); and two answer tokens. The answer token y_0 means bit value 0 and y_1 means bit value 1. At step t, x_t is the supplied token, and F decodes tokens arithmetically without a stored lookup table. Self-pairs a = b are valid tokens: DEMO(a,a,s) asserts that a site's bit XOR itself equals s, and ASK(a,a) queries that XOR. XOR denotes addition modulo two.

Find. Find(i) follows parent pointers from site i and returns its root r_i and the parity h_i accumulated along that path. It does not modify the state.

Temporary values. In the join update, u and v denote the two distinct roots. u is the root with the larger M, and on equal M it is the one with the smaller index. In the readout, z is the bit h_a XOR h_b in {0,1}, and q is a real number in [0,1] equal to the predicted probability of y_1. The symbol y is any vocabulary token, p_t(y) is the next-token distribution, and 1[condition] is the 0/1 indicator. These local values are not persistent memories.
state.name: F
state.type: Fixed protocol and operations; not learned

state.meaning: Initially P[i]=i. It encodes the component forest of the observed constraint graph. Each entry takes O(log d) bits. Roots identify components; they are not learned semantic embeddings.
state.name: P

state.meaning: Initially all zero. H[i] records the inferred XOR of the latent bit at site i and the latent bit at P[i]. Latent site bits themselves are not stored. Root entries remain zero.
state.name: H

state.meaning: Initially all one. M[r] is the size of the component rooted at r. Entries at nonroots are ignored. Union by size bounds parent-path length by O(log d).
state.name: M

state.meaning: Initially false. It becomes true if any demonstration contradicts a previously implied parity, including a self-pair demonstration DEMO(a,a,1). An inconsistent context gets a deliberately uninformative answer distribution rather than an unsupported inferred answer.
state.name: C

update.name: Resolve the current relation
update.plain: For DEMO(a,b,s) or ASK(a,b), traverse the parent paths of a and b, XORing H along each path. If a = b, both calls return the same root and parity, so h_a XOR h_b = 0. Answer tokens do not change the reservoir.

update.latex: \text{If }x_t=\operatorname{DEMO}(a,b,s),\ r_a\ne r_b:\ (u,v)=\begin{cases}(r_a,r_b),& M[r_a]>M[r_b]\ \text{or}\ (M[r_a]=M[r_b]\ \text{and}\ r_a<r_b),\\(r_b,r_a),&\text{otherwise};\end{cases}\quad P[v]\leftarrow u,\ H[v]\leftarrow h_a\mathbin{\mathrm{XOR}}h_b\mathbin{\mathrm{XOR}}s,\ M[u]\leftarrow M[u]+M[v].
update.name: Join independent components
update.plain: For a demonstration whose endpoints have different roots, choose the surviving root u: u is r_a if M[r_a] > M[r_b], or if the sizes are equal and r_a < r_b. Otherwise u is r_b. Let v be the other root. Set P[v] = u, set H[v] = h_a XOR h_b XOR s, and set M[u] = M[u] + M[v]. Because XOR is symmetric, the same parity formula is correct for either attachment direction.

update.name: Check cycle consistency
update.plain: If the endpoints already share a root, compare the supplied parity s with the implied parity h_a XOR h_b. Set C if they disagree. This uses the roots obtained before any update. This also covers a = b. There the implied parity is 0, so DEMO(a,a,0) changes nothing, and DEMO(a,a,1) sets C. This is intended, because a bit XOR itself cannot be 1.

references.why: The supplied abstract describes a fixed contractive graph encoding, stability in the presence of cycles, and a separately adaptive readout. The transplant takes the graph-encoding role but replaces contraction with exact, idempotent constraint closure. The parity union-find algorithm and the gauge-identifiability argument are not claimed to appear in this paper.

source_transplant.change: The contractive numerical encoding is replaced by an idempotent encoding of the solution set of binary graph constraints. The resulting reservoir keeps exact component relations instead of fading graph features. This is a substantial change. Neither parity constraints nor union-find are attributed to the source paper.

card.summary: This is a small, specialized sequence learner for binary relational rules. Its reservoir is a set of named binary sites whose relative values are constrained by demonstrations. It does not evolve a numerical hidden vector. Instead it merges equivalent components and keeps their relative parity. The central theory is that conceptual sample complexity is controlled by graph connectivity: one new bridge can determine every previously ambiguous relation across two components. The mechanism is an exact classical algorithm, not a general language model, and its parity union-find construction is not claimed to be new.
card.title: Gauge-Quotient Constraint Reservoir

toy_example.description: Three demonstrations identify relations among four sites, while a fifth site stays disconnected. A consistent redundant cycle changes nothing, and an inconsistent cycle sets the rejection flag. Roots are chosen by size with ties going to the smaller index, matching the join equation.
toy_example.python:
import json

class Reservoir:
    def __init__(self, d):
        self.P = list(range(d))
        self.H = [0] * d
        self.M = [1] * d
        self.C = False

    def find(self, i):
        h = 0
        while self.P[i] != i:
            h ^= self.H[i]
            i = self.P[i]
        return i, h

    def demo(self, a, b, s):
        ra, ha = self.find(a)
        rb, hb = self.find(b)
        if ra == rb:
            self.C = self.C or ((ha ^ hb) != s)
            return
        if self.M[ra] < self.M[rb] or (self.M[ra] == self.M[rb] and ra > rb):
            u, v = rb, ra
        else:
            u, v = ra, rb
        self.P[v] = u
        self.H[v] = ha ^ hb ^ s
        self.M[u] += self.M[v]

    def p_one(self, a, b):
        ra, ha = self.find(a)
        rb, hb = self.find(b)
        if self.C or ra != rb:
            return 0.5
        return float(ha ^ hb)

r = Reservoir(5)
for event in [(0, 1, 1), (1, 2, 0), (2, 3, 1)]:
    r.demo(*event)
queries = [(0, 2), (0, 3), (1, 3), (0, 4)]
probabilities = [r.p_one(*q) for q in queries]
components = len({r.find(i)[0] for i in range(5)})
r.demo(0, 3, 0)
bad_after_consistent = r.C
r.demo(0, 3, 1)
result = {
    'p_one': probabilities,
    'components': components,
    'bad_after_consistent': bad_after_consistent,
    'bad_after_conflict': r.C,
    'p_one_after_conflict': [r.p_one(*q) for q in queries]
}
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

critic.difference_if_any: Nothing beyond packaging. The card wraps parity union-find in a token protocol (DEMO/ASK/answer tokens with arithmetic decoding). It reports the 'unknown' and 'contradiction' cases as a 0.5/0.5 distribution and calls the data structure a reservoir. There are no learned parameters. The 'structure learning' is just the union operation of the data structure, so there is no learning-rule difference. The O(n log d) time, O(d) memory and idempotence on redundant consistent edges are the standard properties of union by size without path compression. Connectivity-controlled identifiability is the standard rank argument for a GF(2) system on a graph: rank = d − #components.
critic.mapping: The card is Z2-labeled (parity / weighted) union-find, the standard online solver for XOR-pair equations x_a ⊕ x_b = s. This is the same as online 2-coloring and bipartiteness checking, and it is the labeled union-find of W4411260212 specialized to the group Z2. Symbol by symbol: P[i] is the union-find parent pointer parent[i]. H[i] is the edge label (potential) to the parent, label[i] = x_i ⊕ x_{parent(i)}. M[r] is the size field used by union by size. Find(i) is the standard non-compressing find, returning (root, xor of labels along the path). DEMO(a,b,s) on distinct roots is the labeled union: attach root v under root u with label[v] = h_a ⊕ h_b ⊕ s. This is the textbook formula that keeps x_a ⊕ x_b = s after merging. DEMO(a,b,s) on equal roots is the standard cycle-consistency check, flagging a contradiction if h_a ⊕ h_b ≠ s. C is the usual sticky 'unsatisfiable / not bipartite' flag. The readout ASK(a,b) is the standard query: if same root and consistent, return h_a ⊕ h_b, else 'unknown'. The card encodes 'unknown' as probability 0.5, the uniform posterior under fair independent latent bits. The equations coincide line for line, including the tie-breaking rule. The 'gauge' per component is the free global flip of each connected component's 2-coloring, a standard fact about the solution set of a homogeneous-plus-offset GF(2) system on a graph. None of the listed neural forms is a meaningful match (rnn, ssm, linear_attention or hopfield). Any finite state machine is trivially an RNN, but that mapping carries no content. The correct reduction is to this known algorithm.
critic.textbook_why: The cited source construction is the Graph Echo State Network's fixed contractive graph encoding with an adaptive readout. The card does not use it. The equations contain no contraction, no reservoir weights and no fitted readout, so the transplanted object is replaced rather than applied unmodified. What replaces it is itself a textbook algorithm from a different field: parity/labeled union-find with union by size. It is used without modification.
critic.why: The update and readout are exactly Z2-labeled union-find with union by size and a cycle-consistency flag. The card itself says so, and the prior-art search found the same mechanism (labeled union-find, W4411260212). The capability claims follow directly from textbook facts about the algorithm and about XOR systems on graphs. These are one-shot bridging, exact retention under redundant edges, and 0.5 posteriors on disconnected pairs. The card re-describes these as a 'sequence learner' and a 'reservoir'. A known algorithm moved into a sequence-modeling framing is not radical. It also only handles the hand-supplied hypothesis class of pairwise XOR relations, so it would not surprise a researcher who knows union-find or constraint propagation.

capabilities.prediction:
Setup: m = 64, d = 256, s = 2, 128 stored atoms. Query 100 distinct three-cue composites {a, b, c}; the target is v_a + v_b + v_c.

Predictions:
- Accuracy <= 0.3 before any demonstration, because only two atoms can be selected.
- After one DEMO of each such composite, repeating the same queries gives accuracy >= 0.99. Each DEMO is always written, because a three-cue key is generically not 2-sparse in the store. After all 100 writes the store holds 228 <= d episodes, so nothing is evicted.

Why the repaired query is answered correctly: the stored composite key equals the query q = k_a + k_b + k_c, so its normalized score is exactly ||q|| = sqrt(3 + 2(k_a.k_b + k_a.k_c + k_b.k_c)). This is the Cauchy-Schwarz maximum, about 1.73 for these codes. Each atom scores about 1, and a stored composite sharing two cues scores about 2/sqrt(3) = 1.15. The exact composite is therefore selected first, with zero residual.

complexity.constants_notes:
Per-step cost:
- Scoring: at most s passes over at most d stored keys, each one m-dimensional dot product (cached key norms).
- Refit: a pseudoinverse solve on at most s columns, O(s^2 m).
- Key: O(w m) for the key sum.
- Write: O(m + p).

Readout: O(V p) to materialize all logits, or O(p) per token if only the argmax (nearest output code) is needed.

Memory is d(m + p + 1) numbers plus the parameter block, with p <= m.

All claims use s = 2. Nothing grows with n: the store is capped at d.

sample_efficiency.mechanism: One-shot gated writes of unexplained episodes, combined with sparse explaining-away inference at read time. A cue never shown alone is answered by solving over two stored episodes, not by statistical fitting.

prediction.metric: Top-1 accuracy (argmax of p_t equals the true integer) on queries of cues never shown alone.
prediction.statement:
Setup:
- m = 64, d = 256, s = 2, untrained instance (unit Gaussian cue codes, E[y] = y, V = 64 output tokens 0..63).
- 120 disjoint cue pairs (a_i, b_i), which use 240 of the U = 256 cue tokens, with values v ~ Uniform{0..15}.
- Each pair is shown exactly twice: first as the composite DEMO({a_i, b_i}, v_{a_i} + v_{b_i}), and after all composites, as DEMO({a_i}, v_{a_i}). This makes 240 demonstrations, with no eviction.
- Then QUERY({b_i}) for all i.

Prediction: accuracy >= 0.9, pooled over 20 random draws x 120 queries = 2400 queries. This uses two demonstrations per binding and zero demonstrations of the queried cue.

card.core_idea: A one-shot episodic store keeps only the episodes its own s-sparse pursuit cannot explain, and answers a query by solving for the sparsest signed combination of stored episode keys that reproduces the query key, then returning the same combination of the stored values.

extensions.description: For raw text, set X_t to the last w tokens and treat every position as a DEMO of its next token. A learned per-offset code C_j[x] replaces C[x], so that order inside the window is encoded. Claims do not cover this wrapper.

equations.plain: The key is the sum of position-specific codes of the last w tokens.

extensions.name: Window-key language-model wrapper

extensions.description: Periodically fit a slow ridge map W from keys to values on the episodes currently in the store. Then delete episodes that W explains within eps, freeing slots. This is the CLS replay step, outside the core.
extensions.name: Replay consolidation into a slow linear map

extensions.description: Replace FIFO eviction with eviction of the episode selected least often by u2 since it was written.
extensions.name: Least-used eviction

falsifiers: The toy program does not print the expected values. In particular, the query for the never-shown cue b after 'a+b -> 7' and 'a -> 3' does not return 4.0, or the consistent composite 'a+c -> 8' is written.
In the overcomplete compositional-recall setup (m = 64, d = 256, s = 2, 1000 queries), core top-1 accuracy is below 0.95.
In the consolidation setup, more than 5 of 100 consistent composites are written, or any inconsistent composite is not written.

Cost protocol: count m-dimensional vector operations (dot products and axpys) per step on streams of n = 10^3, 10^4 and 10^5 steps (d = 256, m = 64, s = 2, |X_t| <= 3). The claim is refuted if any step exceeds s*d + 32 = 544 such operations, or if the per-token mean changes by more than 10% across n.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: Activation here is not a Hamming-radius set. It is a sequential explaining-away pursuit whose later selections depend on the residual left by earlier ones. Pooling uses signed least-squares coefficients, not counter sums. Hard locations are not fixed random addresses: they are allocated on demand to unexplained episodes.
known_relatives.name: Kanerva Sparse Distributed Memory
known_relatives.relation: Reads by pooling the contents of the hard locations that an address activates. Its capacity can exceed the vector dimension.

known_relatives.name: Orthogonal matching pursuit and sparse coding / online dictionary learning
known_relatives.relation: u2 is OMP used unchanged as the read operation.

known_relatives.claimed_difference:
Their state is a function of G = sum k k^T and H = sum k y^T, or of an order-weighted version, and their readout is linear in the query, so they realize a map of rank <= m.

Here the readout is piecewise linear in q, with a data-chosen support. It is not invariant under the index rotation (K, Y) -> (KQ, YQ), which preserves G and H. It fits d > m episodes exactly.
known_relatives.name: MesaNet / in-context least squares, RLS, DeltaNet, linear attention, SSMs
known_relatives.relation: These also answer queries with a least-squares-like map fitted in context.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: The ALD test and the KRLS prediction use the full dictionary. That is a dense least-squares fit, equivalent to the MesaNet form on the retained set. Here both the gate and the readout use an s-sparse support, which is what allows d > m and the -1 coefficient on near-orthogonal episodes.
known_relatives.name: Kernel recursive least squares with approximate-linear-dependence sparsification
known_relatives.relation: Also admits a sample to its dictionary only if it is not explained by the current dictionary.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: Their weights are nonnegative similarity scores that do not depend on values and are computed per item. Explaining away needs a negative weight on an item with near-zero similarity to the query, set by a joint least-squares refit on the selected support.
known_relatives.name: Modern Hopfield / softmax attention / memory networks with multiple hops
known_relatives.relation: Retrieve values from stored key-value episodes.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: The error gate here is the sparse-explanation residual of the store itself, not a TD error. The store is read by pursuit, not by SOM best-matching-unit distance weighting.
known_relatives.name: Complementary Temporal Difference Learning (CTDL)
known_relatives.relation: A hippocampal store written when the slow system's error is high.

learning.description:
In context, the only learning is the one-shot gated write u4. The store is a dictionary of episodes grown only by unexplained data.

Slowly, theta = (C, E, beta) can be pretrained on many synthetic in-context sequences by minimizing next-token cross-entropy. During this training:
- the support S_t from u2 is treated as a constant;
- gradients flow through the least-squares solution alpha_t = pinv(K_{S_t}) k_t into C, and through yhat_t into E.
Pretraining should lower the mutual coherence of the codes, which enlarges the recoverable sparsity.

All claims below are stated for the untrained instance (random unit Gaussian codes, E[y] = y). The claims test the mechanism, not the training.

equations.latex: \mathcal L(\theta)=-\sum_{t:z_t=\mathrm{DEMO}}\log p_t(y_t),\quad \nabla_\theta \text{ through } \alpha_t=K_{S_t}^{+}k_t \text{ with } S_t \text{ held fixed}
equations.name: pretraining loss
equations.plain: Cross-entropy of the label at each DEMO step. Backpropagate through the least-squares coefficients on the selected support; the selection itself is held fixed.

learning.few_shot_argument:
A binding shown once is written in one shot. A new random key is generically not in the span of any s stored keys, so its pursuit residual is nonzero.

Now take a later query whose key equals an s-sparse signed combination of stored keys, k_q = sum_{i in T} c_i K_i with |T| <= s. Once the pursuit selects exactly T, the refit gives alpha = c with zero residual, and yhat = sum_i c_i v_i. This is exactly the value under an additive binding rule, whether or not this combination was ever shown.

When is T selected? The worst-case guarantee ((2s-1) mu < 1, with mu the mutual coherence) does NOT hold in the claimed setup. For 256 random unit codes in R^64, mu is about 0.6. The claims instead rest on a per-query estimate. For a non-support unit key k_i, k_i . u is approximately N(0, ||u||^2 / m).

Pair query q = k_a + k_b, with rho = k_a . k_b:
- Step 1: each support key scores 1 + rho, while a non-support key scores about N(0, (2 + 2 rho)/m). The margin is z = sqrt(m (1 + rho)/2), which is about 5.7 at m = 64 and rho = 0. The per-key exceedance probability is about 1e-8, and the union over 254 keys is about 1e-5 (about 3e-4 at a 2-sigma rho = -0.25).
- Step 2: the residual is k_b - rho k_a. The true key scores 1 - rho^2, the others score about N(0, (1 - rho^2)/m), and z = sqrt(m (1 - rho^2)), about 8.

Inferred binding (query k_b with stored composite k_a + k_b and atom k_a):
- Step 1: the composite scores 1/sqrt(2), about 0.71, against noise of std 1/8 (z about 5.7).
- Step 2: the residual is about (k_b - k_a)/2. The atom k_a scores 0.5 against noise of std about 0.088 (z about 5.7).

Consequences:
- d one-shot atoms answer on the order of d^s composites.
- A cue never shown alone (b) is answered from one composite (a+b) and one atom (a), because k_b = 1*(k_a + k_b) - 1*k_a is 2-sparse in the store.

The novelty gate keeps explained composites out of the store, so the d slots hold independent information.

Capacity is limited. At most d episodes are retained under FIFO eviction. Composites needing more than s atoms are answered wrongly until one demonstration of them is written.

readout.latex: p_t(v)=\frac{\exp(-\beta\|E[v]-\hat y_t\|^2)}{\sum_{u=1}^{V}\exp(-\beta\|E[u]-\hat y_t\|^2)}
readout.name: next-token distribution
readout.plain:
For every output token v, the logit is -beta * squared distance between its output code E[v] and yhat_t. Apply a softmax over the V tokens.

On DEMO steps this is the prediction made before y_t is revealed; on QUERY steps it is the answer. With E[y] = y, the argmax is the integer token nearest to yhat_t.

state.name: Input specification

state.meaning:
C[x] in R^m is the cue code of cue token x (one row per cue token, U rows), and m is the key dimension. E[y] in R^p is the output code of output token y (one row per output token, V rows), and p is the value dimension. beta is the readout inverse temperature.

The claims use an untrained instance:
- U = 256 cue tokens; rows of C are i.i.d. Gaussian, normalized to unit length;
- V = 64 output tokens 0..63, p = 1 and E[y] = y.

Pretraining (see learning) adapts C and E for natural data.
state.name: theta = (C, E, beta)

state.meaning:
Column i of K_t is the key of a stored episode, and column i of Y_t is its value code. The norm ||K_i|| is cached when the episode is written. The store starts empty.

append_d(M, (k, v)) appends a column pair and drops the oldest pair if the size would exceed d. K_S denotes the columns of K indexed by an ordered index list S, and Y_S likewise for Y.
state.name: M_t = (K_t, Y_t)
state.type: Bounded episodic store, ordered oldest to newest

state.meaning: S_t is the selected support. alpha_t holds the minimum-norm least-squares coefficients on K_{S_t}. r_t = k_t - K_{S_t} alpha_t is the unexplained residual of the query key. yhat_t = Y_{S_t} alpha_t is the predicted value code. yhat_t is the zero vector when S_t is empty.
state.name: (S_t, alpha_t, r_t, yhat_t)
shape: S_t: ordered list of <= s store indices
state.type: Pursuit result at step t (temporary, recomputed every step)

update.name: u1: cortical key
update.plain: k_t = sum of the cue codes C[x] over the nonempty cue set X_t of the current step.

update.latex: r^{(0)}=k_t,\ S^{(0)}=\varnothing;\ \text{for } j=1..s:\ i_j=\arg\max_{i\notin S^{(j-1)}}\frac{|K_{t-1,i}^\top r^{(j-1)}|}{\|K_{t-1,i}\|};\ \text{stop if the max}\le\tau;\ S^{(j)}=S^{(j-1)}\cup\{i_j\},\ \alpha^{(j)}=K_{t-1,S^{(j)}}^{+}\,k_t,\ r^{(j)}=k_t-K_{t-1,S^{(j)}}\alpha^{(j)}
update.name: u2: explaining-away pursuit
update.plain:
Start with residual r = k_t and an empty support. Repeat up to s times:
1. Over stored episodes not yet selected, compute |K_i . r| / ||K_i||. Take the largest, breaking ties by the lowest index.
2. If it is <= tau, stop.
3. Otherwise add that index to the support.
4. Re-solve least squares for k_t on all selected keys, taking the minimum-norm solution alpha = pinv(K_S) k_t (numpy.linalg.lstsq).
5. Set r = k_t minus the fitted combination.
The final support, coefficients and residual are S_t, alpha_t and r_t.

Linear dependence: r is orthogonal to span(K_S) after every refit. A stored key lying in that span therefore scores exactly 0 and is never selected. The pseudoinverse keeps step 4 defined if near-dependent keys are selected numerically. Generic random codes give full column rank, where pinv(K_S) k_t = (K_S^T K_S)^{-1} K_S^T k_t.

update.name: u3: value inference
update.plain: The predicted value code is the same signed combination of the selected stored values: yhat_t = sum_j alpha_t[j] * Y[:, S_t[j]]. Coefficients may be negative.

update.name: u4: novelty-gated one-shot write
update.plain: On a demonstration, store (k_t, E[y_t]) only if the pursuit failed to explain it: either the key residual norm exceeds eps, or the predicted value differs from the true value code by more than eps. If the store is full, drop the oldest episode. Explained demonstrations and queries leave the store unchanged.

non_reduction_argument.broken_invariant:
The parent's mapping relies on two properties:
(i) retrieval is exact match (score 1{x_i = x}) or a lookup in a table derived from an order-independent closure of positive examples;
(ii) the learned structure is the most specific hypothesis containing the observed differences.

In this card, neither holds:
- u2-u3 answer a query whose key matches no stored key with a signed combination sum_j alpha_j Y_{i_j}. The support is chosen by residual correlation after earlier selections (explaining away), and the coefficients come from a joint least-squares refit.
- u4 writes an episode only if that pursuit fails, so the store's contents depend on the solve and on write order. 'a+c -> 8' is dropped after atoms a and c are stored, but it would be stored if shown first.

The neighbouring numeric families share a further invariant: their state is a function of G = sum k k^T and H = sum k y^T (or a decay-weighted version), and their readout is linear in q. Both properties fail here. The readout is piecewise linear in q, with a data-chosen support. It is not invariant under the index rotation (K, Y) -> (KQ, YQ), which preserves G and H exactly. The toy prints 3.0 vs -0.65812 for two stores with identical G and H.
non_reduction_argument.known_family: other_known: exact-match hard-attention cache over a sliding window plus the Helmbold-Sloan-Warmuth most-specific integer-lattice (gcd/HNF closure) learner with a coset-to-label table
non_reduction_argument.why_unrepairable:
Exact cache: the query 'b' has no stored key, so any exact-match cache returns none. There is no closure or HNF step, and the hypothesis class is additive binding over learned codes, not a lattice.

Strongest numeric repair: MesaNet / RLS / delta rule with a learned feature map phi. Its readout H^T (G + lambda I)^{-1} phi(q) is linear in phi(q).
- Explaining away requires phi(k_b) = phi(k_a + k_b) - phi(k_a) for every stored pair. So phi must be additive on the code lattice, that is, linear on span(C), and so of rank <= m.
- The fitted map then has rank <= m and cannot reproduce d > m generic bindings (capability 1).
- A non-additive phi loses explaining away (capability 2).
- Larger lifted states do not help: any state that is a function of (G, H) gives identical outputs for the toy's stores X and Y, while the core gives different ones.

Strongest attention or kernel repair: multi-hop softmax or Hopfield retrieval. Its weights f(k_i, q)/Z are nonnegative, computed per item, and independent of values. The correct answer v_{a+b} - v_a depends with coefficient -1 on an item whose key is nearly orthogonal to the query. Swap v_a with the value of another unrelated stored item: the true answer changes by their difference, but any kernel readout changes only by about |f(k_a, q) - f(k_j, q)|, which is close to 0.

An attend-subtract-reattend stack would have to compute the least-squares refit pinv(K_S) q on a data-chosen support and gate writes on its residual. That is this mechanism, not a member of the family. Its failure would show up on capabilities 2 and 3.

references.why: Supplies the SDM read rule (pool the contents of the hard locations activated by an address). Also supplies the result that SDM capacity can grow independently of the stored-vector dimension, which motivates the overcomplete regime d > m that this card targets. The radius activation is replaced by pursuit activation.

Surveys distributed memories that store more items than their dimension, and bipartite networks that recall by iterative residual correction under linear constraints. The pursuit read is a residual-correcting recall carried out directly over stored episodes.

CTDL writes its hippocampal store when the slow system's error is high (CLS fast/slow split). Here the error gate becomes the store's own sparse-explanation residual, and pretrained cue codes play the slow cortical role.

source_transplant.change:
Three changes to the SDM rule:
- The activated set is chosen by s-step orthogonal matching pursuit on the query residual, not by a Hamming radius.
- Contents are pooled with signed least-squares coefficients, not counter sums.
- Hard locations are allocated on demand as one-shot episodes, not as fixed random addresses.

The CTDL write gate uses the pursuit's key and value residual instead of a TD error, so the same solve both reads and decides what to write.
source_transplant.object: The Kanerva SDM read rule (pool the contents of the hard locations an address activates; capacity beyond the vector dimension), together with CTDL's error-gated write to the hippocampal store

card.summary:
The fast store is a bounded set of episodes (key, value). Keys come from slow, pretrained cue codes; in CLS terms these are the cortical representations.

Retrieval does not look up the most similar episode. It runs s steps of orthogonal matching pursuit over the stored keys. Each step:
- picks the stored key most correlated with the current residual of the query;
- re-fits least-squares coefficients on the keys picked so far;
- subtracts their contribution from the query.
The answer is the same signed combination of the stored values.

A query that matches no stored episode can therefore be answered by inference. Suppose the store holds 'a+b -> 7' and 'a -> 3'. Then the query 'b' resolves to 7 - 3 = 4. This is explaining away: the stored atom a enters with coefficient -1 even though its key is orthogonal to the query.

Writes are gated by the same solve. A demonstration is stored only if the pursuit cannot reproduce both its key and its value. Composites that are consistent with stored atoms are therefore never stored, and capacity goes to genuinely new bindings.

The store may hold more episodes (d) than the key dimension (m). This follows the SDM point that capacity can exceed the vector dimension. Any memory whose readout is linear in the query can realize only a rank-m map, so it cannot exploit this regime.

Cost is O(s d m) per token, with no growth in n.
card.title: Explaining-Away Episodic Store: sparse-pursuit recall with novelty-gated one-shot writes

toy_example.description:
Part 1 uses m = 3, s = 2, d = 8, cue codes a, b, c = unit basis vectors, and E[y] = y.
- Demonstrations, in order: a+b -> 7, a -> 3, c -> 5, a+c -> 8, b+c -> 9.
- 'b' is never shown alone; it is inferred as 7 - 3 = 4.
- 'a+c -> 8' is explained by the stored atoms, so it is not written.
- 'b+c' is 3-sparse in the store at that point, so the s = 2 pursuit predicts 8.5. Its demonstration is therefore written, after which the same query returns 9.

Part 2 builds two stores in R^2 with identical G = sum k k^T and H = sum k v^T (the program's variables GX/GY and CX/CY hold G and H). Store Y is store X with its first two episodes rotated by an orthogonal mixing. The pursuit readout of query e1 differs (3.0 vs -0.65812), while the in-context least-squares readout H^T G^{-1} q is 0.9456 for both. No function of (G, H) can reproduce the core readout.

numpy.linalg.lstsq returns the minimum-norm least-squares solution, which is the pseudoinverse refit of u2. The score test against tau matches u2.
toy_example.python:
import json
import numpy as np

def omp(q, keys, s, tau=1e-9):
    S, alpha, r = [], np.zeros(0), q.copy()
    for _ in range(s):
        best, bi = tau, -1
        for i, k in enumerate(keys):
            if i in S:
                continue
            c = abs(float(k @ r)) / float(np.linalg.norm(k))
            if c > best:
                best, bi = c, i
        if bi < 0:
            break
        S.append(bi)
        K = np.stack([keys[i] for i in S], axis=1)
        alpha = np.linalg.lstsq(K, q, rcond=None)[0]
        r = q - K @ alpha
    return S, alpha, r

def read(keys, vals, q, s=2):
    S, a, r = omp(q, keys, s)
    y = float(sum(a[j] * vals[i] for j, i in enumerate(S))) if S else 0.0
    return y, r

class Store:
    def __init__(self, d=8, s=2, eps=1e-6):
        self.d, self.s, self.eps = d, s, eps
        self.K, self.Y = [], []
    def predict(self, q):
        return read(self.K, self.Y, q, self.s)
    def demo(self, q, v):
        y, r = self.predict(q)
        wrote = bool(np.linalg.norm(r) > self.eps or abs(v - y) > self.eps)
        if wrote:
            self.K.append(q)
            self.Y.append(float(v))
            if len(self.K) > self.d:
                self.K.pop(0)
                self.Y.pop(0)
        return wrote, y

def token(yhat, beta=2.0, V=16):
    logits = [-beta * (v - yhat) ** 2 for v in range(V)]
    return int(np.argmax(logits))

C = {'a': np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]), 'b': np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]), 'c': np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0])}
def key(cues):
    return sum(C[x] for x in cues)

m = Store()
w = []
r1, _ = m.demo(key('ab'), 7); w.append(r1)
r2, p_a = m.demo(key('a'), 3); w.append(r2)
qb, _ = m.predict(key('b'))
r3, _ = m.demo(key('c'), 5); w.append(r3)
r4, p_ac = m.demo(key('ac'), 8); w.append(r4)
bc0, _ = m.predict(key('bc'))
r5, _ = m.demo(key('bc'), 9); w.append(r5)
bc1, _ = m.predict(key('bc'))

KX = [np.array([1.0, 0.0]), np.array([0.0, 1.0]), np.array([0.96, 0.28])]
VX = [3.0, 5.0, 0.0]
cs, sn = 0.8, 0.6
KY = [cs * KX[0] + sn * KX[1], -sn * KX[0] + cs * KX[1], KX[2]]
VY = [cs * VX[0] + sn * VX[1], -sn * VX[0] + cs * VX[1], VX[2]]

def gram(K, V):
    G = sum(np.outer(k, k) for k in K)
    Cv = sum(k * v for k, v in zip(K, V))
    return G, Cv

GX, CX = gram(KX, VX)
GY, CY = gram(KY, VY)
q = np.array([1.0, 0.0])
mesaX = float(CX @ np.linalg.solve(GX, q))
mesaY = float(CY @ np.linalg.solve(GY, q))
ompX, _ = read(KX, VX, q)
ompY, _ = read(KY, VY, q)
gc = float(max(np.max(np.abs(GX - GY)), np.max(np.abs(CX - CY))))

result = {
    'wrote': w,
    'pred_a_demo': round(p_a, 6),
    'query_b': round(qb, 6),
    'query_b_token': token(qb),
    'pred_ac_demo': round(p_ac, 6),
    'query_bc_before': round(bc0, 6),
    'query_bc_after': round(bc1, 6),
    'query_bc_after_token': token(bc1),
    'store_size': len(m.K),
    'X_omp': round(ompX, 6),
    'Y_omp': round(ompY, 6),
    'X_mesa': round(mesaX, 6),
    'Y_mesa': round(mesaY, 6),
    'GC_maxdiff': round(gc, 6)
}
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

critic.difference_if_any:
What remains is a combination of known parts, not a new update.
- The ALD/RAN admission test uses the s-sparse OMP residual instead of the dense projection residual or nearest-centre distance.
- The coupled dictionary holds raw episodes from an in-context token stream instead of image patches or training samples.
- Eviction is FIFO.

The read is textbook OMP plus coupled-dictionary code transfer. The write is error- and novelty-gated exemplar allocation. Swapping the sparse residual into an ALD/RAN-style test is a modest variant, not a new learning rule.
critic.mapping:
Exemplar-dictionary coupled sparse coding (Yang, Wright, Huang & Ma, 'Image super-resolution as sparse representation of raw image patches', CVPR 2008; also sparse-representation regression and classification over raw training samples, Wright et al. SRC) with greedy OMP as the solver. Its dictionary grows by a novelty and error allocation rule in the style of Platt's Resource-Allocating Network (1991) and Engel's ALD sparsification, here tested on the s-sparse residual.

Symbol map:
- K_t (stored keys) = the low-resolution / input dictionary D_l, whose atoms are raw stored exemplars, not learned atoms.
- Y_t (stored values) = the coupled high-resolution / output dictionary D_h. Column i of D_h is paired with column i of D_l.
- u1, k_t = sum C[x] = the input signal to be coded. C is a fixed random (or pretrained) feature map.
- u2 = textbook OMP with sparsity s on D_l. It picks argmax |<d_i, r>| / ||d_i||, re-solves least squares on the support, and updates the residual. The card itself says 'u2 is OMP used unchanged'.
- u3, yhat = Y_S alpha = the coupled-dictionary reconstruction x_h = D_h alpha. The sparse code from the input dictionary is transferred unchanged to the output dictionary.
- u4 = RAN/ALD-style allocation. Add the exemplar (k_t, E[y_t]) as a new dictionary pair when the current approximation leaves key residual > eps or output error > eps. ALD uses the dense projection residual, RAN uses nearest-centre novelty together with error. Here the residual is the s-sparse OMP residual, and either condition triggers a write.
- append_d = a budgeted dictionary with FIFO removal (budgeted kernel/online learners).
- Readout p_t = a Gaussian-distance softmax over output codes, i.e. nearest-integer decoding.
- Pretraining through alpha = K_S^+ k with S fixed = the standard task-driven dictionary learning gradient (Mairal, Bach & Ponce 2012), which differentiates through the support-restricted least-squares code.
critic.textbook_why: The stated source construction is Kanerva SDM (Hamming-radius activation, counter-sum pooling, fixed random hard locations) together with CTDL's TD-error-gated write. The card replaces all three SDM elements with OMP selection, signed least-squares pooling and on-demand allocation, and replaces the TD gate with a pursuit residual. So the stated source construction is materially changed, even though the replacement components are themselves textbook OMP and coupled-dictionary coding.
critic.why:
Escape test, parent mapping: the argument holds.
- u2-u3 do answer non-matching queries with signed least-squares combinations, so retrieval is not exact-match.
- u4 makes store contents order-dependent, so there is no gcd/HNF closure.
- The card's further invariant is also correct. A readout that is piecewise linear on a data-chosen support is not a function of (G, H). The toy's rotation counterexample is valid.
- The MesaNet, RLS and delta-rule repairs fail for the stated rank reason.
- Softmax and Hopfield repairs fail because explaining away needs a coefficient of -1 on a near-orthogonal key. I checked the inferred-binding margins: step 1 scores about 0.71 against noise of about 0.125; step 2 scores 0.5 against about 0.088. The 2-sparse solve then gives exactly (1, -1).
- So the card does not reduce to the parent's cache-plus-lattice learner, nor to linear attention, SSM, RNN or kernel memory.

Closest repair, which succeeds as a reduction to other_known: coupled-dictionary sparse coding over raw exemplar pairs. Sparse-code the input on dictionary D_l and reuse the code on D_h. This is exactly OMP-on-keys followed by alpha-on-values. Add a RAN/ALD-style rule that admits only unexplained samples.
- Yang et al. 2008 even uses raw sampled patch pairs as the dictionary, with signed sparse codes.
- Overcompleteness (d > m), negative coefficients and sparse-recovery capacity are the standard selling points of that literature. They are not new here.
- The card's own known_relatives concedes that OMP is unchanged and that KRLS-ALD gates admission the same way, differing only in dense versus sparse residual.

Why not radical: a researcher who knows sparse coding, super-resolution coupled dictionaries and resource-allocating networks would recognize the mechanism immediately. Moving it into a token-stream memory is a transplant, not a new mechanism.

SRC) with greedy OMP as the solver. Its dictionary grows by a novelty and error allocation rule in the style of Pl
