prior_art.label: prior_art_undertested
prior_art.notes: Close prior work exists: Kanerva-style SDM, which the card says has capacity beyond vector dimension; generic OMP, which the card uses unchanged as its read operation; and OLS-as-attention, which corresponds to the in-context least-squares baseline. The SDM continual-learning papers (W4360103626, W4417332370) test related memory claims but not the pursuit-based, residual-gated write mechanism. No listed paper tests the central overcomplete-recall or explaining-away capability at the stated scale (m=64, d=256, s=2, 2400-query protocol), so the label is undertested rather than tested. No listed paper shows the central claim fails, so known_disproven does not apply. The card's own SDM reference (W825574500) does not appear in the results and is not cited. The label is a judgement from abstracts only, not full texts.
queries: sparse orthogonal matching pursuit associative memory
Kanerva sparse distributed memory capacity exceeding dimension
episodic memory explaining away sparse coding recall
novelty-gated one-shot write episodic memory complementary learning systems
in-context least squares linear attention memory rank limitation

capabilities.prediction: Accuracy follows the slot-collision law A(K) = (B/2K)(1 - exp(-2K/B)) within +/-0.05, where 2K counts the writes (each cue and each value token writes once). This gives 0.88 at K = 512, 0.79 at K = 1000 and 0.43 at K = 4096. Accuracy does not change when d is varied from 16 to 256 at fixed B. A d-wide recurrent state would instead degrade once K exceeds about d.
capabilities.task: Associative recall capacity versus number of pairs K at random initialization. B = 4096, d = 64, N = 256, k = 8, w = 1. The 2K cue and value tokens are distinct. There is one query per sequence.

capabilities.prediction: Each filler token writes only under its own key, so the binding survives with probability (1 - 1/B)^(F+1), about exp(-F/B), independent of L once every filler token has appeared. Accuracy is 0.78 +/- 0.05 for every L from 10^4 to 10^6. If the filler is instead a fixed cycle of 8 tokens, which becomes non-surprising after the first cycle, accuracy is at least 0.95 for any L.
capabilities.task: Distance-independent recall with surprising filler. One binding, then L filler tokens drawn uniformly from F = 1000 distinct tokens (disjoint from the cue), then the query. B = 4096, w = 1, d = 64, N = 256, k = 8.

capabilities.prediction: Query accuracy is at least 0.8 after a single demonstration, for both trained and held-out offsets. Accuracy with 4 demonstrations differs from accuracy with 1 by at most 0.05, because later demonstrations hit the slot, are predicted correctly, and trigger no write.
capabilities.task: One-shot rule transfer. Items 0..63, prompts 'x -> x+c' with an offset c drawn per sequence, one demonstration, then queries on new items. Pretrained only on offsets c in {1..8}; tested on held-out c in {9, 10}. d = 64, N = 256, k = 8, B = 4096, w = 2 (the cortex at '->' sees x).

capabilities.prediction: The pretrained key at '->' is item-invariant, so all 32 pairs write one shared slot and only the last residual survives. Accuracy on the last shown pair is at least 0.9. Accuracy on the earlier 31 shown pairs and on unshown items is each at most 1/32 + 0.05. This is the predicted price of rule-invariant keys: the core cannot hold specifics and rules under the same key.
capabilities.task: Arbitrary-map sequences given to the same model pretrained on offset rules (w = 2): a random permutation of 32 items per sequence, each pair shown once in the form 'x -> y', then queries.

complexity.constants_notes: Per-token costs: encoder w*d^2, expansion N*d, top-k selection O(N), hash h1 O(k), tag comparison O(k), one slot read or write O(d), and readout V*d (the same as any softmax language model). Memory is the table, B*(d+k) entries, which is O(B d) because k <= d, plus O((V + N + w d) d) parameters. None of this depends on n. Training adds O(W (N + d)) = O(W N) per token for the key loss: W inner products of N-dimensional soft codes, plus the O(d) tau test for each s in the window. Inference has no such term. There is no n^2 term and no per-token search over history.

sample_efficiency.mechanism: Binding is done by an overwrite whose recalled value e_y - z(c) cancels the cortical prediction exactly. One-shot associative recall therefore needs no gradient training at all. It only needs distinct keys for distinct cues, which a random P and a random U provide when w = 1. Gradient training is needed only to shape the keys and the cortical geometry for rule transfer.

prediction.metric: one-shot associative recall accuracy at random initialization (zero training tokens). K = 64 key-value pairs over 128 distinct tokens, each pair shown once, then one query of a uniformly random studied key per sequence, averaged over sequences. w = 1, d = 64, N = 256, k = 8, B = 4096, tau = 0.5, E entries N(0, 1/d).
prediction.statement: An untrained model, with E, U, P and W_o all random Gaussian, recalls the queried value with accuracy at least 0.95. Each of the 128 tokens is surprising once and writes once, so there are 2K = 128 writes. The binding write of pair i is followed by 2(K - i) + 1 later writes, each of which overwrites it with probability 1/B. Averaged over i, survival is (B/2K)(1 - exp(-2K/B)) = 0.985. The worst case is the first pair, with 127 later writes, giving exp(-127/4096) = 0.969.

card.core_idea: A slow cortical predictor proposes the next-token embedding; a fast hippocampal table, addressed in O(1) by a hashed k-winners-take-all code of the cortical state, stores the cortex's residual error in one shot and adds it back whenever the same code recurs.

extensions.description: Replace the overwrite with a per-slot running mean using a write count c[a], so that k noisy demonstrations average out. This breaks the core's prediction that extra shots add nothing.

equations.latex: M[a_t] \leftarrow M[a_t] + \tfrac{1}{c[a_t]+1}(e_{x_{t+1}} - z_t - M[a_t]),\; c[a_t] \leftarrow c[a_t]+1

extensions.name: Running-mean encoding for noisy rules

extensions.description: Write each episode under each of its k (k-1)-subsets as well as under the full key, and read from the first subset that hits. Recall then tolerates one active unit drifting, at k times the write cost.
extensions.name: Partial-cue pattern completion

extensions.description: Compute two keys from two expansion projections, one item-specific and one item-invariant. Write to both and read from the item-specific slot first. This would let one model hold arbitrary pairs and transfer rules together, removing the tradeoff predicted in the arbitrary-map capability.
extensions.name: Dual keys for specifics and rules

extensions.description: Between sequences, replay table entries (address code, residual) as extra training targets for W_o and U. Residuals that are stored again and again then move into the slow cortex and stop using slots. This is the hippocampus-to-neocortex transfer described in the consolidation literature.
extensions.name: Replay consolidation

falsifiers: Recall accuracy versus K tracks the state width d instead of the slot law A(K) = (B/2K)(1 - exp(-2K/B)). For example, accuracy collapses near K of about d = 64 even with B = 4096, or deviates from the law by more than 0.05 at K = 512, 1000 or 4096. That would show capacity is not set by the addressed table.
A randomly initialized model with w = 1, B = 4096 and K = 64 scores below 0.95 on one-shot recall. That would refute the claim that residual cancellation makes binding training-free.

On the offset-rule task, a pretrained model scores at least 0.8 on trained offsets but below 0.8 on held-out offsets 9 and 10. That would show the stored residual is not item-invariant, so rule transfer does not come from the residual mechanism.
Zeroing the table H at query time leaves one-shot recall above 0.2 in a trained model. That would mean binding is carried by the cortical path, not the episodic store.

In the surprising-filler test with F = 1000 fixed, recall accuracy drops by more than 0.1 between L = 10^4 and L = 10^6. That is twice the stated +/-0.05 tolerance, and it would contradict the prediction that forgetting depends only on the number of distinct colliding keys.

In the arbitrary-map test, the offset-pretrained model recalls earlier (not last) shown pairs at accuracy above 0.3. That would mean its keys are not item-invariant, contradicting the account of how rule transfer arises.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: Keys are hashed, tagged k-subsets addressing B >> d slots. A read is one O(d) lookup, not a d x d matrix product. Capacity is set by B through the collision law, not by d. The stored quantity is the slow predictor's residual, which makes recall exact (h = e_y) without training and lets stored corrections transfer as rules. Writes are gated by surprise against the combined prediction.
known_relatives.name: Linear attention / delta-rule fast weights (Transformers are RNNs, DeltaNet-style updates)
known_relatives.relation: Written as a matrix recurrence, a write is S_t = (I - g_t e_a e_a^T) S_{t-1} + g_t e_a rho_t^T. This is a gated delta rule with learning rate 1 and a one-hot key over B slots. We do not claim the write rule is new.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: The fast process is an addressable table indexed by a sparse code of the slow state, not a decaying scalar. It is written by one-shot overwrite and forgets only through collisions.
known_relatives.name: Two-state fast/slow motor adaptation model
known_relatives.relation: Same additive decomposition of the output into slow plus fast, with the fast process driven by error.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: Those keep all n past contexts (memory O(n d)), search for nearest neighbours among them, and store tokens. Here memory is a fixed set of B slots with exact-code lookup, only surprising events are written, and the stored values are residuals of the cortical prediction. These residuals transfer to new items when the cortical codes are translation-equivariant.
known_relatives.name: Cache language models / kNN-LM
known_relatives.relation: Both retrieve next-token information from earlier contexts.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: Reformer still attends with a softmax over all bucket members and keeps O(n) keys. Product-key memories are slow parameters trained by SGD. Here the table is written within the sequence, holds at most one value per slot, and has no softmax over history.
known_relatives.name: Reformer (LSH attention) and product-key memory
known_relatives.relation: Both use hashing or top-k keys to address memory.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: There is no dense decaying state and no readout from a summed superposition. Each memory item sits in its own addressed slot, so interference is an all-or-nothing collision whose rate does not grow with the number of items stored.
known_relatives.name: Mamba / SSMs / RWKV / RetNet
known_relatives.relation: All have constant per-token cost and constant memory.

learning.description: The slow parameters E, U, W_o and P are trained across many sequences by gradient descent. The training forward pass uses the same hard table as inference. Stored residuals are kept as differentiable functions of the parameters (e_{x_{s+1}} - z_s), so the next-token loss trains E, U and W_o through both the cortical path and the recalled path. The key projection P cannot be differentiated through TopK and hashing, so it is trained by an auxiliary consolidation loss. For each position t, G_t is the set of earlier positions s, inside a training-only window of W positions, whose residual added to z_t would have made position t non-surprising. This is the same tau criterion as the write gate, and it costs O(d) per s. The loss pulls the soft code of t toward the soft codes of the positions in G_t, so that keys collide exactly when reusing an episode helps. lambda weights the auxiliary loss, T0 is the temperature of the soft code, and T1 is the temperature of the code-overlap softmax. No parameter is updated at inference. Within a sequence, only the table H changes.

equations.name: total loss
equations.plain: L = sum_t -log p_t(x_{t+1}) + lambda * sum_t Lkey_t

equations.latex: \mathcal{L}^{key}_t = -\log \frac{\sum_{s\in G_t} \exp(\langle q_t,q_s\rangle/T_1)}{\sum_{s=t-W}^{t-1} \exp(\langle q_t,q_s\rangle/T_1)},\; q_t=\mathrm{softmax}(P u_t/T_0),\; G_t=\{s\in[t-W,t-1]: \lVert e_{x_{t+1}}-(z_t+e_{x_{s+1}}-z_s)\rVert \le \tau\}
equations.name: key consolidation loss
equations.plain: q_t = softmax(P@u_t/T0) (an N-vector); G_t = {s in [t-W, t-1] : norm(E[x_{t+1}] - (z_t + E[x_{s+1}] - z_s)) <= tau}; Lkey_t = -log(sum over s in G_t of exp(q_t.q_s/T1) / sum over all s in the window of exp(q_t.q_s/T1)); skip Lkey_t when G_t is empty

learning.few_shot_argument: The mechanism is a one-shot residual overwrite at a pattern-separated address. Suppose context c is followed by y and the model is surprised. Then the slot at h1(kappa(c)) stores rho = e_y - z(c), tagged with kappa(c). A later context c' with kappa(c') = kappa(c) reads h = z(c') + e_y - z(c). (1) Binding: if c' looks the same as c to the encoder, then z(c') = z(c), so h = e_y exactly and y is the readout maximum for any parameter values. One exposure is enough and no training is needed. (2) Rule transfer: h = e_{y'} exactly when z(c') - z(c) = e_{y'} - e_y and the key ignores item identity. The first condition holds when the cortex represents items equivariantly and represents the rule as a translation of the cortical code. Slow training through the next-token loss and the key loss is what produces this geometry. After that, a rule shown once applies to new items. Extra exposures add nothing in the core, because the write is an overwrite, not an average. This has a cost: when keys are item-invariant, all pairs of a sequence share one slot, so only the most recent residual is kept.

readout.latex: p_t(v) = \mathrm{softmax}_v\big(-\beta \lVert e_v - h_t \rVert^2\big)
readout.name: nearest-embedding softmax
readout.plain: logits[v] = -beta * sum((E[v] - h_t)**2); p_t = softmax(logits) over the V tokens

state.meaning: Token embeddings. Row e_v is the embedding of token v. V is the vocabulary size and d is the model width. Positions before the start of the sequence use the zero vector. At initialization, entries are i.i.d. N(0, 1/d).
state.name: E

state.meaning: Slow cortical encoder taps over the last w tokens. They are combined through a fixed elementwise nonlinearity phi (GELU in experiments, identity in the toy) to give the cortical state u_t in R^d.
state.name: U

state.meaning: Cortical prediction map. z_t = W_o u_t is the slow system's prediction of the next token's embedding.
state.name: W_o

state.meaning: Expansion projection, analogous to entorhinal-to-dentate pattern separation. The indices of the k largest coordinates of P u_t (N expansion units, k of them active) form the sparse conjunctive key kappa_t. This key is a sorted k-tuple of 0-based indices in {0..N-1}.
state.name: P

state.meaning: Hippocampal store with B slots. Each slot a holds two parts. M[a] in R^d is a stored cortical residual. T[a] in {0..N-1}^k is the full key kappa that last wrote the slot; the sentinel 'empty' means the slot is unused. Comparing tags is an exact O(k) tuple comparison. The table is reset to all empty at the start of each sequence.
state.name: H = (M, T)
state.type: fast episodic table: M is real, T is integer

state.meaning: k is the number of active units in the key. tau is the surprise threshold for writing, a Euclidean distance in embedding space. beta is the inverse temperature of the readout. r is the integer base of the address hash h1 (r = 31 in the toy, drawn uniformly from [2, 2^61 - 2] in experiments).
state.name: theta_h

update.name: cortical state
update.plain: u_t = phi(sum over j=0..w-1 of U[j] @ E[x_{t-j}]), where E[x] is the zero vector for positions before the sequence start

update.name: cortical prediction
update.plain: z_t = W_o @ u_t

update.name: pattern-separated address
update.plain: kappa_t = sorted tuple of the indices (0-based) of the k largest entries of P @ u_t; a_t = (sum over j=1..k of (kappa_t[j]+1) * r**j) % (2**61 - 1) % B

update.name: recall (add stored residual on hit)
update.plain: hit = (T[a_t] == kappa_t) as an exact tuple comparison; h_t = z_t + (M[a_t] if hit else 0)

update.latex: g_t = \mathbb{1}\big[\lVert e_{x_{t+1}} - h_t \rVert > \tau\big];\; \text{if } g_t:\; M[a_t] \leftarrow e_{x_{t+1}} - z_t,\; T[a_t] \leftarrow \kappa_t
update.name: surprise-gated one-shot encoding
update.plain: after x_{t+1} is observed: if norm(E[x_{t+1}] - h_t) > tau then M[a_t] = E[x_{t+1}] - z_t and T[a_t] = kappa_t (overwrite); otherwise leave the table unchanged

references.why: Supplies the CLS division of labor, used directly as the architecture. The hippocampus is a sparse, pattern-separated conjunctive index that learns in one shot; this is our hashed top-k key and overwrite table. The neocortex is a slow, distributed learner of shared structure; this is our gradient-trained encoder and predictor. Switching between encoding and recall is modulated dynamically; this is our surprise gate.

Supplies the fast-plus-slow adaptive-process decomposition: net output is the sum of a fast and a slow process, and the fast process learns from error. We take from it the additive output h = z + recalled residual and the rule that the fast system stores the slow system's error.

Systems consolidation, in which the hippocampus guides the reorganization of neocortex and existing knowledge sets the rate of consolidation, motivates the key consolidation loss: slow learning shapes which cortical features the hippocampal index binds on. It also motivates the replay extension.

source_transplant.change: In the source, the fast process is a single decaying scalar state. Here it becomes a hash-addressed table of B vector slots. The slots are indexed by the k-winners-take-all code of the slow (cortical) state, which plays the role of the pattern-separation step. The fast process learns the slow process's residual by one-shot overwrite instead of by incremental decay. A hard surprise threshold on prediction error switches between encoding and recall. Forgetting happens only through slot collisions, never through decay.
source_transplant.object: The two-state (fast + slow) error-driven adaptation model: net output = slow-process output + fast-process output, and the fast process learns from the slow process's error. It is combined with the CLS hippocampus, a sparse, pattern-separated conjunctive index that switches between encoding and recall according to novelty.

card.summary: This card uses the complementary learning systems division of labor directly as a sequence model. The neocortex is a slow, distributed, gradient-trained predictor. It maps a short window of tokens to a predicted embedding z_t, and it also supplies the representation that the hippocampus indexes. The hippocampus is a fixed-size table of B slots. A slot is addressed by hashing the sparse, pattern-separated top-k code of the cortical state, and it is tagged with that code. A slot is written in one shot, by overwrite and only when the model is surprised, with the cortical residual e(next) - z_t. Reading is a single lookup that adds the stored residual to the cortical prediction. When a context recurs exactly, the bound token is reproduced without any training: h = z + (e_y - z) = e_y. A context that differs only in features the cortex treats equivariantly receives the stored correction as a rule, which gives one-shot rule transfer. The cost per token does not depend on n. Memory is a fixed table of B slots. Capacity is set by the number of slots B through a hash-collision law, not by the state width d.
card.title: Residual Episodic Index: a hash-addressed hippocampal store of cortical prediction errors

toy_example.description: A hand-set 2-D instance. Items 0..5 are embedded at e(i) = (i, -1) and a separator S = 6 at (0, 1). Settings: w = 2, phi = identity, k = 1, N = 2, B = 8, r = 31, tau = 0.5, beta = 1. The cortical state is u_t = (first coordinate of the previous token, second coordinate of the current token), so at S the cortex predicts a copy of the previous item. The key P u_t separates 'current token is S' from 'current token is an item'. The address is h1(kappa) = ((sum_j (kappa_j + 1) 31^j) mod (2^61 - 1)) mod 8, and the tag is the full key. The sequence '3 S 4 1 S 2 4 S' encodes the rule y = x + 1. At the first S the table is empty: the model predicts 3, is surprised, and stores the residual e(4) - e(3) = (1, 0). At the second S it recalls (1, 0) and correctly predicts 2, so no write happens. At the third S it predicts 5 for the new item 4, where the cortex alone would predict 4. Item positions also write under their own key, without affecting the S slot.
toy_example.python:
import json
import numpy as np
S = 6
E = np.array([[i, -1.0] for i in range(6)] + [[0.0, 1.0]])
U0 = np.array([[0.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]])
U1 = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0]])
Wo = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, -1.0]])
P = np.array([[0.0, 1.0], [0.0, -1.0]])
k, B, tau, beta, r = 1, 8, 0.5, 1.0, 31
M = np.zeros((B, 2))
T = [None] * B
seq = [3, 6, 4, 1, 6, 2, 4, 6]
def h1(kappa):
    return sum((i + 1) * r ** (j + 1) for j, i in enumerate(kappa)) % (2 ** 61 - 1) % B
preds, hits, writes = [], [], 0
cortex_final, p_final = None, None
for t in range(len(seq)):
    prev = E[seq[t - 1]] if t > 0 else np.zeros(2)
    u = U0 @ E[seq[t]] + U1 @ prev
    z = Wo @ u
    kappa = tuple(sorted(np.argsort(-(P @ u))[:k].tolist()))
    a = h1(kappa)
    hit = T[a] == kappa
    h = z + (M[a] if hit else 0.0)
    logits = -beta * ((E - h) ** 2).sum(axis=1)
    if seq[t] == S:
        preds.append(int(np.argmax(logits)))
        hits.append(int(hit))
    if t + 1 < len(seq):
        tgt = E[seq[t + 1]]
        if np.linalg.norm(tgt - h) > tau:
            M[a] = tgt - z
            T[a] = kappa
            writes += 1
    else:
        cortex_final = int(np.argmax(-((E - z) ** 2).sum(axis=1)))
        p = np.exp(logits - logits.max())
        p = p / p.sum()
        p_final = round(float(p[5]), 3)
print(json.dumps({'pred_at_sep': preds, 'hit_at_sep': hits, 'writes': writes, 'cortex_only_final': cortex_final, 'p_final_correct': p_final}))

critic.difference_if_any: Three things are left. (1) Keys are hard, sparse and hashed: one-hot over B >> d slots, chosen by TopK+hash, plus an exact tag check that returns zero instead of a superposed or wrong value on a miss. This is a choice of phi (a fixed, non-differentiable feature map) and an eviction policy, not a new update. It is why capacity follows a B-collision law rather than a d law. That follows directly from phi mapping into R^B with orthogonal keys. (2) The value is the residual of a slow base predictor rather than a raw projection of the token, so recall cancels the base prediction exactly. This is a reparameterization of v_t with a skip connection. (3) The key projection P is trained by an auxiliary contrastive loss on soft codes, with positives defined by whether reusing a residual would have avoided surprise. This is an extra gradient-trained objective (a surrogate for a non-differentiable key), not a different learning rule for the fast state, which stays the standard gated delta rule.
critic.mapping:
Let a_t = h1(kappa_t) and phi(k_t) = phi(q_t) = e_{a_t}, a one-hot vector over the B slots, computed from the cortical state u_t through the fixed hash of TopK_k(P u_t). The fast state S_t in R^{B x d} is the table M. The value is v_t = rho_t = e_{x_{t+1}} - z_t, which is the target minus the slow prediction. The write gate g_t = 1[||e_{x_{t+1}} - h_t|| > tau] is in {0,1}.

Update: S_t = (I - g_t e_{a_t} e_{a_t}^T) S_{t-1} + g_t e_{a_t} v_t^T. This is the gated delta rule with learning rate beta_t = g_t and a unit-norm one-hot key. Because the key is one-hot, the delta-rule erase-then-write is exactly the card's overwrite M[a_t] <- rho_t. The card writes this equation itself.

Readout: y_t = S_{t-1}^T phi(q_t) = M[a_t], and the card adds it to the skip/base path: h_t = z_t + y_t.

Cortical path: z_t = W_o phi(sum_j U_j e_{x_{t-j}}) is a w-token convolutional/MLP feature map, the kind of short conv that already precedes DeltaNet/Mamba-style layers. The readout softmax(-beta ||e_v - h_t||^2) is a tied-embedding output layer with an RBF logit, which differs from the dot-product logit only by a per-token norm bias.

Tag check: 1[T[a]=kappa] is equivalent to using a one-hot key over the full C(N,k) code space (exact-key delta memory) and then storing it in a B-entry hash table with eviction on collision. This is an implementation of the same exact-key associative map with bounded capacity, not a new recurrence.
critic.textbook_why: The cited source object is the two-state fast/slow adaptation model: output = slow + fast, with the fast process being a single decaying scalar driven by error. The card replaces the scalar with a hash-addressed table of vector slots, replaces decay with a one-shot overwrite, and adds a surprise gate. These changes to the construction come from the CLS account and computer-science hashing, not from the textbook two-state equations. The construction is therefore modified rather than transplanted verbatim, even though the result coincides with a known ML mechanism.
critic.why: The per-token computation is a gated delta-rule fast-weight memory, linear attention with a delta update. The keys are one-hot vectors over B slots produced by a fixed hash of a top-k code. Values are residuals e_{x+1} - z_t. The readout is added to a short-window predictor. The card itself concedes that the write is S_t = (I - g e_a e_a^T) S_{t-1} + g e_a rho^T. The headline properties follow from choosing a sparse orthogonal feature map phi of dimension B, which is the well-known capacity argument for linear attention with higher-dimensional or one-hot feature maps. These properties are capacity set by B rather than d, exact one-shot binding, and all-or-nothing collisions. The CLS and two-state-adaptation vocabulary (cortex, hippocampus, pattern separation, consolidation) renames a short-conv base model plus a delta-rule memory. Nothing here would surprise a researcher who knows DeltaNet and fast weight programmers.

learning.description: Learning is exact algebraic identification, not weight adaptation. The hidden operation is assumed to be a three-permutation isotope of addition modulo a prime, with hidden permutations alpha_h, beta_h and gamma_h. Comparing row 1 with row 0 gives P. In hidden coordinates P is translation by the nonzero element delta = alpha_h(1)-alpha_h(0) mod p, so it is a single p-cycle. Walking that cycle recovers the output arrays gamma and gamma_inv, up to the unavoidable affine gauge. The column then gives every recovered left coordinate alpha, and row 0 gives every recovered right coordinate beta. The resulting tensor is reused at every MUL node, and the postfix syntax tree supplies the contraction graph. A new calibration set overwrites the identified operation. Trees have exponential growth: a height-h tree can have 2^h leaves, yet evaluation keeps at most h+1 messages. This is the only geometric property the core uses.
learning.few_shot_argument: Three calibration records suffice. Each record has p outputs, so these are three structured demonstrations, not three scalar examples. Together they contain 3p-2 distinct operation entries. Since D_1[b]=op(1,b) and D_0[b]=op(0,b), gamma_h(P(y)) = gamma_h(y) + delta mod p with delta = alpha_h(1)-alpha_h(0) nonzero. Because p is prime, the orbit of P visits every output. The walk assigns gamma(P^j(s_0)) = j, and gamma_h(P^j(s_0)) = gamma_h(s_0) + j*delta. Therefore gamma(y) = (gamma_h(y)-gamma_h(s_0))/delta mod p, an affine function of the hidden coordinate. Using gamma_h(s_0) = alpha_h(0)+beta_h(0), we get alpha(a) = gamma(op(a,0)) = (alpha_h(a)-alpha_h(0))/delta and beta(b) = gamma(op(0,b)) = (beta_h(b)-beta_h(0))/delta. Hence alpha(a)+beta(b) = gamma(op(a,b)) mod p for all a and b, so gamma_inv[(alpha[a]+beta[b]) % p] = op(a,b). Every undemonstrated entry is therefore forced within the stated hypothesis family. Nested expressions need no further demonstrations, because every internal node uses the same identified tensor. No conclusion extends to unrestricted binary tables or to noisy data.

readout.latex: q_t(c)=\begin{cases}S_{\mathrm{top}}(c),&\text{after a valid ASK and }0\leq c<p,\\0,&\text{after a valid ASK and }p\leq c<V,\\1/V,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
readout.name: Next-token distribution
readout.plain: Immediately after a valid ASK, the root message S_top gives the probabilities on the p operand/output labels, and control tokens get probability 0. At every other position, return U. The core predicts answers to structured requests. It does not claim to model the protocol-token stream itself.

readout.latex: \hat{y}_t=\min\{c:\ q_t(c)=\max_{c'}q_t(c')\}.
readout.name: Emitted answer token
readout.plain: After a valid ASK, emit the most probable label (argmax of q_t), breaking ties by the smallest label. In the core, S_top is one-hot, so the argmax is unique and equals the exact answer.

state.meaning: Sizes: p is a fixed prime, n is the number of input tokens, and V = p+5 is the vocabulary size, which is also the length of every next-token distribution. Operand/output labels are the integers 0 through p-1. There are five control tokens: ROW0, ROW1, COL0, MUL and ASK. A ROW0 record lists the p outputs for left operand 0 and right operands 0 through p-1. ROW1 does the same for left operand 1. COL0 lists the outputs for right operand 0 and left operands 0 through p-1. The admissible unknown operation op satisfies gamma_h(op(a,b)) = (alpha_h(a)+beta_h(b)) mod p. Here alpha_h, beta_h and gamma_h are the hidden permutations of the p labels that generate the data. They are never observed, their zero points are gauge-dependent, and they are distinct from the recovered arrays alpha, beta and gamma stored in Z. Notation in the equations: a, b, c, x and y range over operand labels; j in 0..p-1 indexes steps along a permutation cycle; t indexes input tokens; I[condition] is the indicator; e_x is the length-p one-hot vector of x; q_t(c) is the next-token probability of token c; U denotes the uniform distribution on the V tokens; division by a nonzero residue means multiplication by its inverse mod p.
state.name: Protocol
state.type: Fixed algebraic prior and token protocol; no learned parameters

state.meaning: D has three rows: D_0 for ROW0, D_1 for ROW1 and D_col for COL0. All entries start unfilled. Duplicate observations at the two row-column intersections (D_0[0]=D_col[0] and D_1[0]=D_col[1]) must agree. Calibration records are assumed exact and complete. The core rejects an inconsistent record instead of repairing it, with rejection as defined in H. A calibration tag arriving after Z has been compiled starts a new calibration set: D is reset to unfilled before the tag's record is written.
state.name: D

state.meaning: Z stores five recovered lookup arrays on p labels, written without the subscript h. P is the row-comparison permutation. gamma maps labels to cycle coordinates, and gamma_inv is its inverse array, so gamma_inv[gamma[y]] = y. alpha holds the recovered left coordinates and beta the recovered right coordinates. Each recovered array differs from its hidden counterpart alpha_h, beta_h or gamma_h by the affine gauge given in learning. P^j means j-fold application of P. s_0 denotes the cycle start label D_0[0]. Z is uninitialized before calibration succeeds and becomes uninitialized again whenever a new calibration set starts or a rejection occurs. There are no gradient-trained weights. The implicit p-by-p-by-p constraint tensor is defined by these arrays and is never allocated.
state.name: Z
state.type: Compiled permutation block (lookup arrays over Z_p coordinates)

state.meaning: S holds the current postfix evaluation frontier. Each message is a distribution over the p labels. u denotes the second-to-top message, v the top message, and m their contracted replacement. S_top denotes the top message. For an expression tree of height h, where h is the number of MUL nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path, the stack never holds more than h+1 messages. With the core's deterministic operand tokens, all messages stay one-hot.
state.name: S
state.type: Variable-length stack of normalized nonnegative messages

state.meaning: H holds three things: a mode, a cursor r with 0 <= r <= p, and a validity flag that is true exactly when Z holds a successfully compiled operation. The mode selects calibration-row ingestion, expression ingestion or response. A calibration tag sets its mode and resets r to 0. If Z was compiled, the tag also starts a new calibration set: it sets the flag false and marks Z uninitialized. Reject means the following. Set the flag false, mark Z uninitialized and clear D and S. Then output U at every position until a fresh complete set of ROW0, ROW1 and COL0 records compiles successfully. ASK is valid only when the flag is true and the expression stack holds exactly one message. After the answer token is emitted, the next expression starts with an empty stack. This reset does not erase D or Z.
state.name: H
state.type: Finite parser control with bounded integer cursor

update.name: Ingest calibration
update.plain: In a calibration mode, write the operand token x into the selected row of D at cursor r, then increment r. Exactly p tokens complete a record. Reject (as defined in H) on an out-of-range label, a control token before the record is complete, or a conflicting intersection. When all three records of the current set are complete, run the next two compilation steps once for that set. A later calibration set triggers a fresh compilation that overwrites Z.

update.name: Identify the output cycle
update.plain: First check that D_0 and D_1 each contain every label exactly once. If either row repeats a label, reject (as defined in H) without building P. Otherwise, for each right operand b, set P[D_0[b]] = D_1[b]. Start at y = s_0 = D_0[0]. For j = 0..p-1, if gamma[y] is already set, reject; otherwise set gamma[y] = j and gamma_inv[j] = y, then set y = P[y]. After the loop, reject unless y == s_0.

update.name: Compile the shared operation
update.plain: Set alpha[a] = gamma[D_col[a]] for every a and beta[b] = gamma[D_0[b]] for every b. Reject unless alpha and beta are permutations and gamma_inv[(alpha[a]+beta[b]) % p] reproduces every calibration entry. On success, store the arrays in Z and set the validity flag true. In the recovered gauge this fixes alpha(0)=beta(0)=0 and alpha(1)=1.

update.name: Push a leaf
update.plain: In expression mode, an operand token x appends its one-hot vector e_x to the stack.

update.name: Contract a binary node
update.plain: On MUL, pop the right message v, then the left message u. Reject on stack underflow or if the validity flag is false. Set m to zeros. For every pair (a,b), add u[a]*v[b] to m[gamma_inv[(alpha[a]+beta[b]) % p]]. Push m. Each input pair has exactly one output, so m stays normalized.

references.why: Supplies the principle that a parsimoniously structured tensor can have identifiable latent factors from limited measurements. Its channel-identification assumptions are not imported, and the paper is not claimed to prove the three-slice theorem.

Supplies explicit grammatical derivations as tensor-contraction graphs and the importance of keeping predicate/argument order. The learned distributional word tensors are replaced with an algebraic constraint tensor identified from context.

Supplies the link between hierarchy and exponential growth. Only the tree property is used: leaves can grow as 2^h with height h, while postfix evaluation keeps at most h+1 frontier messages. No hyperbolic embedding machinery is used.

source_transplant.change: Statistical tensor decomposition is replaced with an exact identification procedure for a prime-order cyclic-isotope constraint tensor. Externally supplied CCG derivations are replaced with an explicitly delimited postfix grammar. From the hyperbolic-hierarchy survey only the exponential-growth property of trees is used: a tree of height h has up to 2^h leaves, while postfix evaluation needs at most h+1 frontier messages. No hyperbolic coordinates or embeddings are used. The papers motivate these transplants. The three-slice identification result and its proof are proposed here and are not attributed to them.
source_transplant.object: Low-rank tensor identifiability; grammatical tensor-network contraction along derivation trees; exponential volume growth of trees (hyperbolic hierarchy)

card.summary: The learner handles a deliberately restricted but compositional sequence language. Its inputs are postfix expressions whose binary operation is an unknown relabeling of addition modulo a prime. Three calibration records identify the operation exactly, including entries never demonstrated. Later expressions are evaluated by contracting one shared constraint tensor along each expression's syntax tree. The central theoretical claim is an identification theorem for this tensor family. It is not a claim of general natural-language competence. The only geometric fact used is the exponential growth of trees: a tree of height h has up to 2^h leaves, while postfix evaluation keeps at most h+1 frontier messages. No embedding or attention mechanism is required. The price of exact identification is an explicit algebraic prior and three records containing 3p-2 distinct demonstrated entries.
card.title: Slice-Identified Tree Algebra Circuits

toy_example.description: A hidden p=5 nonassociative isotope supplies two rows and one column. The program identifies the recovered coordinate arrays, including gamma_inv, completes all 12 unseen entries, and contracts four postfix trees. The answer is the argmax of the root distribution, with ties going to the smallest label. Only calibration entries are passed to the learner. The hidden table is used afterwards only to check completion.
toy_example.python:
import json

p = 5
hidden_alpha = [0, 2, 4, 1, 3]
hidden_beta = [0, 1, 3, 4, 2]
hidden_gamma = [0, 3, 1, 4, 2]
hidden_inverse = [0] * p
for label, coordinate in enumerate(hidden_gamma):
    hidden_inverse[coordinate] = label

def hidden(a, b):
    return hidden_inverse[(hidden_alpha[a] + hidden_beta[b]) % p]

row0 = [hidden(0, b) for b in range(p)]
row1 = [hidden(1, b) for b in range(p)]
col0 = [hidden(a, 0) for a in range(p)]

P = [0] * p
for b in range(p):
    P[row0[b]] = row1[b]
gamma = [-1] * p
gamma_inv = [-1] * p
y = row0[0]
for j in range(p):
    assert gamma[y] == -1
    gamma[y] = j
    gamma_inv[j] = y
    y = P[y]
assert y == row0[0]
alpha = [gamma[y] for y in col0]
beta = [gamma[y] for y in row0]
assert sorted(alpha) == list(range(p))
assert sorted(beta) == list(range(p))

def learned(a, b):
    return gamma_inv[(alpha[a] + beta[b]) % p]

seen = {(0, b) for b in range(p)}
seen |= {(1, b) for b in range(p)}
seen |= {(a, 0) for a in range(p)}
assert all(learned(a, b) == hidden(a, b) for a, b in seen)
unseen = [(a, b) for a in range(p) for b in range(p) if (a, b) not in seen]
correct = sum(learned(a, b) == hidden(a, b) for a, b in unseen)

def contract(tokens):
    stack = []
    for token in tokens:
        if token != '*':
            message = [0.0] * p
            message[token] = 1.0
            stack.append(message)
        else:
            right = stack.pop()
            left = stack.pop()
            message = [0.0] * p
            for a in range(p):
                for b in range(p):
                    message[learned(a, b)] += left[a] * right[b]
            stack.append(message)
    assert len(stack) == 1
    return stack[0]

def answer(tokens):
    distribution = contract(tokens)
    return max(range(p), key=lambda label: distribution[label])

ordered = answer([2, 4, '*', 3, 1, '*', '*'])
reversed_order = answer([4, 2, '*', 1, 3, '*', '*'])
left_grouped = answer([1, 2, '*', 3, '*'])
right_grouped = answer([1, 2, 3, '*', '*'])
result = {
    'calibration_entries': len(seen),
    'unseen_entries': len(unseen),
    'unseen_correct': correct,
    'inferred_alpha': alpha,
    'inferred_beta': beta,
    'inferred_gamma': gamma,
    'ordered_answers': [ordered, reversed_order],
    'grouped_answers': [left_grouped, right_grouped],
    'root_distribution': [round(x, 6) for x in contract([2, 4, '*', 3, 1, '*', '*'])]
}
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

critic.difference_if_any: LEARNING_RULE: The transition tensor T is not trained by gradient descent and is not estimated spectrally. It is set by a hand-derived exact identification procedure. That procedure assumes T is a three-permutation isotope of (Z_p, +) and builds the row-quotient permutation P = row1 o row0^{-1}. It then walks the p-cycle of P to recover gamma up to affine gauge, and reads alpha from col0 and beta from row0. This fixes all p^2 entries from 3p-2 observed entries. The procedure is classical quasigroup-isotopy reasoning: an isotope of an abelian group is determined by a row, a column and the group law, and here the group law is recovered from a second row. It is a symbolic solver for a narrow, prespecified hypothesis family, not a general learning mechanism.
critic.mapping: Inference reduces to a shift-reduce evaluation of a tree-structured tensor network (a recursive neural tensor network or Socher-style RNTN without nonlinearity, equivalently a weighted or deterministic bottom-up tree automaton run by a pushdown stack, as in SPINN shift-reduce TreeRNNs). The symbols map as follows. (1) Leaf embedding: the operand token x maps to the one-hot e_x. This is the TreeRNN leaf embedding with an identity embedding matrix, and pushing it is the SHIFT operation. (2) Composition: MUL maps to the REDUCE operation, h_parent = T(h_left, h_right). The card's u is h_left, v is h_right and m is h_parent. The composition tensor is T[c,a,b] = I[c = gamma_inv((alpha[a]+beta[b]) mod p)], a single shared p x p x p transition tensor applied at every internal node with no nonlinearity. This is exactly the bilinear term of the RNTN, and the transition tensor of a weighted tree automaton over state set {0..p-1}. (3) Frontier: the stack S is the standard shift-reduce stack, and its depth bound h+1 is the usual postfix-evaluation property. (4) Readout: q_t = S_top is the root representation used as the output distribution, and the answer is its argmax. Because T is a 0/1 functional tensor and leaves are one-hot, every message stays one-hot. The circuit is therefore literally a deterministic bottom-up tree automaton whose transition function is the quasigroup op. The card itself concedes that tree contraction is not new.
critic.textbook_why: The tree-contraction half is the textbook grammatical tensor-network / RNTN construction, applied unchanged with a postfix grammar replacing CCG derivations. The cited tensor-identifiability work (low-rank statistical decomposition) is not used as stated. It is replaced by an exact cycle-walking isotope identification, which changes the learning construction itself. The hyperbolic source contributes only the trivial tree-growth fact.
critic.why: The per-token computation is shift-reduce evaluation of a shared bilinear composition tensor along a parse tree, which is a TreeRNN/RNTN or weighted tree automaton with one-hot states. The card acknowledges this. The only non-standard element is the in-context 'learning' rule. That rule is an exact algebraic identification valid only under a strong built-in prior: the op must be an isotope of Z_p with p prime, and the data must be noiseless and complete. Restricting a hypothesis class to a p-parameter-ish family and solving it in closed form from structured probes is classical combinatorial reasoning about Latin squares and group isotopes. It would not surprise a researcher who knows tree-structured networks or program synthesis. It does not transfer to any task outside that family, and the card says so. The capability claims follow directly from the construction being an exact symbolic evaluator, so they reflect the hard-coded prior rather than a new sequence mechanism.

The core cannot recover from the conflicting example without starting a new context.
capabilities.task: Contradiction certification

complexity.constants_notes: There are exactly two operations, and V=d+5. A single seed may cause O(d) propagation work. F is updated in place, and each source is expanded at most once over the whole context, so total expansion work is O(d). Each of the m <= n/3 demonstrations also costs O(1) to enqueue and check its seed, even when the source is already assigned. Total closure work is therefore O(d+m), which is O(d+n). Parser steps and query execution cost O(1) per token. Writing out each V-dimensional distribution costs O(d) per token, which gives the stated O(nd) total. If point masses and uniform distributions are returned in compressed form, the total cost is O(n+d). The supplied tables take 4d entries. No cost depends quadratically on n.

sample_efficiency.mechanism: A demonstrated binding fixes its entire forward orbit through naturality. A cyclic source system therefore has a unique compatible translation after one anchor.

prediction.metric: Exact target accuracy after one demonstration
prediction.statement: Take d=64, T[0,i]=(i+1) mod 64 and T[1,i]=2i mod 64. Draw any permutation pi of {0,...,63} and set U[a,j]=pi(T[a,pi^{-1}(j)]). Provide one correct anchor D i pi(i). The core then predicts all 64 source targets with accuracy 1.0, with no pretraining and no further demonstrations.

card.core_idea: Learn a translation between two finite transition systems by compiling one demonstrated binding into every binding that naturality forces, then reuse the resulting map on arbitrarily long compositions.
falsifiers: On the d=64 benchmark (T[0,i]=i+1 mod 64, T[1,i]=2i mod 64, U conjugated by a permutation) with one correct anchor, any missing entry, wrong target, or contradiction after closure refutes the one-anchor identification claim or its implementation.
After complete correct closure on that benchmark, any incorrect answer on an L/R query word refutes the compositional transport claim, including words longer than every demonstrated sequence.

If total closure work over a context with m demonstrations grows faster than O(d+m), the amortized closure claim is false. Examples are expansions of already assigned sources on repeated demonstrations, or per-demonstration O(d) copying of F. A concrete test: 1000 repeated demonstrations of the same correct anchor at d=64 must cost at most 64 expansions plus 1000 constant-time seed checks.

On the two-component d=64 benchmark with one anchor, the coverage claim is refuted by any non-uniform answer distribution on a query in the unanchored component, by any assignment of an unanchored source, or by any wrong answer in the anchored component.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: The proposed sequence architecture compiles in-context demonstrations into a persistent partial natural transformation, detects conflicts, and executes compositional queries. It does not claim a new theorem about equivariant maps or a new general-purpose graph-isomorphism algorithm.
known_relatives.name: Equivariant maps, natural transformations, and automaton-morphism propagation
known_relatives.relation: The central mathematics is established: a map that commutes with the transition operations is determined on a generated orbit by its value at an anchor.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: This core has finite-set fibers and exact forced assignments. It has no learned vector-bundle layers, Laplacian diffusion, or continuous message aggregation. Its one-shot guarantee comes from reachability and naturality, not from universal approximation.
known_relatives.name: Order-equivariant and sheaf neural networks
known_relatives.relation: Both express compatibility with morphisms and local-to-global structure.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: This core does not merge sites into equivalence classes or maintain relative parity. It learns a directed map between two supplied transition systems, including noninvertible operations and noncommutative compositions. Bindings propagate through the source and target tables, not through pairwise relative relations.
known_relatives.name: Parity constraint reservoirs and union-find binding systems
known_relatives.relation: Both can propagate a small number of demonstrations through symbolic consistency constraints.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: The learned state is a partial discrete morphism built by worklist completion. There is no update of the form S_t=A_t S_{t-1}+B_t x_t, no differentiable hidden-state evolution, and no optimization of parameters at inference time. The guarantees depend on explicit transition structure, a restriction these general sequence models do not require.
known_relatives.name: Mamba, RWKV, linear attention, and test-time-training layers
known_relatives.relation: These also process streams without quadratic attention and can adapt their predictions from context.

learning.description: There are no gradient-trained parameters. Learning completes a partial natural transformation from the supplied tables A and the demonstrated bindings, using FIFO_A. If a compatible total translation exists, every assignment that closure produces agrees with every such translation that satisfies the demonstrations. The procedure is deliberately incomplete on unanchored components. It does not search over possible extensions, and it does not claim that an unassigned symbol is globally unconstrained. A detected contradiction certifies that no compatible translation satisfies all observed demonstrations.
learning.few_shot_argument: The mechanism is orbit generation under naturality. Suppose every source symbol is reachable from one demonstrated source through the two operations. Then repeatedly enforcing phi(T[a,i])=U[a,phi(i)] determines the target of every source, so one correct binding identifies the entire map, provided a compatible map exists. More generally, k anchors suffice if the union of their forward reachable sets covers the source system. Without such coverage, the core leaves some entries unassigned. This is a conditional one-shot identification theorem. It is not a claim about learning the transition tables, and it is not a claim about learning arbitrary language from one example.

readout.latex: p_t(v)=\begin{cases}\mathbf{1}\{v=F_t[r_t]\},&b_t=\mathrm{answer},\ c_t=\mathrm{false},\ F_t[r_t]\ne\bot,\\\mathbf{1}\{v\in\{0,\ldots,d-1\}\}/d,&b_t=\mathrm{answer}\text{ otherwise},\\1/V,&b_t\ne\mathrm{answer}.\end{cases}
readout.name: Certified answer or explicit uncertainty
readout.plain: p_t(v) is the probability of vocabulary token v (one of V=d+5 tokens) after processing token t. The indicator 1{condition} is one when the condition holds and zero otherwise. In answer mode, if c is false and F[r] is assigned, put probability one on F[r]. Otherwise in answer mode, put probability 1/d on each numeric token and zero on the five control tokens. In every other mode, put 1/V on every token.

state.meaning: A stacks two tables, each of shape [2,d]. A[0,a,i]=T[a,i] is the source table and A[1,a,i]=U[a,i] is the target table. The first index selects source (0) or target (1). The second index a in {0,1} selects the operation: 0 is L and 1 is R. The third index i in {0,...,d-1} is a symbol, where d is the number of symbols in each system. Every entry is a symbol in {0,...,d-1}. The tables are supplied with the task and are not inferred from demonstrations. The intended unknown translation phi obeys phi(T[a,i]) = U[a,phi(i)]. The operations need not commute, be linear, or be invertible.
state.name: A

state.meaning: F[i], for i in {0,...,d-1}, is either an assigned target symbol in {0,...,d-1} or the unassigned marker bottom. Every entry starts at bottom. F is a single array that is modified in place. F_{t-1} and F_t name its contents before and after input token t. F holds at most d bindings, one per source symbol.
state.name: F
state.type: learned partial symbolic map, updated in place

state.meaning: c starts false. It becomes true, permanently, when propagation requests two different targets for the same source. c_{t-1} and c_t denote its value before and after input token t.
state.name: c

state.meaning:
B=(b,r,e) holds the parser mode b, a register r, and an emitted event e. The modes are idle, demo_source, demo_target, query_source, word, and answer. The register r stores a source symbol. The event e is either none or seed(i,j) with i,j in {0,...,d-1}. Parse_A is the deterministic transition function:
- idle accepts D or Q and enters demo_source or query_source.
- demo_source stores a numeric token in r and enters demo_target.
- demo_target, on a numeric token j, emits seed(r,j) and returns to idle.
- query_source stores a numeric token in r and enters word.
- word replaces r by T[0,r] on L or by T[1,r] on R, so operations apply left to right. On ? it enters answer.
- answer consumes one numeric answer token and returns to idle.
Every step first sets e=none. Invalid inputs reset the parser to idle without emitting an event. A demonstration is therefore D i j. A query is Q i, then any number of L/R operations, then ?, then its answer.
state.name: B
state.type: finite-state parser with one integer register

state.meaning: W holds the source-target pairs (x,y) proposed during one call of FIFO_A. It is empty between input tokens. Each call pushes one seed. Each first assignment pushes two more pairs, and there are at most d first assignments. W therefore never holds more than 2d+1 entries.
state.name: W
state.type: transient FIFO queue of proposed bindings

state.meaning: z_t is input token t, for t from 1 to n, where n is the context length. The vocabulary has the numeric tokens 0,...,d-1 and five control tokens D, Q, L, R, ?, so its size is V=d+5. Numeric tokens name source symbols in demonstrations and queries, and target symbols in answers.
state.name: z

update.name: Parse and execute a compositional query
update.plain: Apply the finite-state parser specified in B to token z_t. In word mode, L and R update the register immediately through T[0,.] or T[1,.], and no operation history is kept. The output event e_t is none or seed(i,j).

update.name: Compile forced bindings
update.plain:
If e_t is none, or c is already true, leave F and c unchanged. Otherwise e_t = seed(i,j), and the procedure FIFO_A(F,(i,j)) runs. It modifies F in place, with no copy, and returns the updated (F, c):
- Set W = [(i,j)].
- While W is nonempty and c is false, pop (x,y) from the front of W:
  - If F[x] is bottom, set F[x] = y, then append (T[0,x], U[0,y]) and (T[1,x], U[1,y]) to the back of W.
  - Else if F[x] == y, do nothing.
  - Else set c = true and empty W.
An assigned source is never expanded again, so the total expansion work over a whole context is O(d).

references.why: Supplies the categorical compatibility viewpoint: equivariant vector bundles over face categories, and the connection between order-equivariant and category-equivariant models. The transplant replaces continuous fibers and learned layers with finite-set representations and exact completion of a demonstrated compatible map. The paper is not cited as establishing this card's one-anchor sequence-learning guarantee.

source_transplant.change: Vector-space fibers become finite sets. The face category becomes the free category with one object and two generating operations. A compatible map between two such finite-set representations is learned by propagating demonstrated bindings. The core uses discrete naturality instead of learned linear equivariant layers, diffusion, or a universal-approximation construction.
source_transplant.object: Equivariant vector bundles over face categories and the compatibility of maps with the category's morphisms

card.summary: A specialized symbolic sequence learner that learns translations between known transition systems. Two operations act on source symbols, and corresponding operations act on target symbols. A demonstration supplies one source-to-target binding. Naturality propagates that binding through the source system, assigns target values, and detects incompatible assignments. If every source symbol is reachable from the demonstrated symbol, one example determines the entire translation. Queries may contain operation strings of any length; they are executed without storing their history. This is not a general language model. Its strong sample-efficiency result depends on supplied transition tables, noiseless examples, and the assumption that the unknown translation respects those transitions.
card.title: Naturality Compiler: One-Anchor Learning of Compositional Transports

toy_example.description: Two noncommuting operations on four source symbols are conjugated by the translation [2,0,3,1]. The program uses the core parser and in-place FIFO closure. One demonstration recovers the full map. The queries L then R and R then L give different targets. A contradictory demonstration then forces the specified uniform fallback.

critic.difference_if_any: Nothing in the mechanism is new beyond packaging. The known homomorphism-extension closure is wrapped in a token-stream parser (D i j / Q i w ?). Its failure and undefined cases are exposed as uniform output distributions. The amortized O(d+m) bound is the standard property of the algorithm: each state is assigned once. Nothing is learned except the partial map h itself, which the classical algorithm computes in the same way. The transition tables are supplied, not learned.
critic.mapping: The card is the standard worklist (Hopcroft–Karp-style) closure for extending a homomorphism between two deterministic automata over the alphabet {L,R}. Equivalently, it extends a morphism of finite M-sets for the free monoid M={L,R}*. Symbol by symbol: the source table T[a,i] is the source automaton's transition function delta_1(i,a). U[a,j] is the target automaton's transition function delta_2(j,a). The partial map F is the candidate homomorphism h. A demonstration seed(i,j) is the initial pair (i,j) pushed on the pending-pair stack. The FIFO_A loop pops (x,y). If h(x) is undefined, it sets h(x)=y and pushes (delta_1(x,a), delta_2(y,a)) for each letter a. If h(x)=y already, it skips. If h(x) differs from y, it reports failure. This is exactly the textbook procedure for testing whether a state pair generates a functional simulation or homomorphism. Without union-find it is the directed version of the Hopcroft–Karp 1971 DFA equivalence check, and it is congruence-closure-style propagation of the constraint h(delta_1(x,a)) = delta_2(h(x),a). The contradiction bit c is that algorithm's 'not a homomorphism' verdict. Parse_A is a fixed DFA that runs a word: r <- delta_1(r,a) letter by letter, which is ordinary automaton execution. The readout p_t is a lookup h(r), with a uniform distribution when h(r) is undefined or c is set. No component falls outside this algorithm plus a hand-coded tokenizer.
critic.textbook_why: The cited source (equivariant vector bundles over face categories) is changed substantially: vector fibers become finite sets and learned layers are removed. But that change lands exactly on the textbook construction of category and automata theory. This is the morphism of finite M-sets (deterministic automata) over a free monoid on two generators, determined on the orbit of one generator and computed by the standard pending-pair worklist with conflict detection. The card adds only a token-stream parser and a uniform-fallback readout. The update, the invariant (naturality) and the inference procedure are unmodified from the standard algorithm.
critic.why: The update is a worklist that propagates a functional constraint h(delta_1(x,a))=delta_2(h(x),a) from a seed pair through two supplied deterministic transition tables, and fails on conflict. That is the classical algorithm for checking or extending an automaton homomorphism or simulation (the directed relative of Hopcroft–Karp equivalence and congruence closure). The one-anchor identification result is the textbook fact that a morphism of monoid actions is determined on the orbit of a generator. Noncommutative compositional generalization follows trivially from executing the word in the source DFA and looking up h. It is not a renamed RNN, SSM or linear attention. Forcing it into an RNN would only be the trivial 'any finite-state machine is an RNN'. But it is a well-known symbolic algorithm moved into a sequence-model framing with given tables. A researcher who knows automata theory would not be surprised by it.

prior_art.label: prior_art_undertested
prior_art.notes: The underlying fact that a morphism commuting with transitions is determined on a generated orbit by its value at one point is standard. Equivariant and categorical frameworks (W7167581049) and labeled union-find binding propagation (W4411260212) address closely related mechanisms. Finite-state transducer learning for translation (W2071991030) is the closest prior work on learning translations between transition systems. None of the retrieved papers tests one-anchor compositional transport in sequence learning at comparable scale, and the card's d=64 sample-efficiency and coverage predictions have no empirical support in these results. No retrieved paper shows the central claim fails, so known_disproven does not apply.

one-shot learning morphism propagation finite automata
