capabilities.prediction: Top-1 accuracy >= 0.95 and mean probability on the correct value >= 0.8. Accuracy changes by at most 0.02 when 0 to 4000 filler tokens are inserted. The precondition, checked directly on the trained model, is that all filler-involving pairs have K0 <= kappa = 1e-3. In that case filler bigrams are never imprinted and cannot evict key-value imprints, and the 32 filler right species add at most 32 * kappa = 0.032 to any key's denominator 1 + (K y)_q.
capabilities.task: One-shot associative recall: the sequence k1 v1 k2 v2 ... k8 v8 followed by a query k_i. 8 random keys from tokens 0-31, 8 random values from tokens 32-95, V = 128, r = 8, P_max = 64, J = 3. Variant: 0 to 4000 filler tokens from 96-127 are inserted before the query.

capabilities.prediction: The held-out value is the top-1 prediction in >= 90% of trials, and its mean probability over trials is >= 0.30. Row-local ablation on the same trained model (same E, F, beta and imprint table): p_loc(v) = K[q,v] / sum_{v': a[v']=1} K[q,v'], over tokens present in context, which is what a count cache or one-hot linear-attention readout gives. The query key's row has no imprints, so p_loc(v) = K0[q,v]/sum K0[q,.] over the 8 inventory values, up to keys present with K0 <= kappa. Under a random bijection the held-out value is uniform over the inventory and independent of q's prior row, so E[p_loc(held-out)] = 1/8 exactly. The measured mean over 1000 trials is predicted to lie in 1/8 ± 0.02. The gap between the mean model probability and the mean row-local probability is >= 0.15, and it comes only from the conservation coupling.
capabilities.task: Elimination (mutual exclusivity): the context lists an inventory of m = 8 value tokens, then demonstrates 7 of the 8 pairs of a random bijection between 8 keys and the 8 values, then queries the 8th key, which was never demonstrated. 1000 trials with fresh random keys, values and bijections.

capabilities.prediction: At convergence the bound parts satisfy exactly C_qa/C_qb = (K0_qa/K0_qb) e^{beta (k_a - k_b)} y_a/y_b. With no other binder, y_v = 1/(1 + K_qv x_q), so log(C_qa/C_qb) is strictly increasing in k_a - k_b. Each unit step changes it by an amount in (0, beta]. The step equals beta in the weak-binding limit K_qv x_q << 1 and is compressed under saturation. Measurable: with K0_qa/K0_qb in [0.8, 1.25], p(a) > p(b) in >= 95% of trials with k_a > k_b, and every measured unit-step increment of log(C_qa/C_qb) lies in [0, beta + 0.05].
capabilities.task: Graded conflicting evidence: key q is shown with value a k_a times and with value b k_b times (k_a + k_b <= 4). No other key in context binds a or b.

capabilities.prediction: For K <= 16, accuracy >= 0.9. For K = 32, eviction (smallest count, ties broken by least recent increment) keeps only the last 16 imprints, so overall accuracy is 0.5 ± 0.1. The last 16 pairs score >= 0.9. The first 16 score <= 0.1, because each evicted key spreads its mass over the roughly 16 values left free, which is the elimination effect at chance. A fixed state cannot hold more than P_max one-shot bindings.
capabilities.task: Capacity limit: one-shot recall of K = 8, 16 or 32 pairs with P_max = 16 (other settings as in the first task). Value->key bridge pairs have K0 <= kappa, so each key-value pair uses exactly one imprint.

complexity.constants_notes: Each sweep costs O(V r) for E(F^T y) and F(E^T x), plus O(P_max) for the sparse correction over the imprint table, where each record caches K0_ij, computed in O(r) at insertion. The gate test and the minimum-count eviction scan cost O(r + P_max) per token. Each token runs J warm-started sweep pairs, and the claims take J = 3 as a fixed constant, so the true cost is about 2 J (2 V r + P_max). The readout row K[q,:] costs O(V r), the same order as an LM output projection of width r. x, y and a take 3V memory, and the table takes 5 P_max numbers. Nothing depends on n, because the table has at most P_max records. Training with implicit differentiation adds a CG solve of at most 50 iterations, each with a matvec costing O(V r + P_max). The initial state is x_0 = y_0 = a_0 = 0 with an empty table.

sample_efficiency.mechanism: The gated imprint e^beta on K_ij plus re-equilibration. One demonstration of a binding shifts the equilibrium enough to dominate the readout, with no test-time gradient step. Pretraining only learns the role prior E F^T (which token types bind), the scalar beta and the background u. It never learns the bindings themselves.

prediction.metric: In-context exposures per new key-value pair needed to reach top-1 recall >= 0.95. Setup: K = 8 pairs per sequence, V = 128 split into keys 0-31, values 32-95 and filler 96-127, r = 8, P_max = 64, J = 3, measured on 1000 held-out sequences with fresh random pairings.
prediction.statement: One demonstration of each pair gives top-1 recall >= 0.95 and mean p(correct) >= 0.8, which matches the first capability claim. Pretraining protocol: one pass over synthetic recall sequences with fresh random pairings, Adam with learning rate 1e-2 and batch 32, and held-out recall evaluated every 100 sequences. Secondary prediction: the median over 5 seeds of the number of pretraining sequences seen before held-out one-shot recall first reaches 0.95 is <= 3000. This is plausible because only 2Vr + V + 1 parameters are trained and no binding is stored in weights.

card.core_idea: Each observed adjacent token pair (i, j) lowers the standard free energy of a complex C_ij in a reversible binding network X_i + Y_j <-> C_ij, whose species totals are set by which tokens are present in context; the next-token distribution is the bound fraction of the current token's species at the network's unique detailed-balanced equilibrium (the Birch point), so competing bindings deplete each other through conservation laws.

extensions.description: Replace the unit totals with learned per-token capacities s^L_i and s^R_j, so that function words can bind many successors. This relaxes the one-to-one bias of the core for natural text. The sweeps stay the same, with a replaced by a ⊙ s.

equations.latex: x \leftarrow (a \odot s^L) \oslash (\mathbf{1} + K y),\quad y \leftarrow (a \odot s^R) \oslash (\mathbf{1} + K^{\top} x)

extensions.name: Learned stoichiometric capacities

extensions.description: Following finite stochastic CRN semantics (W2008591003), use small integer molecule counts and sample the stationary distribution of the binding network. At unit counts this gives exact discrete matchings instead of fractional bindings, which is useful for strict permutation tasks.
extensions.name: Finite-count stochastic regime

extensions.description: Add reactions X_i + Z_k + Y_j <-> C_ikj, imprinted by triples (w_{t-2}, w_{t-1}, w_t), with their own capped repertoire. This conditions bindings on a two-token context, for example 'relation r applied to key k'. Conservation still couples all complexes through the shared totals.
extensions.name: Trimolecular complexes for two-token contexts

falsifiers: On the elimination task (m = 8, 7 pairs shown, inventory listed, 1000 trials), the mean probability the trained model gives the held-out value exceeds the mean row-local ablation probability (p_loc(v) = K[q,v]/sum over present tokens of K[q,.], with the same E, F, beta and imprint table) by less than 0.15. That would show the conservation coupling adds nothing.

One-shot associative recall with K = 8 pairs (V = 128, r = 8, P_max = 64, J = 3) fails to reach top-1 accuracy 0.95, the threshold of the first capability claim, with one exposure per pair after pretraining, but reaches it with two or more. That would refute the claim that a single e^beta imprint plus re-equilibration is enough.
With V, r and P_max fixed, measured time per token grows by more than 10% when context length goes from n = 1,000 to n = 64,000. That would refute the n-independent cost claim.

With J = 3 warm-started sweep pairs per token, the readout differs from the fully converged Birch-point readout by total variation distance > 0.05 on more than 5% of recall-task positions. In that case the constant J in the cost claim does not hold, and the true cost includes a growing convergence factor.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: The readout is not a linear or row-local function of the state. It is the minimizer of a convex free energy under per-token conservation laws, and that minimizer couples every row to every column. p(v | q) depends on how strongly other keys bind v. This is why elimination works. A row-local readout of the same affinities gives an undemonstrated key's held-out value exactly 1/m in expectation over random bijections, whatever the prior row.
known_relatives.name: Linear attention (Transformers are RNNs) / count-based cache language models
known_relatives.relation: The imprint update N_t = N_{t-1} + gate * e_{w_{t-1}} e_{w_t}^T is an additive outer-product accumulator with one-hot features. It is the state update of linear attention or a bigram cache (an S_t = S_{t-1} + B x_t form), and we say so plainly.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: Those methods scale an n x n position-by-position attention matrix, which is quadratic in n. Here the scaled matrix is a token-type by token-type affinity whose context-dependent part has at most P_max entries. The transport is unbalanced: the free monomers x and y absorb unmatched mass, and that free fraction is the fallback to u. The equilibrium constants are written by gated in-context co-occurrence, not by query-key dot products.
known_relatives.name: Sinkhorn / optimal-transport attention (doubly stochastic attention normalization)
known_relatives.relation: Matrix scaling of a positive kernel to prescribed marginals is the same mathematics as the binding equilibrium with conserved totals. Entropic OT is a special case of Birch's theorem.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: Those models have no conserved quantities and no global equilibrium readout. Their state decays and is gated, so no conservation law forces bindings to compete. Here nothing decays. Capacity is a hard cap on distinct complexes with eviction, and inference is constrained free-energy minimization.
known_relatives.name: Mamba / RWKV / RetNet / xLSTM
known_relatives.relation: Linear-time recurrent sequence models with fixed-size state.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: Here competition is not a heuristic normalization. It is the exact equilibrium of a detailed-balanced mass-action network, with a uniqueness guarantee (the Birch point), a convex objective, and a closed-form implicit gradient. The mixing weight on the background u is the free concentration x_q, which the chemistry determines. It is not a learned gate.
known_relatives.name: Cross-situational word-learning models with competition (mutual exclusivity) and pointer-sentinel mixtures
known_relatives.relation: Psychology models of word-object mapping use competition between candidate mappings. Pointer-sentinel models mix a copy distribution with a background distribution.

learning.description: E_raw, F_raw, b and l are trained by next-token cross-entropy on pretraining sequences. There are two equivalent options. (1) Backpropagate through the J unrolled sweep pairs. (2) Differentiate through the converged Birch point by the implicit-function theorem, using the closed form below. On the support of a_t, use log coordinates sigma = log x and tau = log y. The Hessian of G in (sigma, tau) at the equilibrium is H = [[Id, C], [C^T, Id]], where Id is the identity matrix on the support and C_ij = K_ij x_i y_j. The diagonal blocks are Id because x_i(1 + (Ky)_i) = a_i = 1 there. H is symmetric positive definite because G is strictly convex in (sigma, tau). The adjoint system H [lambda; mu] = [x ⊙ dL/dx; y ⊙ dL/dy] is solved by conjugate gradients. CG starts from lambda = mu = 0 and stops when the residual norm is at most 1e-6 times the norm of the right-hand side, or after 50 iterations, whichever comes first. Each matvec C z costs O(V r + P_max). The gradient with respect to K is a rank-2 dense term plus sparse parts, so it is never materialized. It is pushed to E, F and beta through K = K0 ⊙ exp(beta N). Nothing is updated by gradient at test time. All in-context adaptation is the imprint table plus re-equilibration.

equations.latex: G(x,y) = \sum_{i: a_t[i]=1} (x_i - a_t[i]\log x_i) + \sum_{j: a_t[j]=1} (y_j - a_t[j] \log y_j) + \sum_{ij} K_t[i,j]\, x_i y_j,\quad (x^*,y^*) = \arg\min_{x,y>0} G
equations.name: free energy whose minimizer is the readout state
equations.plain: Setting the gradient of G to zero gives exactly x_i = a_t[i]/(1 + (K y)_i) and y_j = a_t[j]/(1 + (K^T x)_j). G is strictly convex in (sigma, tau) = (log x, log y) on the support of a_t, so the minimizer is unique and the alternating sweeps (exact block minimization) converge to it. Off the support, x_i = y_j = 0.

equations.name: training loss
equations.plain: loss = - sum over positions t of log p_t[w_{t+1}].

equations.latex: \begin{pmatrix} \mathrm{Id} & C \\ C^{\top} & \mathrm{Id} \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\lambda\\ \mu\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} x\odot \partial_x \mathcal{L} \\ y \odot \partial_y \mathcal{L}\end{pmatrix},\quad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial K_{ij}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial K_{ij}}\Big|_{\text{explicit}} - (\lambda_i + \mu_j)\, x_i y_j
equations.name: implicit gradient through the Birch point
equations.plain: Solve for lambda and mu by CG on the support of a_t (initial guess 0, stop at relative residual <= 1e-6 or 50 iterations), with C z = x ⊙ (K (y ⊙ z)) and C^T z = y ⊙ (K^T (x ⊙ z)). Then dL/dK[i,j] = explicit_ij - (lambda[i] + mu[j]) * x[i] * y[j], where explicit_qv = (dL/dp[v]) * x[q] * y[v] for the readout row q and 0 elsewhere. Chain rule: dK[i,j]/dE[i,k] = F[j,k] * exp(beta*N[i,j]), dK[i,j]/dF[j,k] = E[i,k] * exp(beta*N[i,j]), dK[i,j]/dbeta = N[i,j] * K[i,j]. So dL/dE is the rank-2 dense part -((x⊙lambda) y^T + x (y⊙mu)^T) times F, plus row q and the sparse corrections on S_t.

learning.few_shot_argument: One exposure of a gated pair (i, j) (K0_ij > kappa) multiplies K_ij by e^beta, a learned free-energy drop. At the new Birch point, the complex C_ij = K_ij x_i y_j takes most of X_i's unit total as soon as e^beta K0_ij is large compared with the competing terms in 1 + (K y)_i. So one demonstration is enough for recall. k demonstrations give an affinity K0_ij e^{k beta}, so conflicting evidence enters the equilibrium constants multiplicatively. The conservation law y_j + sum_i C_ij = a_j makes the readout of key q depend on every other key's bindings. A value bound strongly elsewhere has a small free concentration y_j, so the probability of an undemonstrated key moves to the values that are still free. This is how a rule shown for m-1 of m items determines the m-th. The inference is done by chemical equilibration (free-energy minimization within the stoichiometric class). It is neither a gradient step nor a stored lookup.

readout.latex: p_t(v) = K_t[q,v]\, x_q\, y_v + x_q\, u_v, \quad q = w_t,\; u = \mathrm{softmax}(l)
readout.name: bound-plus-free fraction of the current token's left species
readout.plain: p[v] = K[q,v]*x[q]*y[v] + x[q]*u[v], with q the current token and u = softmax(l). The last x sweep sets x[q] = 1/(1 + Ky[q]) and a[q] = 1, and u sums to 1, so sum_v p[v] = x[q]*(Ky[q] + 1) = 1 exactly, even before full convergence.

state.meaning: Phi is the column concatenation of two V x r blocks. V is the vocabulary size and r is the prior rank. E = Phi[:, :r] and F = Phi[:, r:] each have shape V x r, so the block has 2Vr numbers. They give the prior equilibrium constants K0 = E F^T >= 0 between left species X_i and right species Y_j. This is the pretrained notion of which token types can bind which, for example keys binding values. Pairs with K0_ij <= kappa (a fixed constant, kappa = 1e-3) are treated as non-binding and are never imprinted.
state.name: Phi = [E | F]
state.type: learned parameter block, nonnegative (E = softplus(E_raw), F = softplus(F_raw))

state.meaning: The imprint free energy is beta = softplus(b) > 0, so each imprint multiplies K_ij by e^beta. The background distribution is u = softmax(l), a point in the probability simplex over V tokens. It receives the unbound fraction of the current token's left species. Only b and l are stored. beta and u are always computed from them.
state.name: (b, l)
state.type: learned parameters: scalar b and logit vector l

state.meaning: N_t is stored only as this table. The notation N_t[i,j] means the count of the record (i, j) if one exists, and 0 otherwise. In other words, N_t is the logical V x V matrix that is zero off the table and is never materialized. N_t[i,j] counts how often token j directly followed token i with K0_ij > kappa. S_t = {(i,j): N_t[i,j] > 0} is the set of stored pairs, with |S_t| <= P_max. P_max is the number of distinct complex species the reaction volume holds, a fixed size independent of n. last_increment_step is used to break eviction ties. cached K0_ij is computed in O(r) when the record is created. N_0 is empty.
state.name: N_t (imprint table)
state.type: sparse table of at most P_max records (i, j, count, last_increment_step, cached K0_ij)

state.meaning: a_t[i] = 1 if token i has occurred in w_1..w_t, else 0, with a_0 = 0. It is the conserved total of both X_i and Y_i, and it is the same a_t that appears in the free energy G. Tokens that are absent contribute no species.
state.name: a_t

state.meaning: x_t[i] is the free (unbound) concentration of X_i at the current equilibrium estimate, with 0 <= x_t[i] <= a_t[i] and x_0 = 0. A newly injected species starts fully free (x[i] = 1).
state.name: x_t

state.meaning: y_t[j] is the free concentration of Y_j at the current equilibrium estimate, with 0 <= y_t[j] <= a_t[j] and y_0 = 0. A newly injected species starts at y[j] = 1. A small y_j means value j is already consumed by other bindings.
state.name: y_t

update.name: gated imprint with capped complex repertoire
update.plain: if t >= 2 and dot(E[w_{t-1}], F[w_t]) > kappa: if a record (w_{t-1}, w_t) exists, increment its count and set last_increment_step = t; otherwise create it with count 1, last_increment_step = t, and cached K0. If the table now holds more than P_max records, delete the record with the smallest count, breaking ties by the smallest last_increment_step. Pairs at or below kappa (for example filler bigrams or value->key bridges, which have near-zero prior affinity) never enter the table, so they cannot evict real bindings.

update.name: species injection (new mass enters free)
update.plain: if a[w_t] == 0: a[w_t] = 1; x[w_t] = 1; y[w_t] = 1. All other entries are unchanged. Together with x_0 = y_0 = a_0 = 0, this fixes the warm start of the sweeps at every t, including t = 1.

update.latex: K_t = (E F^{\top}) \odot \exp(\beta N_t),\quad (K_t y)_i = E_i^{\top}(F^{\top} y) + \sum_{j:(i,j)\in S_t} K^0_{ij}\,(e^{\beta N_t[i,j]}-1)\, y_j
update.name: context-written equilibrium constants (never materialized)
update.plain: Ky = E @ (F.T @ y); then for each record (i,j) in the table: Ky[i] += K0[i,j]*(exp(beta*N[i,j]) - 1)*y[j]. Likewise KTx = F @ (E.T @ x); for each record (i,j): KTx[j] += K0[i,j]*(exp(beta*N[i,j]) - 1)*x[i]. A row or column with no record receives no correction. K0[i,j] is read from the record's cache.

update.name: free right-species sweep
update.plain: for each j: y[j] = a[j] / (1 + KTx[j]). This is exact minimization of G over log y with x fixed.

update.name: free left-species sweep (alternates with the y sweep, J times per token)
update.plain: for each i: x[i] = a[i] / (1 + Ky[i]). The pair (y sweep, then x sweep) runs J times per token, where J is a fixed integer (J = 3 in all claims). It starts from the warm start given by the previous token and the injection step. The fixed point is the unique Birch point C_ij = K_ij x_i y_j with x_i + sum_j C_ij = a_i and y_j + sum_i C_ij = a_j.

references.why: Source of the central object. Detailed-balanced chemical reaction networks have product-form mass-action equilibria (generalized Boltzmann machines), and conservation laws condition those equilibria. I take the binding equilibrium C_ij = K_ij x_i y_j under conserved totals, together with its free-energy characterization, and use it as the inference step of a sequence learner whose equilibrium constants are written by the context.

Finite stochastic CRN semantics with integer molecule counts. It is used only in the 'finite-count stochastic regime' extension, where the deterministic Birch point is replaced by the stationary distribution of a finite-count network. The core does not depend on it.

source_transplant.change: In chemistry the equilibrium constants are fixed. Here the context writes them. Each observed adjacent pair with prior affinity above a threshold multiplies K_ij by e^beta, starting from a learned low-rank prior E F^T. Species totals are injected when a token occurs. The equilibrium is tracked by warm-started alternating sweeps instead of being simulated in time. The bound and free fractions of the current token's left species are read out as a next-token distribution.
source_transplant.object: The detailed-balanced mass-action equilibrium of reversible binding reactions X_i + Y_j <-> C_ij with equilibrium constants K_ij and stoichiometric conservation laws: C_ij = K_ij x_i y_j, with x_i + sum_j C_ij = total_i and y_j + sum_i C_ij = total_j. It is the unique positive equilibrium in its compatibility class (the Birch point) and the minimizer of the Gibbs free energy. The cited paper identifies it as a product-form equilibrium, a generalized Boltzmann machine whose conservation laws condition the distribution.

card.summary: Tokens are species. The first time a token i occurs, one unit of a 'left' species X_i and one unit of a 'right' species Y_i are injected, and both start out free. Each observed adjacent pair (w_{t-1}, w_t) whose learned prior affinity exceeds a fixed threshold kappa multiplies the equilibrium constant of the reversible reaction X_{w_{t-1}} + Y_{w_t} <-> C_{w_{t-1} w_t} by e^beta. The constants start from a learned low-rank nonnegative prior K0 = E F^T. The model holds the mass-action, detailed-balanced equilibrium of this binding network. That equilibrium is unique in each stoichiometric compatibility class (Birch's theorem). It minimizes a convex free energy and is found by warm-started alternating fixed-point sweeps on the free concentrations x and y. The prediction after token q is the vector of complexes C_qv, plus the free fraction x_q routed to a learned background distribution u. Every value species has a total of 1 that all keys share, so the readout is not row-local. A value already bound strongly by another key is depleted, which pushes a never-demonstrated key toward the values that are still free. This is elimination, or mutual-exclusivity inference. A per-row normalization of the same affinities gives the held-out value only 1/m in expectation. The state is a sparse imprint table capped at P_max gated entries plus O(V) concentrations, so cost per token does not depend on n. Training differentiates through the equilibrium in closed form. In log coordinates, the Hessian of the free energy at the Birch point is [[Id, C], [C^T, Id]], where C is the complex matrix.
card.title: Birch-Point Binding Chemistry: in-context bindings as the mass-action equilibrium of a reversible binding network under conservation laws

toy_example.description: Six tokens: keys 0, 1, 2 and values 3, 4, 5. The role prior K0 = E F^T with r = 1 lets only keys (left species) bind values (right species), each with K0 = 1. E and F are set directly to their post-softplus values, using exact zeros as the limiting case. The sequence [5, 0, 3, 1, 4, 2] first shows value 5 (inventory), then the pairs (0 -> 3) and (1 -> 4), then the query key 2, which was never paired. The bridge pairs (5,0), (3,1) and (4,2) have K0 = 0 <= kappa, so the gate does not imprint them. beta = ln 9, so demonstrated pairs have K = 9. All mass starts free (x = y = a, the injection rule). Alternating sweeps run to convergence. By uniqueness of the Birch point, this equals the per-token warm-started procedure run to convergence. The equilibrium is x = y = 1/4 for the demonstrated keys and values and 1/2 for key 2 and value 5. Key 2's bound mass therefore goes twice as much to the still-free value 5 as to each depleted value (elimination). Its free fraction of 1/2 goes to the uniform background over values. The row-local baseline is uniform (1/3 each).
toy_example.python:
import json
import numpy as np
V = 6
E = np.array([1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0], dtype=float).reshape(V, 1)
F = np.array([0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1], dtype=float).reshape(V, 1)
K0 = E @ F.T
kappa = 1e-3
beta = np.log(9.0)
u = np.array([0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1], dtype=float) / 3.0
seq = [5, 0, 3, 1, 4, 2]
N = np.zeros((V, V))
a = np.zeros(V)
prev = None
for w in seq:
    if prev is not None and K0[prev, w] > kappa:
        N[prev, w] += 1.0
    a[w] = 1.0
    prev = w
K = K0 * np.exp(beta * N)
x = a.copy()
y = a.copy()
for _ in range(500):
    y = a / (1.0 + K.T @ x)
    x = a / (1.0 + K @ y)
def readout(q):
    return K[q] * x[q] * y + x[q] * u
p2 = readout(2)
p0 = readout(0)
r = lambda v: [round(float(t), 4) for t in v]
out = {
    "x_free_keys": r(x[:3]),
    "p_q2_values": r(p2[3:]),
    "p_q0_values": r(p0[3:]),
    "rowlocal_q2": r(K[2, 3:] / K[2, 3:].sum()),
    "rowlocal_q0": r(K[0, 3:] / K[0, 3:].sum()),
    "argmax_q2": int(np.argmax(p2)),
    "mass_q2": round(float(p2.sum()), 4)
}
print(json.dumps(out))

critic.difference_if_any: The normalization is over token types, not over positions. The card scales a V x V type-by-type kernel whose context part is a capped sparse count table. It does not scale an n x n position matrix, so cost is independent of n. The marginals are binary presence indicators, and the dustbin potential is pinned to 1 rather than given a fixed marginal. The equilibrium is tracked incrementally with J warm-started sweeps per token. The column-coupling effect (elimination / mutual exclusivity) is precisely what Sinkhorn normalization adds over row-softmax, and it is known in OT matching (SuperGlue's one-to-one assignment bias). The learning rule (cross-entropy with BPTT or implicit differentiation through the scaling fixed point) is not new.
critic.mapping: Update: N_t = N_{t-1} + gate * e_{w_{t-1}} e_{w_t}^T is the linear-attention state S_t = S_{t-1} + phi(k_t) v_t^T. Here phi(k_t) = e_{w_{t-1}} and v_t = e_{w_t} are one-hot, and a binary gate 1[K0 > kappa] is applied. This is a gated bigram/count cache, and the card concedes it. The P_max cap with min-count eviction is a fixed-size LFU cache over the same outer-product state. The effective kernel K = (E F^T) ⊙ exp(beta N) is a low-rank learned bilinear prior times an exponentiated count cache. That is a kernel over token types, with log K_ij = log(E_i·F_j) + beta N_ij acting as the 'attention logit'. Readout: the fixed point x_i = a_i/(1+(Ky)_i), y_j = a_j/(1+(K^T x)_j) is alternating Sinkhorn/matrix scaling of the kernel K to marginals a. P_ij = x_i K_ij y_j is the transport plan with row potential x and column potential y. The '+1' terms are a dustbin row and column with kernel entry 1 whose scaling is pinned at 1. This is exactly SuperGlue-style unbalanced Sinkhorn with slack: the free monomer is the dustbin mass. The readout p(v) = P_qv/a_q + x_q u_v takes row q of a Sinkhorn-normalized kernel and sends the dustbin mass to a learned background distribution, as a pointer-sentinel mixture does. Taken together, the card is Sinkhorn (doubly stochastic, OT) normalized attention (Sinkformer / Sparse Sinkhorn / SuperGlue dustbin) applied to a vocabulary-indexed one-hot linear-attention/bigram-cache state. Training through the fixed point by implicit differentiation is standard differentiable Sinkhorn (Hessian [[Id, C],[C^T, Id]] in log-potentials).
critic.textbook_why: The core object is the textbook detailed-balanced mass-action equilibrium of reversible binding reactions under conservation laws (the Birch point, the Gibbs free-energy minimizer). It is computed by the standard alternating fixed point, and the card does not change its equations. The card's changes are only in the inputs: equilibrium constants written by a gated count of token bigrams on top of a learned low-rank prior, and totals set by token presence. It then adds a next-token readout with a background distribution. The construction itself is unmodified.
critic.why: The state update is a gated, capped one-hot outer-product accumulator, which is linear attention or a bigram cache. The card says so itself. The only non-standard part is the readout, and that is matrix scaling of a positive kernel to prescribed marginals with slack. In other words it is unbalanced Sinkhorn normalization with a dustbin, a known attention normalization (Sinkformers, Sparse Sinkhorn attention) and a known one-to-one matching layer (SuperGlue). The card admits that entropic OT is the same mathematics. Its mutual-exclusivity capability is the textbook consequence of column constraints in Sinkhorn assignment. Calling it a binding equilibrium under conservation laws renames the row and column potentials as free concentrations. Applying the scaling to type-level counts instead of positions changes cost but not the mechanism. A researcher familiar with Sinkhorn attention and cache language models would not be surprised.

prior_art.notes: Close prior work exists on both sides of the mechanism. The Hessian and detailed-balance geometry of chemical reaction networks with stoichiometric constraints (2112.12403, W4286111474, W4226282717) covers the equilibrium math, but not sequence learning. Gated linear attention (W4389713725) covers the additive outer-product state update, which the card itself acknowledges as a relative. For the elimination/mutual-exclusivity capability, W2954931071 and W4205957729 test related claims. W2954931071 reports that standard networks lack the ME bias, and W4205957729 studies ME in pragmatic agents. Neither tests the conservation-coupled binding-equilibrium mechanism, and none of the found papers reports empirical results for the proposed model's capabilities (recall accuracy, elimination probabilities, capacity limits, or cost scaling). The claimed capabilities are therefore undertested rather than tested or disproven. No found paper shows the central claim fails. The primary reference 2205.06313 named in the card does not appear in the search results, so it is not cited here.

capabilities.prediction: Take two components of 8 sites each (d = 16, K = 6), each internally connected by consistent demonstrations. Before a bridge, all 64 cross pairs get probability exactly 0.5. After one correctly labeled bridge demonstration, H^(K) predicts all 64 cross pairs correctly by sign, for any alpha, beta > 0. Cross distances are at most 15, which is at most 2^(K-1) = 32.
capabilities.task: One-shot relational bridge

capabilities.prediction: Demonstrate one isolated pair r times with the true parity and w < r times with the wrong one. The prediction is exactly p(correct) = (1 + tanh(alpha (r - w)))/2, because the iterate is constant from k = 1 on. With alpha = 2, r = 3 and w = 2, this is 0.982. The parent's union-find sets its sticky flag at the first conflict and returns 0.5 on every later query.
capabilities.task: Majority under conflicting repeats (where union-find freezes)

capabilities.prediction: In any consistent context, adding a consistent demonstration on an already connected pair (a,b) strictly increases |H^(K)_ab|. This change leaves the union-find quotient, and every union-find answer, unchanged. The toy program prints a concrete case: chain 0-1-2 versus chain 0-1-2 plus edge (0,2).
capabilities.task: Graded confidence from path redundancy

capabilities.prediction: Use the pretraining distribution of mechanism.learning: d = 32, 96 demonstrations, all before the queries, on uniformly random pairs, each parity flipped with probability 0.1. Queries are on uniformly random connected pairs, and theta is pretrained as specified. On fresh contexts, mean sign accuracy is at least 0.80, with ties counted as 0.5. Baseline: Z2-labeled union-find with a sticky flag, which outputs 0.5 on every query once any DEMO has contradicted its stored parity. A spanning forest on 32 sites has at most 31 edges, so at least 65 of the 96 DEMOs close a cycle or repeat a pair. Each such edge, given the past, is consistent with probability at most 0.9, since its own flip is independent. The flag is therefore unset before the first query with probability at most 0.9^65 < 0.0011. The baseline's expected accuracy is then at most 0.5 + 0.5 * 0.0011 < 0.501.
capabilities.task: Noisy random relational graphs

complexity.constants_notes: All three bounds are worst case. A DEMO token costs O(1), two additions. Only an ASK token triggers the K = ceil(log2 d) + 2 dense d x d matrix products of update[2], so the per-token worst case is O(d^3 log d). The total O(n d^3 log d) is the worst case, reached when ASK tokens follow changes of E throughout the sequence. With the caching rule (reuse H^(K) while E is unchanged) the same bound tightens to n + m d^3 log d up to constants, where m <= n is the number of ASK tokens that follow a change of E. In the pretraining protocol, all DEMOs precede all ASKs, so m = 1. Memory is the d x d table E plus one working matrix, independent of n. Capacity is d sites. The table stores signed multiplicities of up to d(d-1)/2 site pairs. It is not a general associative store.

sample_efficiency.mechanism: Gauge covariance plus monotone repeated squaring inside the fixed-depth Picard solve. Every pair connected by demonstrations receives a strictly nonzero entry of H^(K) whose sign is the product of the latent signs.

prediction.metric: Sign accuracy of H^(K) on the three undemonstrated unordered pairs among four sites after demonstrations on edges (0,1), (1,2), (2,3)
prediction.statement: Here d = 4, so K = ceil(log2 4) + 2 = 4, and the maximum distance 3 is at most 2^(K-1) = 8. For every one of the 16 noiseless latent assignments and for every alpha, beta > 0, the predicted bit on pairs (0,2), (0,3) and (1,3) is correct. No pretraining is needed for this claim.

card.core_idea: Answer a relational query by running K = ceil(log2 d) + 2 Picard steps of a learned Ornstein-Zernike-style closure equation H = tanh(alpha E + beta offdiag(H H)) over the in-context evidence graph, so that signed relations compose through chains by matrix squaring and saturate instead of shrinking.

extensions.description: Replace tanh(alpha e + beta gamma) with f_theta(e, gamma) = (g_theta(e, gamma) - g_theta(-e, -gamma))/2, clipped to (-1,1), for a small MLP g_theta. The odd symmetrization keeps gauge covariance. Monotonicity in (e, gamma) is guaranteed only if g_theta is constrained to be monotone.
extensions.name: Odd MLP closure

extensions.description: Track the direct correlation C separately instead of approximating C by H, with Gamma = M ⊙ (C H), H = M ⊙ f(E, Gamma) and C = H - Gamma. This is closer to the source, but the monotonicity proof is lost.

equations.plain: Gamma = M*(C@H); H = M*tanh(alpha*E + beta*Gamma); C = H - Gamma; iterate K times.

extensions.name: Full Ornstein-Zernike split

extensions.description: Replace the fixed depth K with Picard iteration until max |H^(k) - H^(k-1)| < tol. On consistent contexts the iterates converge monotonically to the least fixed point. On inconsistent contexts convergence is not guaranteed, so the core keeps the fixed-depth readout.
extensions.name: Solve to convergence

falsifiers: Suppose a consistent demonstration graph on d sites, with K = ceil(log2 d) + 2 and alpha, beta > 0, gives some connected pair the wrong sign in H^(K), or a probability of exactly 0.5. That refutes the gauge-covariance and repeated-squaring argument.

A disconnected pair whose probability differs from exactly 0.5 refutes the support argument for H^(K). So does an added consistent demonstration on an already connected pair that fails to raise |H^(K)_ab| strictly, which refutes the monotonicity argument.

On the noisy random-graph benchmark (d = 32, 96 demonstrations before the queries, flip probability 0.1, theta pretrained as in mechanism.learning), mean sign accuracy below 0.80 refutes the noise-robustness claim.

Fit a resolvent readout with an elementwise squash, p = (1 - tanh(g [(lambda I - E)^{-1}]_ab))/2, with (lambda, g) fit on that benchmark. If it matches this card's probabilities within 0.01 on every query, the claimed non-reduction to the in-context least-squares family is refuted in practice.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: Union-find answers depend only on the quotient (component partition and relative parity), and a contradiction freezes them. Here the answer is a graded function of multiplicities, path counts and path lengths. It is computed by a fixed-depth nonlinear solve over the whole evidence table, and it aggregates conflicting evidence.
known_relatives.name: Z2-labeled union-find (the parent's reduction)
known_relatives.relation: It solves the same noiseless XOR-pair protocol and gives the same signs on consistent contexts.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: A linear-attention or lookup readout returns E_ab, which is 0 for every undemonstrated pair. The readout here is the K-th Picard iterate of a transcendental matrix equation that is quadratic in H and depends on all of E. For an undemonstrated pair it returns a value that depends on every path. That value is neither a linear read S^T phi(q) nor an elementwise function of one.
known_relatives.name: Linear attention / exact-match count table over one-hot pair keys
known_relatives.relation: The persistent state E is an additive sum of one-hot signed writes, which is an n-gram-like count table. This is conceded.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: The resolvent is rational in E and adds walk contributions linearly. Its magnitudes shrink as eps^L with distance L, or blow up near criticality. Here the contributions pass through a saturating closure at every squaring step, so long chains do not shrink and each chain term is bounded by 1.
known_relatives.name: MesaNet / in-context least squares and resolvent (walk-sum) readouts
known_relatives.relation: A readout [(lambda I - E)^{-1}]_ab also propagates signed evidence along walks and gets signs right on consistent graphs.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: The core works in the graded, signed, learned regime. The answer depends on evidence counts and path redundancy, and alpha and beta are fit by pretraining. The boolean limit discards exactly the information that the noisy and graded claims test.
known_relatives.name: Transitive closure by repeated boolean matrix squaring
known_relatives.relation: With boolean signs and alpha, beta -> infinity, the iteration becomes R <- E or R R, which is classical closure.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: BP passes per-edge messages, and mean-field solves for site magnetizations. Here the solve runs directly on the all-pairs correlation matrix through the Ornstein-Zernike split, with a matrix-product chain term, and it is truncated at a fixed depth K tied to graph diameter by repeated squaring. It is not a token-driven recurrence: the iteration runs over solver steps on the state-dependent operator H H.
known_relatives.name: Mean-field / belief-propagation inference on a pairwise Ising model; deep equilibrium models
known_relatives.relation: These are related self-consistent inference schemes on graphs, and an equilibrium layer solved by iteration.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: Those filters are linear polynomials in a fixed Laplacian and shrink signals toward low frequency. Here the graph is built from the context, and propagation is nonlinear and saturating.
known_relatives.name: Graph reservoirs with spectral filters (MRGNN, Fairing filter, 2507.12963)
known_relatives.relation: Both propagate signals over a graph with a fixed, non-learned propagation law and fit few parameters.

learning.description: Only theta = (a0, b0) is learned, with alpha = softplus(a0) and beta = softplus(b0). The closure form, the depth K and the protocol are fixed. The pretraining distribution is also the benchmark distribution of claims.capabilities[3]. Set d = 32, so K = 7. Draw latent bits z in {0,1}^d uniformly. Draw 96 DEMO tokens on unordered pairs {a,b}, a != b, chosen uniformly with replacement. The order (a,b) is a fair coin. The parity is s = z_a XOR z_b, flipped independently with probability 0.1. All 96 DEMO tokens come first. Then come 32 queries, each on a uniformly random pair that is connected in the demonstration graph. Each query appears as ASK(a,b) followed by its correct answer token. Answer tokens do not change E. Optimization: 20,000 contexts, Adam with learning rate 0.01, batch 64, initialization a0 = b0 = 0. Gradients are backpropagated through the K unrolled iterations of update[2].

equations.latex: \mathcal L(\theta)=-\sum_{t:\,x_t=\operatorname{ASK}(a,b)}\log p_t\bigl(y^{*}_t\bigr),\qquad y^{*}_t=\begin{cases}y_0 & z_a=z_b\\ y_1 & z_a\ne z_b\end{cases}
equations.name: Pretraining loss
equations.plain: y*_t is the correct answer token at an ASK(a,b) position: y_0 if the latent bits satisfy z[a] == z[b], else y_1. It is the answer token that follows the ASK in the training context. The loss is the sum of -log p_t(y*_t) over ASK positions, where p_t is the readout distribution computed from H^(K). Minimize over (a0, b0) by gradient descent through the K unrolled iterations.

learning.few_shot_argument: All statements concern the readout H^(K) and hold for every alpha, beta > 0. (0) Support. For any E, consistent or not, H^(k)_ab = 0 at every k whenever a and b lie in different connected components of the demonstration graph. By induction, H^(k-1) is zero across components, so (H H)_ab is zero there and E_ab = 0. Disconnected pairs therefore get exactly 0.5. (1) Gauge covariance. Take a consistent context with latent signs z in {+1,-1}^d, and let D = diag(z). Then E = D|E|D, and every iterate satisfies H^(k) = D A^(k) D, where A^(k) is the k-th iterate for the all-positive problem |E|. This holds because tanh is odd, D commutes with the mask M, and (D H D)(D H D) = D (H H) D. So the sign of H^(K)_ab is exactly z_a z_b whenever A^(K)_ab > 0. (2) Monotonicity. On |E| >= 0 the map is entrywise monotone and starts at 0, so A^(k) is entrywise nondecreasing, nonnegative and bounded by 1. It therefore converges to the least fixed point A*, and A^(K) <= A* entrywise. The truncated readout is a lower bound of A* with the same support and signs. (3) Repeated squaring. After iteration 1, every demonstrated pair has A_ab = tanh(alpha|E_ab|) > 0. Suppose all pairs at graph distance <= 2^(k-1) are positive after iteration k. Take a pair (a,c) at distance <= 2^k. It has a midpoint b with both halves at distance <= 2^(k-1), so the term A_ab A_bc is > 0 and all other terms are >= 0. The pair is therefore positive after iteration k+1. Since 2^(K-1) >= 2d > d-1, K iterations cover every connected pair. Consequences: a spanning tree of demonstrations on any set of sites fixes the sign of every pair among them. A single bridge between two internally connected components makes every cross pair connected, at distance at most d-1, so every cross pair gets the correct sign in H^(K). (4) Graded answers. An extra consistent demonstration on a connected pair (a,b) raises alpha|E_ab|. By monotonicity of every iterate in |E|, it strictly raises A^(K)_ab, because A^(K)_ab = tanh(alpha|E_ab| + beta G_ab) with G_ab nondecreasing. (5) Conflict. A conflicting demonstration subtracts from E instead of freezing the learner. For an isolated pair, (H H)_ab = 0 at every iterate, so H^(k)_ab = tanh(alpha E_ab) for all k >= 1, exactly.

readout.latex: x_t=\operatorname{ASK}(a,b):\ h=H^{(K)}_{ab}\ (a\ne b),\ h=1\ (a=b);\quad p_t(y_1)=\tfrac{1-h}{2},\ p_t(y_0)=\tfrac{1+h}{2},\ p_t(\text{other})=0;\qquad \text{non-ASK } x_t:\ p_t(y_0)=p_t(y_1)=\tfrac12.
readout.name: Relational posterior from the K-th iterate
readout.plain: p_t is the next-token distribution over the V token ids. After ASK(a,b), let h = H^(K)[a,b] (the K-th iterate of update[2]) if a != b, and h = 1 if a == b. Put probability (1-h)/2 on id 3*d*d+1 (y_1), (1+h)/2 on id 3*d*d (y_0), and zero on every other id (stored sparsely). At non-ASK positions, put 0.5 on y_0 and 0.5 on y_1.

state.meaning: d >= 2 is the number of sites, indexed 0..d-1. n is the context length, and the size of E never depends on n. E starts at zero. E[a,b] = (number of DEMO(a,b,0) and DEMO(b,a,0) tokens) minus (number of DEMO(a,b,1) and DEMO(b,a,1) tokens). It plays the role of the pair potential. It is the only persistent state, and only update[1] (Evidence write) changes it. update[0] (Token decoding) decodes the token vocabulary of size V = 3*d*d + 2.
state.name: E

state.meaning: Working matrix of the truncated closure solve in update[2]. It is reset to zero at each solve and holds H^(k) after iteration k, for k = 1..K, where K = ceil(log2 d) + 2. M = 1 - I is the d x d off-diagonal mask, so H has zero diagonal. ⊙ is the elementwise product, and tanh acts elementwise. The readout uses only H^(K). H^(K)[a,b] in (-1,1) is the inferred signed correlation of the bits at sites a and b: near +1 means same, near -1 means different, and exactly 0 means there is no evidence path.
state.name: H
state.type: Real symmetric matrix (solver iterate, total pair correlation)

state.meaning: alpha weights the direct evidence and beta weights the indirect (chain) correlation inside the closure tanh(alpha e + beta gamma). They are parameterized as alpha = softplus(a0) and beta = softplus(b0) and fit by the pretraining in mechanism.learning. Every provable claim holds for every alpha, beta > 0.
state.name: theta

update.latex: \text{id}<2d^2:\ \operatorname{DEMO}(a,b,s),\ a=\lfloor \text{id}/2d\rfloor,\ b=\lfloor \text{id}/2\rfloor \bmod d,\ s=\text{id}\bmod 2;\quad 2d^2\le\text{id}<3d^2:\ \operatorname{ASK}(a,b),\ j=\text{id}-2d^2,\ a=\lfloor j/d\rfloor,\ b=j\bmod d;\quad \text{id}=3d^2:\ y_0;\quad \text{id}=3d^2+1:\ y_1.
update.name: Token decoding
update.plain: Given a token id in 0..3*d*d+1: if id < 2*d*d, it is DEMO(a,b,s) with a = id // (2*d), b = (id // 2) % d, s = id % 2. Else if id < 3*d*d, it is ASK(a,b) with j = id - 2*d*d, a = j // d, b = j % d. id == 3*d*d is answer token y_0 (bit 0, 'same'). id == 3*d*d+1 is answer token y_1 (bit 1, 'different').

update.latex: x_t=\operatorname{DEMO}(a,b,s),\ a\ne b:\quad \sigma=1-2s,\qquad E_{ab}\leftarrow E_{ab}+\sigma,\quad E_{ba}\leftarrow E_{ba}+\sigma.
update.name: Evidence write
update.plain: x_t is the decoded token at position t. On DEMO(a,b,s) with a != b, set sigma = 1 - 2*s (+1 means same bit, -1 means different bit), and add sigma to E[a,b] and to E[b,a]. DEMO(a,a,s), ASK and answer tokens leave E unchanged.

update.latex: H^{(0)}=0,\qquad H^{(k)}=M\odot\tanh\!\Bigl(\alpha E+\beta\, M\odot\bigl(H^{(k-1)}H^{(k-1)}\bigr)\Bigr),\quad k=1,\dots,K,\qquad K=\lceil\log_2 d\rceil+2.
update.name: Truncated closure solve (K Picard steps of the Ornstein-Zernike split with learned closure)
update.plain: At an ASK token, start from H = zeros(d,d). Repeat exactly K = ceil(log2 d) + 2 times: G = M * (H @ H), the indirect correlation through one intermediate site, then H = M * tanh(alpha*E + beta*G). The output is H^(K), the K-th iterate. There is no convergence test. The depth is fixed and the readout is defined as H^(K) whether or not the iteration has converged. On consistent contexts the iterates are monotone and H^(K) is a lower bound, in magnitude, of the least fixed point, with the same signs and support. On inconsistent contexts convergence is not claimed, and only H^(K) is used. The result can be cached until E changes.

non_reduction_argument.broken_invariant: The mapping relies on the parent's answers being a function of an idempotent quotient state, the partition plus the relative parity, maintained by a textbook closure algorithm. That algorithm discards every redundant consistent edge, and the first contradiction collapses all answers to 0.5. In this card, update[1] (Evidence write) keeps signed multiplicities. The readout is H^(K), the K-th Picard iterate of H = M ⊙ tanh(alpha E + beta M ⊙ (H H)) computed by update[2]. It depends on evidence counts, on the number and length of independent paths, and on conflicting evidence. Two contexts with identical union-find states, chain 0-1-2 with and without edge (0,2), give different H^(K)_02 (toy output confidence_rises_with_redundant_path = true). Contexts that union-find maps to 'contradiction' get majority answers (toy p_one_noisy_majority = 0.018 rather than 0.5).
non_reduction_argument.known_family: other_known: Z2-labeled (parity) union-find with union by size and a sticky consistency flag
non_reduction_argument.why_unrepairable: No relabeling of parent pointers, labels and sizes can reproduce H^(K), because H^(K) is not a function of the quotient: the toy exhibits two contexts with the same quotient and different outputs. Repair 1, union-find with per-edge counts, still discards cycle-closing edges. Keeping those edges and aggregating evidence over all paths with saturation is exactly the solve in update[2]. Repair 2 is the strongest known-family repair. It keeps E as a linear-attention or count-table state and reads it with the in-context least-squares/resolvent form y = [(lambda I - E)^{-1}]_ab, followed by an elementwise squash. This readout is a rational function of E with linearly additive walk contributions. H^(K), by contrast, is a K-fold composition of elementwise tanh and matrix squaring. To match it, the resolvent would have to apply saturation after every composition step, a nonpolynomial function of every partial path sum, and no choice of (lambda, g) or lifted linear state supplies that. Repair 3 views the solve as an RNN or DEQ. It fails because the iteration is quadratic in H (operator H H, not a fixed W), runs over solver steps rather than tokens, and is truncated at a depth set by repeated squaring rather than solved to equilibrium. Repair 4, boolean transitive closure, matches only in the limit alpha, beta -> infinity, where the graded and noisy claims fail.

references.why: Source of the transplanted object: the Ornstein-Zernike decomposition of total correlation into direct and indirect (chain) parts, closed by a closure relation. The perspective's proposal to learn closures with machine learning motivates learning the closure parameters (alpha, beta). The discretization to context sites, the h*h approximation of the chain term, the odd tanh closure and the fixed-depth truncation are this card's own changes.

Its spectral analysis of graph reservoirs shows that repeated linear Laplacian filtering shrinks signals toward low-frequency components (over-smoothing), and that a pass-band filter is needed to smooth without shrinkage. This motivated a saturating rather than linear propagation law, so that relations survive long chains. The Fairing algorithm itself is not used.

source_transplant.change: Particles become the d discrete sites named in the context, and the pair potential u becomes the signed demonstration count E. The spatial convolution c*h becomes a matrix product over intermediate sites. The indirect correlation gamma = rho c*h is approximated at lowest order by H H (taking c ~ h), and rho is absorbed into beta. The HNC closure h = exp(-u + gamma) - 1 is replaced by a learned odd closure h = tanh(alpha e + beta gamma). This closure commutes with sign flips, so signed relations compose by multiplication. Instead of solving to convergence, the equation is run for exactly K = ceil(log2 d) + 2 Picard steps from h = 0, and the K-th iterate is the readout. On consistent contexts this iterate is a monotone lower bound of the least fixed point, with the same signs and support. One design choice comes from 2507.12963, which shows that repeated Laplacian filtering on a graph reservoir shrinks signals toward low frequency. Propagation here therefore uses a saturating closure rather than a linear diffusion or resolvent, so evidence passes along long chains without shrinking.
source_transplant.object: The Ornstein-Zernike relation h = c + rho c*h (total correlation = direct correlation + indirect correlation through chains of intermediate particles), closed by a closure relation h = F(u, gamma) with gamma = h - c (HNC/PY-type closures, and the machine-learned closures the perspective proposes)

card.summary: This is a small, specialized in-context learner for binary relational rules. It uses the same DEMO/ASK protocol as its parent, but it keeps no quotient or union-find structure. A demonstration only adds a signed count to a pair-evidence table E over d sites. At a query, the learner runs a fixed number K = ceil(log2 d) + 2 of Picard iterations, starting from H = 0, on a self-consistent equation from liquid-state theory for the full matrix of pair correlations H. The readout is that K-th iterate H^(K): a truncated, fixed-depth computation, not the converged solution. The Ornstein-Zernike split writes total correlation as direct plus indirect correlation. The indirect part is approximated by chains through one intermediate site (H H). A learned odd closure, tanh(alpha e + beta gamma), maps direct evidence e and indirect correlation gamma to total correlation. Each iteration doubles the path length that propagation reaches, so K iterations reach every connected pair. The equations have a sign-gauge covariance. On consistent contexts this gives provably correct parities on every connected pair and exactly 0.5 on disconnected pairs. On consistent contexts the iterates also rise monotonically toward the least fixed point. Unlike union-find, the answer is graded. It rises with redundant independent paths, takes the majority under conflicting repeats, and does not freeze after a contradiction. None of these quantities is a function of the partition-plus-parity quotient that union-find stores.
card.title: Ornstein-Zernike Relation Closure: in-context relations as a fixed-depth Picard solve of a learned correlation-closure equation

toy_example.description: Five sites with alpha = beta = 2 and K = 5. The readout is the 5th Picard iterate. (1) Three chain demonstrations: queries (0,2), (0,3) and (1,3) get the correct predicted bits, and the disconnected pair (0,4) gets exactly 0.5. (2) Adding a consistent redundant edge (0,2) to the chain 0-1-2 strictly raises the confidence on (0,2), although union-find's state is unchanged. (3) An isolated pair demonstrated 3 times as same and 2 times as different gives majority probability (1 - tanh(2))/2 = 0.018 on bit 1, where union-find would freeze at 0.5. A tie gives exactly 0.5.

critic.difference_if_any: Only parameterization choices remain. The weights are tied across the K layers, and just two scalars are learned (alpha and beta, through softplus). The depth is set to ceil(log2 d)+2 so that repeated squaring covers diameter d-1. The odd activation gives sign equivariance and monotone iterates from 0. None of these changes the form of the update or the readout, and the closure-equation framing is a renaming. The learning rule is ordinary backprop through the unrolled layers on next-token NLL, so there is no learning-rule difference.
critic.mapping: The state and write rule are a count table over one-hot pair keys, which the card concedes is linear attention or an n-gram table. Each DEMO(a,b,s) adds sigma = 1-2s at key (a,b) and at (b,a), so E is the signed adjacency matrix of the in-context evidence graph. The readout is a weight-tied, single-channel 2-FWL / PPGN pair network (Maron et al. 2019, Provably Powerful Graph Networks) run on that adjacency. The same block appears as the triangle multiplicative update in AlphaFold2's pair stack and as the triangular composition of the Edge Transformer (Bergen et al. 2021). Symbol by symbol: (1) The PPGN pair feature tensor X^(l) in R^{d x d x c} becomes H^(k), with c = 1. (2) In the PPGN block X^(l+1) = m4([X^(0), m1(X^(l)) @ m2(X^(l))]), m1 and m2 are the identity, and the matrix product over the intermediate node index is H^(k-1) H^(k-1). m4(u, v) = tanh(alpha u + beta v) is a one-unit layer with input skip u = X^(0) = E. (3) The diagonal mask M is the usual zeroing of self-pair channels. (4) The depth is K = ceil(log2 d) + 2 tied layers. With H^(0) = 0, layer 1 is tanh(alpha E), which serves as the input embedding. (5) The readout p = (1 ± H_ab)/2 is a fixed head on one pair entry. The equations match line for line. That every pair at distance <= 2^(k-1) is reached after k layers is the standard repeated-squaring argument for transitive closure (Fischer-Meyer, Munro), and it is also why 2-FWL/PPGN layers double their reachable path length. Gauge covariance H -> D H D is the switching equivalence of signed graphs (Harary) carried through an odd activation. Any network built only from matrix products and odd elementwise maps has this property. Overall, the card is a linear-attention/count-table memory plus a looped, tied, two-parameter PPGN (soft signed transitive closure) readout computed at query time.
critic.textbook_why: The textbook object is the Ornstein-Zernike relation h = c + rho c*h, closed by HNC or PY (h = exp(-u+gamma) - 1) and solved to convergence. The card changes that construction in three ways: it sets c ≈ h so the chain term becomes H H, it replaces HNC with an odd closure tanh(alpha e + beta gamma), and it truncates at a fixed depth starting from h = 0. The resulting equations are no longer the source's construction.
critic.why: The escape argument holds against its stated target. update[1] keeps signed multiplicities, and the update[2] readout is not a function of the union-find quotient. I checked both toy cases. Adding (0,2) to the chain 0-1-2 raises A_02 from tanh(beta G) to tanh(2 + beta G). The isolated conflict gives tanh(2(3-2)) = 0.964, so p_one = 0.018. Union-find, including the per-edge-count repair, cannot reproduce these outputs. The argument also correctly rules out the resolvent repair, because the resolvent is rational in E and has no saturation between compositions. However, why_unrepairable never names the strongest repair. Its Repair 3 dismisses RNN/DEQ because the iteration is quadratic in H rather than built on a fixed W. That reasoning fails, because quadratic pair-composition layers of the form H <- f(E, H H) are exactly the PPGN / 2-FWL block, AlphaFold's triangle multiplicative update and the Edge Transformer's triangular update. Tying weights across a fixed depth is the standard looped or recurrent-depth variant of such networks. The closest repair is also the one that succeeds: a count-table memory read out by a tied, single-channel PPGN with input skip and tanh. Equivalently, it is soft signed transitive closure by repeated squaring, which the card itself concedes in the alpha, beta -> infinity limit. The capability claims follow directly from that construction: correct signs on connected pairs, exactly 0.5 on disconnected pairs, rising confidence with redundant paths, and majority voting on an isolated pair. This is a known pair-network readout on a known memory, renamed in liquid-state-physics terms. It would not surprise a researcher who knows GNNs, 2-WL networks or transitive closure.

prior_art.label: prior_art_undertested
prior_art.notes: Learned closures for the Ornstein-Zernike equation exist (W3160405605 learns a bridge-function closure from data; W4226337467 uses neural-network closures that reduce to HNC for hard spheres; W4391177851 uses physics-informed networks to solve OZ for bulk fluids). These cover the closure-learning ingredient in liquid-state physics, but none applies an OZ-style fixed-depth Picard solve to in-context binary relational sequence learning. W7138934227 tests a related claim, that transformers learn XOR-style rules beyond interpolation, at small scale on a cellular automaton, which is similar in task but not in mechanism. No found paper tests the card's claims: one-shot bridge inference, graded confidence from path redundancy, or the noisy random-graph benchmark at d=32. Those remain untested, so the label is undertested rather than tested. No result shows the central sign-correctness claim fails, so known_disproven does not apply. The card's non-reduction argument against union-find (parent not in results) and against resolvent readouts is not checked by any retrieved paper. The source paper 2311.05167 cited in the card does not appear in the search results and is not cited here. The card's own sign-correctness and monotonicity arguments are not evaluated against the literature.

capabilities.prediction: Accuracy = 1.000 with exact integer arithmetic, and zero facts are rejected. Any single error refutes the lemma. Every label's largest entry is at most 21^15, so it has at most 1 + 15 log2(21), about 66.9 bits.
capabilities.task: In-context transitive inference on random taxonomies with 500 nodes, depth <= 15 and at most 20 children per node. Facts arrive in a random admissible order (each parent placed before its children). There are 2000 queries: half positive (ancestor at distance >= 2) and half negative (siblings, cousins, reversed pairs).

capabilities.prediction: Accuracy = 1.000. The chain node at depth D has label exactly L^D = [[1,0],[D,1]], so its entries grow linearly in D, far below the general bound.
capabilities.task: Deep chains and depth extrapolation. A single chain of depth 1000 whose top node is the first top-level root. Each chain node is the first child of its parent, and distractor branches are attached to chain nodes only after the chain child's fact. Queries cover pairs up to 1000 levels apart.

capabilities.prediction: Accuracy = 1.000. A child's largest entry is at most (j + 2) <= 10001 times its parent's, so it has at most log2(10001), about 13.3, more bits. No branching limit is set in advance, unlike ping-pong constructions with a fixed generator count.
capabilities.task: Extreme branching: one parent with 10,000 children (child indices 0..9999), plus grandchildren under random children. 2000 queries, half positive, half negative (siblings and reversed pairs).

capabilities.prediction: All cross-hierarchy queries are answered 'no' (accuracy 1.000). The three roots get distinct codewords C(0), C(1), C(2) under rho, and no root's word is a prefix of another's.
capabilities.task: Forest in one context: three disjoint hierarchies with interleaved facts, and 600 cross-hierarchy queries.

capabilities.prediction: Accuracy = 0.500 exactly. Every second-parent fact is rejected by the admissibility gate, because its child is already labeled. Ancestors in the tree of accepted facts are a subset of DAG ancestors, so every query is answered 'no'. All 500 negatives are correct, and all 500 second-parent-only positives are wrong.
capabilities.task: Scope limit: DAGs (multiple inheritance). The DAG has 500 nodes, and 30% of non-root nodes have a second parent. Every parent is placed before its children, and the first parent fact for each child is accepted. The test set has 1000 queries with X != Y: 500 pairs where Y is an ancestor of X only through paths that use a second-parent edge, and 500 pairs where Y is not an ancestor of X in the DAG.

complexity.constants_notes: Definitions. D is the maximum depth of a node below the virtual root rho (rho has depth 0 and a top-level root has depth 1). For a node with path rho -> ... -> X, j_i is the child index used at level i (j_i = 0 for a first child). J is the largest child index used in the context, and beta = J + 2. Costs are in bit operations; time and total also include expected O(1) hash lookups per token. Bound: all entries are nonnegative, and every entry of M[Y] C(j) is at most (j + 2) times the largest entry of M[Y]. Hence the largest entry of M[X] is at most prod_i (j_i + 2) <= beta^D, with at most 1 + sum_i log2(j_i + 2) <= 1 + D log2(beta) bits. A fact costs one big-by-small 2x2 product, O(D log beta) bit operations. A query costs one big-by-big 2x2 product (8 multiplications, 4 additions, 4 sign tests), O((D log beta)^2) bit operations with schoolbook multiplication. Every query product is at most beta^(2D) in absolute value. So when D log2(beta) <= 31, all arithmetic fits in signed 64-bit words, and the per-token cost is O(1) word operations plus expected O(1) hash lookups. This is the sense in which the per-token cost is independent of n: n never enters, only D and beta do. Memory holds m <= n + 1 labels of O(D log beta) bits each. No optimality claim is made for this label length.

sample_efficiency.mechanism: One-write label composition, combined with unique factorization in SL(2,Z>=0) and the prefix code {U^j L}, makes every transitive ancestor relation a function of two labels, each written once.

prediction.metric: Minimum number of presentations per edge needed for accuracy 1.000 on a held-out query set. Setup: random trees with 500 nodes, depth D <= 15 and child index J <= 19 (at most 20 children per node). Each edge appears as one fact, in a uniformly random order subject to admissibility (each parent before its children). The held-out set has 2000 queries: 1000 positives (Y an ancestor of X at tree distance >= 2, so the pair never co-occurs in a fact) and 1000 negatives (X != Y, Y not an ancestor of X, drawn uniformly). Arithmetic uses exact arbitrary-precision integers. Results are averaged over 20 random trees.
prediction.statement: Showing each parent-child edge exactly once, in any admissible order, yields accuracy exactly 1.000 on all 2000 held-out queries for every one of the 20 trees. The minimum number of presentations per edge is therefore 1. No repetition and no worked examples of transitive inference are needed.

card.core_idea: Each symbol introduced in context as a child of an already-placed parent is labeled, in one multiplication, with an integer hyperbolic isometry M_X = M_parent * C(j) from the free monoid SL(2,Z>=0); ancestry between any two symbols, including pairs never shown together, is then exactly the nesting of their Farey geodesic half-planes, decided by one 2x2 integer product, M_Y^{-1} M_X, that has no negative entry exactly when Y is an ancestor-or-self of X; that product costs O(1) word operations whenever label entries fit in 64-bit words.

extensions.description: Replaces rejection of a fact X < Y when X is already a top-level root, which happens when facts arrive bottom-up. Each node stores a parent pointer and a relative label in SL(2,Z), and absolute labels are composed during find with path compression. Re-rooting X under Y replaces X's relative label by C(K[Y]) times the inverse of X's old root codeword. The cost is amortized near-constant per fact.

equations.plain: M_abs[X] = M_abs[par[X]] @ M_rel[X], compressed during find

extensions.name: Group-valued union-find for out-of-order facts

extensions.description: The continued-fraction expansion of the interval endpoint a/c recovers the U/L word of M[X], and with it the child-index path. The LCA of X and Y is the longest common codeword prefix, and its depth is the number of L letters in that prefix. Both are computed in O(D) by Euclid's algorithm.
extensions.name: Depth and lowest-common-ancestor readout

extensions.description: A small trained tagger maps natural-language spans (for example 'a robin is a kind of bird') to (X, '<', Y) and (X, '?', Y) events that feed the core. Only the tagger is gradient-trained, and the relational memory stays exact.
extensions.name: Learned fact parser

extensions.description: Instead of rejecting a second-parent fact, a node keeps one label per parent path. A query answers yes if any pair of labels passes the nesting test. Cost grows with the number of paths.
extensions.name: Multiple inheritance via label sets

falsifiers: On a fact stream with no rejected facts (admissible order, single inheritance), the exact-integer implementation returns any wrong answer to an ancestor query. That would refute the unique-factorization or prefix-code argument.
Some label has a largest entry above prod_i (j_i + 2) along its path, or a node at depth D on a first-child chain from the first top-level root has a label other than [[1,0],[D,1]].

Instrument the query readout with a counter of integer multiplications, additions and sign tests on matrix entries, excluding hash lookups. Use trees with D = 10 and child indices <= 4 (beta = 6, so D log2 beta = 25.9 <= 31 and every value fits in int64). Measure contexts of n = 10^3, 10^4, 10^5 and 10^6 tokens. The prediction is exactly 8 multiplications, 4 additions and 4 sign tests per query at every n. Any query whose count differs from this, at any n, refutes the n-independence claim.

Replace the prefix code by the non-prefix codeword set C'(0) = L, C'(j) = U^j for j >= 1. Every C'(j) still has determinant 1 and nonnegative entries, and every j is covered. Then build trees in which every internal node has at least 3 children, and ask 1000 sibling queries 'c2 ? c1', where c1 and c2 are the children with indices 1 and 2 of a common parent. The prediction is that these are answered 'yes' (wrongly), since M[c2] = M[c1] U. If accuracy stays at 1.000 on these queries, the prefix-code condition is not what makes the test exact.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: Those embeddings are gradient-fitted, approximate, offline and in floating point. Here the labels are exact integer isometries, written online in one step per fact, and the ancestry test is provably exact.
known_relatives.name: Poincare / hyperbolic prototype embeddings of hierarchies (e.g. 2209.05842)
known_relatives.relation: Same geometric principle: hierarchies are embedded in negatively curved space, and membership is decided geometrically.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: The contribution is to use this encoding as the in-context memory of a sequence learner, with a streaming parse-gate-write-read loop and an exact transitive readout from one 2x2 product, framed as horizon nesting in the hyperbolic plane. The encoding is not claimed as new mathematics.
known_relatives.name: Nested-interval / Farey-fraction tree encodings (database literature) and the Stern-Brocot tree
known_relatives.relation: The encoding itself, a tree node as a Farey interval, is known.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: The product is not applied to the previous step's state. It is applied to the stored label of the parent, selected by content. The state is a symbol-indexed table rather than one recurrent vector, and the readout compares two entries algebraically.
known_relatives.name: SSMs / linear attention (S_t = A_t S_{t-1} + B_t x_t), unitary or group-structured RNNs
known_relatives.relation: The write is a product of input-dependent matrices.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: There is no scan or softmax over the context. A transitive query that would need D retrieval hops, or D layers in a transformer, is answered by one 2x2 product, because the path is already composed into the label.
known_relatives.name: Key-value memory / attention retrieval
known_relatives.relation: The core stores per-symbol values and looks them up by key.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: Those encode one stack in a single real and need exact reals. This card encodes a whole tree, one exact-integer label per node, with arbitrary branching, and decides ancestry between any two nodes without popping.
known_relatives.name: Siegelmann-Sontag Cantor-set stack encodings / fractal RNN encodings
known_relatives.relation: Discrete nested structure is encoded in numbers via contracting maps.

learning.description: The core has no gradient-trained parameters. Learning is the in-context write rule, one 2x2 matrix product per accepted fact. C is fixed in closed form and eps is a smoothing constant. Learned components, such as a parser from natural text to facts or a model of non-relational tokens, are extensions.

equations.name: correctness lemma (tree of accepted facts)
equations.plain: For X, Y in dom(M): Y is an ancestor-or-self of X in the tree of accepted facts  iff  inverse(M[Y]) @ M[X] has all entries >= 0

learning.few_shot_argument: One presentation of each edge suffices, for algebraic reasons. (0) The admissibility gate guarantees that accepted facts form a forest under rho: X is new when attached, so it has no descendants yet and no cycle can form. (1) Associativity. The single write M[X] = M[Y] C(j) folds X's whole ancestor chain into X's label, so M[X] = C(j_1) C(j_2) ... C(j_D), the codewords along the path from rho. (2) Unique factorization. Every determinant-1 integer matrix with nonnegative entries is a unique word in U and L; this is the Stern-Brocot theorem, i.e. Euclid's algorithm. Distinct nodes have distinct paths, hence distinct words and distinct labels. R = M[Y]^{-1} M[X] is nonnegative iff M[X] = M[Y] W for some (possibly empty) U/L word W, iff Y's U/L word is a prefix of X's. (3) Prefix code. Every codeword has exactly one L, at its end. Y's word is empty (rho) or ends in L, so the prefix ends on a codeword boundary of X's path. It is therefore the word of an ancestor-or-self of X, and by distinctness that node is Y. Geometrically, X's horizon half-plane lies inside Y's. Every transitive pair is decided by two labels, each written once, and the decision is exact for pairs never shown together.

state.meaning: C(j) = U^j L = [[1+j, j],[1,1]] for child index j >= 0, where U = [[1,1],[0,1]] and L = [[1,0],[1,1]] are the Stern-Brocot generators. They freely generate the monoid SL(2,Z>=0) of determinant-1 integer 2x2 matrices with all entries >= 0. {U^j L : j >= 0} is a prefix code, because each word ends at its single L.
state.name: C

state.meaning: Horizon label of each introduced symbol. m <= n + 1 is the number of distinct symbols introduced by accepted facts so far, plus the virtual root rho with M[rho] = I. As a Moebius map, M[X] = [[a,b],[c,d]] sends the geodesic (0, inf) of the upper half-plane to the Farey geodesic (b/d, a/c).
state.name: M
state.type: hash table: symbol -> exact (arbitrary-precision) integer matrix in SL(2,Z>=0)

state.meaning: Number of children already attached to each symbol. This is the index j of the next child slot. K[rho] counts the top-level roots.
state.name: K

state.meaning: The last three tokens (x_{t-2}, x_{t-1}, x_t). Here x_t is the token at position t of a context of length n over a vocabulary of size V. V contains four reserved tokens: '<' (fact operator), '?' (query operator), 'yes' and 'no'. All other tokens are symbols.
state.name: buf

state.meaning: Smoothing mass 0 < eps < 1, spread uniformly over the V tokens so that the readout is a proper distribution. The default is 1e-3.
state.name: eps

update.name: parse (runs once per position t, after x_t enters buf)
update.plain: X, o, Y = buf. If X or Y is a reserved token, or o is neither '<' nor '?': no state change. If o == '<': run the admissibility gate. If o == '?': compute the readout and do not write.

update.latex: \mathrm{accept}(X<Y) \iff X \notin \mathrm{dom}(M) \;\wedge\; X \ne Y; \quad \text{rejected facts change no state}
update.name: admissibility gate (checkable rejection rule)
update.plain: if X in M or X == Y: reject (no state change at all, so no root is created for Y); else: run root creation, then attach. A stream is in admissible order iff no fact is rejected, i.e. every parent's own parent fact precedes every fact that names it as a parent. The correctness lemma is stated for the tree formed by accepted facts. Example: after 'mammal < animal', the fact 'animal < life' is rejected and 'life' stays unlabeled.

update.name: root creation (accepted facts only)

update.latex: j \leftarrow K[Y],\; M[X] \leftarrow M[Y]\,C(j),\; K[Y] \leftarrow j+1,\; K[X] \leftarrow 0
