update.name: Exact constraint update
update.plain:
Apply the first matching case, with x the query label and y the response label.

- If already rejected, stay rejected.
- With fewer than three anchors:
  - an input equal to some alpha_i must repeat beta_i, otherwise reject;
  - a new input whose output is already some beta_i is rejected;
  - a new input with a new output is appended as row r+1.
- With three anchors, keep the state if y = T_A(x); otherwise reject.

By sharp three-transitivity, U sets r = -1 exactly when the compatible set H_A becomes empty.

update.name: Per-token parser transition
update.plain: On a query token w, save it as s and switch to the response phase; the posterior does not change. On a response token w, apply U to (s, w), write the returned pair into the A and r fields, and return to the query phase.

references.why: Supplies the framing of communication as inference. Speaker and listener share a generative model, and observations update the inferred causes so as to suppress prediction error. The projective cause proposed here replaces those causes; it is not claimed to appear in this source.

Supplies variational free energy as an inference objective. Here its exact discrete minimizer becomes a uniform distribution over the compatible group transformations. The source does not supply the projective-group representation or the three-anchor guarantee.

source_transplant.change: Continuous latent causes and approximate perceptual updates are replaced by a discrete projective-group latent cause whose posterior coset is represented exactly. Generic surprise-reducing action is replaced by a query that maximizes the expected reduction of posterior entropy. The projective-group construction is proposed here and is not attributed to these papers.
source_transplant.object: Variational free energy minimization for a shared generative model of communication

card.summary: A small sequence learner with no trained parameters. It reads query symbols and response symbols that come from one unknown projective transformation over a finite field. It does not compress history into a numerical recurrent state, and it does not enumerate hypotheses. Instead it represents the exact posterior as a group coset fixed by at most three anchors. Three distinct demonstrations identify the transformation, so every symbol not yet seen can be predicted exactly. This is a deliberately narrow algebraic prototype, not a claim of general language competence. The hypothesis it is meant to carry over is that few-shot learning can come from eliminating the symmetries of a generative cause rather than from fitting token associations.
card.title: Projective-Coset Active Inference

toy_example.description: On the projective line with p = 5, the hidden map is z -> (2z+1)/(z+1), with projective handling of zero denominators and infinity. The active policy picks the smallest unanchored label in {0,1,2,3} and so requests inputs 0, 1 and 2. The program checks the ambiguous posterior before the third response, reconstructs the full map, and rejects a contradictory fourth response. In the code, anchors holds the (alpha_i, beta_i) rows, and frame(u1, u2, u3) is M(u_1,u_2,u_3).

critic.difference_if_any: Nothing beyond the choice of hypothesis class and its compact encoding. Because the class is sharply 3-transitive, the version space can be stored as at most three anchor pairs instead of an enumerated set. The update is plain consistency filtering and the readout is the textbook posterior predictive. There are no learned parameters, so there is no learning rule to differ. The hypothesis family (one PGL(2,p) map per episode) is hard-wired into the transition function, which is why the card itself admits it cannot hold several bindings or several maps.
critic.mapping:
The card is the candidate-elimination (version-space) algorithm, with the Bayes-optimal posterior predictive, for the hypothesis class G = PGL(2,p) acting on P^1(F_p). It is packaged as a hand-coded finite-state transducer over the token stream.

(1) Hypothesis space: H = PGL(2,p) with a uniform prior pi. H_A is the version space, meaning the hypotheses consistent with all labeled examples so far.

(2) State: (A, r) is a compressed boundary representation of the version space. Sharp 3-transitivity means the set of hypotheses consistent with r <= 3 distinct pairs is exactly the coset determined by those pairs, so storing the pairs stores H_A.

(3) Update: U(A,r,x,y) is the candidate-elimination step with an indicator likelihood 1[g(x)=y]. Its cases are:
- keep a consistent duplicate;
- collapse to the empty version space (r = -1) when a pair breaks injectivity or functionality;
- append a new constraint;
- at r = 3, test the example against the unique remaining hypothesis.

(4) Reconstruction: T_A = M(beta)^{-1} M(alpha) is the classical three-point Möbius interpolation, i.e. the cross-ratio normal form. Each frame matrix M(u1,u2,u3) sends (u1,u2,u3) to (infinity,0,1).

(5) Response readout: P_next on response tokens is the Bayes posterior predictive under the uniform prior on H_A.
- r = 3: a point mass at T_A(s).
- s anchored: a point mass at beta_i.
- s unanchored, r < 3: uniform over the V-r unused outputs, because the coset acts regularly on them.
- empty version space: uniform fallback.

(6) Free-energy equation: KL(q||pi) - E_q log 1[g in H_A] is minimized by the exact posterior. This is the standard identity that variational inference with an unrestricted q recovers Bayes' rule, so the free-energy layer adds no mechanism.

(7) Active policy: a_star is a membership query in the Angluin sense, or equivalently a query-by-committee query. Every unanchored point has equal information gain, so the policy reduces to 'query any unqueried point', with a fixed tie-break.

(8) Sequence-model form: the parser (phi, s) together with (A, r) is a finite-state machine with a fixed, non-learned transition and readout.
critic.textbook_why: The cited source object is variational free-energy inference in active-inference models of communication, which uses continuous latent causes and approximate predictive-coding updates. The card changes this construction in its equations: it substitutes a discrete PGL(2,p) latent cause with an indicator likelihood, and it uses exact posterior conditioning instead of approximate updates. So it is not that construction applied unmodified. The parts it puts in are themselves textbook constructions: three-point Möbius reconstruction (cross-ratio frames) and version-space or Bayes conditioning, used without change.
critic.why:
The card's own known_relatives concede that the posterior is a noiseless version space and that the three-anchor guarantee is the standard sharp 3-transitivity theorem. The equations confirm it:
- U is candidate elimination.
- T_A is three-point Möbius interpolation via frame matrices.
- The readout is the uniform posterior predictive.
- The active policy is a trivial membership query.

The free-energy framing collapses to exact Bayes, since the minimizer of KL(q||pi) restricted to H_A is the conditional prior. The card is not a renamed RNN, SSM or linear attention. That is only because it is not a learned sequence architecture at all: it is a hand-coded finite-state learner for one fixed algebraic hypothesis class.

The exact few-shot results follow directly from building the true generative group into the transition function. Researchers who know version spaces, exact learning with queries, or projective geometry would find nothing surprising here. Moving a known mechanism into a token-stream interface is a transplant, not a new mechanism. The prior-art classifier likewise found the group-theoretic core and the active-query component standard.

prior_art.notes: The group-theoretic core is standard: PGL(2,p) is sharply 3-transitive on the projective line, so three distinct anchors fix one map, and |PGL(2,101)| = 1,030,200 with V-2 compatible maps after two anchors. The 3-transitivity papers (W3092974681, W2055311656) supply this background but do not address learning. Active query selection that reduces hypothesis ambiguity is addressed in the active-learning literature (W20801799, W2134948265, W2743911451), which tests similar claims at small scale. None of the retrieved work tests exact few-shot identification and next-token prediction for a sequence learner with this bounded state, so the sequence-learning capability is undertested. No retrieved paper refutes the central claims; I checked the counting and the 3-anchor identification claims and found them consistent. Several search results are unrelated (e.g., W4391751021, W7126168518) and were not cited.

In every one of the 4 possible positions of the exception in the order:
- accuracy on the exception is at least 0.85;
- accuracy on the unseen items is at least 0.8.

The exception key keeps all k units and outranks the schema key, which has k' < k units. A store without consolidation (rule b disabled) scores at most 0.1 on the unseen items.

capabilities.prediction:
Each surprising token inserts one entry, giving 2K entries. Consolidation almost never fires, because random residuals are about 1.4 apart, well above tau. Recall therefore follows LRU survival:
- accuracy is at least 0.95 for 2K <= B;
- for 2K > B, accuracy is within 0.05 of B/(2K).

At every K, the largest and smallest accuracies across d in {16, 64, 256} differ by at most 0.03, with 1000 sequences per setting.

complexity.constants_notes: The subset test K_j ⊆ kappa_t costs O(k) per entry with bitsets, so a read or a consolidation scan is O(B k). An inverted index from code units to entries would reduce this to the entries that touch kappa_t, but the bound uses the plain scan. The encoder (w d^2), expansion (N d) and readout (V d) costs match a small softmax model. None of these depend on n. Training adds O(Omega N) per token for the code loss and nothing at inference. There is no n^2 term and no search over past tokens. B is a fixed hyperparameter, for example 512.
complexity.time_per_token: O(B k + d (N + V + w d))
complexity.total_sequence: O(n (B k + d (N + V + w d)))

sample_efficiency.mechanism: Transfer appears after exactly two agreeing demonstrations, because the intersection of two codes is the first point at which item units leave the key. A single exact recurrence binds without any training, because the recalled residual cancels the cortical prediction exactly. Gradient training is needed only for two things: to make the cortex equivariant (equal residuals for the same rule), and to separate rule-context units from item units in P.

prediction.metric: Accuracy on held-out items (never shown in the sequence) on the offset-rule task 'x -> x+c', with items 0..63 and offset c drawn per sequence. The model is pretrained on offsets 1..8 and tested on held-out offsets 9 and 10, with d = 64, N = 256, k = 8, m = 2, B = 512, w = 2, tau = 0.5. Accuracy is measured after exactly 2 demonstrations, and separately after exactly 1.
prediction.statement: After 2 demonstrations, held-out-item accuracy is at least 0.8 on held-out offsets. After 1 demonstration it is at most 0.1, because the single key still contains item units and so does not fire on new items. The jump from 1 to 2 demonstrations is at least 0.6. With 4 demonstrations, accuracy differs from the 2-demonstration accuracy by at most 0.05, because demonstrations 3 and 4 hit the schema and are not surprising.

card.core_idea: A fast store holds (sparse key, cortical residual) episodes; when a surprising new episode carries a residual that a stored episode already predicts, the two consolidate into one entry whose key is the intersection of their sparse codes, and a read returns the residual of the most specific stored key contained in the current code, so two demonstrations of a rule produce a schema that applies to unseen items while a once-shown exception stays specific.

extensions.description: When rule (b) fires, also average the residual over the consolidated episodes using a count c_j, so that noisy rules sharpen with more shots.

In the rule-plus-exception task, either of these happens: exception accuracy falls below 0.85 while unseen-item accuracy stays at or above 0.8, or unseen-item accuracy falls below 0.8 while exception accuracy stays at or above 0.85. Either would refute specificity-ordered retrieval as the way schema and exception coexist.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: In the delta rule, a stored value sits at the address phi(k_t), which is computed from its own token and never changes afterwards; a read is S^T phi(q). Here a later write moves an existing value to a new address K_j ∩ kappa_t. Whether and where it moves depends on comparing the stored value rho_j with the new residual. A read is a max over the subset lattice of stored keys, not a linear functional of the state.

learning.description:
The slow parameters E, U, W_o and P are trained across many sequences by gradient descent. The hard store is used in the forward pass.

All discrete decisions of the store are constants in the backward pass. These are: which entries exist, their keys K_j (including any shrinking by rule (b)), which entry wins a read, and which rule fires on a write. No gradient flows through a key or through a key change.

Each stored residual is kept as a differentiable function of the parameters. It equals the residual of the episode that last set it: rho_j = e_{x_{r+1}} - z_r, where r is the step at which the entry was inserted by rule (c) or last overwritten by rule (a). Consolidation by rule (b) leaves rho_j, and therefore its gradient path, unchanged.

When entry j wins a read at step t, the next-token loss at t sends gradient into E, U and W_o through two paths: the current z_t and that stored rho_j, that is, through e_{x_{r+1}} and z_r at the creation step r.

P receives no gradient from the next-token loss, because TopK is not differentiable. It is trained only by an auxiliary code-overlap loss over a training-only window of Omega earlier positions. The loss pushes the soft codes of two positions to overlap when their episode residuals agree within tau, and to be disjoint when they do not. As a result, units shared by same-residual contexts come to encode the rule context, and units that differ encode item identity. That is the geometry intersection needs.

No parameter changes at inference; only H changes within a sequence.

equations.plain: L = sum_t -log p_t(x_{t+1}) + lambda * sum_t Lcode_t

learning.few_shot_argument:
The mechanism is consolidation by code intersection, triggered by residual agreement.

(1) One shot binds. A surprising episode (context c, next y) inserts an entry with key kappa(c) and residual e_y - z(c). A later context c' with the same code finds the entry, because kappa(c) is a subset of kappa(c'). It reads h = z(c') + e_y - z(c) = e_y. With w = 1 at random initialization, distinct cues get distinct k-sets, and a k-set contains another k-set only if they are equal. So binding needs no training.

(2) Two shots make a rule. Take demonstrations 'a -> a+c' and 'b -> b+c'. If the cortex is equivariant, they have equal residuals, since both translate by c. Their codes share the rule-context units R but differ in the item units. The second demonstration is surprising: the first key contains item-a units that are absent from the second code, so there is no hit. The residual agrees within tau, so rule (b) shrinks the key to R. Every later code at that context contains R, so the correction applies to every new item.

(3) Exceptions survive. An exception item shown once has a residual that disagrees with the schema, so it is inserted with its full k-unit key. That key is more specific than R, so it wins whenever its item recurs.

One demonstration therefore gives binding but not transfer, and two agreeing demonstrations give transfer. This step from one to two is the core's signature prediction.

readout.name: nearest-embedding softmax
readout.plain: logits[v] = -beta * sum((E[v] - h_t)**2); p_t = softmax(logits) over the V tokens

state.meaning: Token embeddings. Row e_v is the embedding of token v. V is the vocabulary size and d is the model width. Positions before the start of the sequence use the zero vector.
state.name: E

state.meaning: Cortical encoder taps over the last w tokens. They are combined through a fixed elementwise nonlinearity phi (GELU in experiments, identity in the toy) to give the cortical state u_t in R^d.
state.name: U

state.meaning: Cortical prediction map. z_t = W_o u_t is the slow system's prediction of the embedding of the next token.
state.name: W_o

state.meaning: Expansion projection onto N code units. The set of indices of the k largest entries of P u_t is the sparse code kappa_t, a subset of {0..N-1} of size k.
state.name: P

state.meaning:
Hippocampal notebook, reset to empty at the start of each sequence. Entry j has three parts:
- K_j is a variable-size set of code-unit indices. It starts as a full code kappa_t and can only shrink, by intersection.
- rho_j in R^d is a stored cortical residual.
- s_j is the integer time step of the entry's last use.

The number of entries and the key sizes are decided by the data.
state.name: H
state.type: fast episodic store: a list of at most B entries (K_j, rho_j, s_j)

state.meaning:
Five hyperparameters:
- k is the number of active code units.
- B is the maximum number of entries.
- m >= 1 is the minimum overlap |K_j ∩ kappa_t| needed to consolidate.
- tau is the surprise and residual-agreement threshold, a Euclidean distance in embedding space.
- beta is the inverse temperature of the readout.
state.name: theta_h

update.name: cortical state
update.plain: Step 1 of token t: u_t = phi(sum over j=0..w-1 of U[j] @ E[x_{t-j}]), with E[x] = 0 for positions before the start.

update.name: cortical prediction and sparse code
update.plain: Step 2: z_t = W_o @ u_t; kappa_t = set of indices of the k largest entries of P @ u_t (ties broken by lower index).

update.latex: J_t = \{j : K_j \subseteq \kappa_t\},\; j^*_t = \arg\max_{j\in J_t} (|K_j|, s_j^{\mathrm{old}}),\; h_t = z_t + \mathbb{1}[J_t\neq\emptyset]\,\rho_{j^*_t};\ \text{then } s_{j^*_t} \leftarrow t
update.name: subsumption read
update.plain: Step 3: J = entries whose key is a subset of kappa_t. If J is nonempty, win = the entry in J with the largest |K|, ties broken by the largest s, using the s values as they were before step t; h_t = z_t + rho_win. If J is empty, h_t = z_t. Step 4: if win exists, set s_win = t now, before observing x_{t+1} and before any write at step t.

update.name: surprise and residual
update.plain: Step 5, after x_{t+1} is observed: g_t = norm(E[x_{t+1}] - h_t) > tau; rho_t = E[x_{t+1}] - z_t (the residual of the current episode; it is distinct from the stored residual rho_j of entry j).

update.latex: \text{(a) if } J_t\neq\emptyset \wedge K_{j^*_t}=\kappa_t:\ \rho_{j^*_t}\leftarrow\rho_t;\ \text{(b) else if } C_t=\{j: \lVert\rho_j-\rho_t\rVert\le\tau,\ |K_j\cap\kappa_t|\ge m\}\neq\emptyset:\ c=\arg\max_{j\in C_t}(|K_j\cap\kappa_t|, s_j),\ K_c\leftarrow K_c\cap\kappa_t,\ s_c\leftarrow t;\ \text{(c) else insert } (\kappa_t,\rho_t,t)\text{, evicting } \arg\min_j s_j \text{ if } |H|=B
update.name: three-way write (only if g_t = 1)
update.plain:
Step 6, only if g_t. All s values here are those after step 4, so s_win = t already.
(a) If a winner exists and K_win == kappa_t: rho_win = rho_t.
(b) Otherwise let C = entries with norm(rho_j - rho_t) <= tau and len(K_j & kappa_t) >= m. If C is nonempty, pick c in C with the largest overlap (ties: largest s). Set K_c = K_c & kappa_t and s_c = t. rho_c is unchanged.
(c) Otherwise, if len(H) == B, remove the entry with the smallest s. Then append (kappa_t, rho_t, t).

non_reduction_argument.broken_invariant:
The parent's mapping relies on three properties:
(i) The address of a stored value is phi(k_t), a function of the writing token's features only, fixed at write time.
(ii) The state is S_t = (I - g e_a e_a^T) S_{t-1} + g e_a v_t^T, so each value stays in the row it was written to until overwritten.
(iii) The read is the linear functional S^T phi(q), gated by an exact tag match.

My write rule (b) breaks (i) and (ii). It moves an existing value rho_c from address K_c to a new address K_c ∩ kappa_t. Whether it moves is decided by comparing the stored value with the new residual, ||rho_c - rho_t|| <= tau. Where it moves depends on both the old stored key and the current code. The new value rho_t is discarded, not written.

My read (update 3) breaks (iii). It is an argmax over {j : K_j ⊆ kappa_t} of (|K_j|, s_j): a specificity selection over a data-dependent subset lattice, not an exact match or a similarity-weighted sum.
non_reduction_argument.known_family: linear_attention: gated delta rule with one-hot hashed keys plus tag-gated eviction (exact-key associative memory)
non_reduction_argument.why_unrepairable:
The strongest repair is to lift the key space to all 2^N subsets, with one row of S per subset, and to use a query feature map that marks every subset of kappa_t. Two things then fail.

First, the read would sum the values of all contained keys, while the mechanism must return only the most specific one, with a recency tie-break. That is a max over rows chosen by a key order, which no fixed linear functional of S computes. A learned feature map cannot know which rows are occupied, because that depends on past data.

Second, consolidation must erase row K_c and write the same stored value into row K_c ∩ kappa_t. This is a copy of stored content between rows, conditioned on a distance test between stored content and the current residual. A delta-rule step S - beta k k^T S + beta k v^T writes a value v_t computed from the current token, at a key computed from the current token. It cannot read rho_c out of S, test it against rho_t, and relocate it, because both the gate and the key would have to depend nonlinearly on S_{t-1}.

Adding a gate or decay cannot express the relocation, and a second memory beside the first would need the same state-dependent copy. Making the key a function of S_{t-1} through an elementwise nonlinearity gives h = f(W h + U x), an RNN. That cannot represent this either, because its state would have to encode the lattice of up to B variable-size subsets and a specificity argmax with exact recall.

The order of writes also matters non-diagonally. Consider rule demonstrations a and b and an exception e. Showing a, b, e yields a schema plus an exception entry, while showing a, e, b yields the same read result through different entries. In a delta-rule model, by contrast, swapping writes at distinct addresses never changes any row, and that commutation is exactly what the critic's check would exploit.

references.why: Supplies the Go-CLS principle that a memory consolidates only when it is predictable and consolidation aids generalization. This is our rule (b): consolidate only when a stored residual already predicts the new episode. It also supplies the tension between memorization and generalization, which the specificity-ordered read resolves by keeping exceptions specific.

Supplies the goal of a learned sparse representation under which online updates generalize without interference. We train P so that rule context and item identity land on separate sparse units, which is what makes code intersection a generalization step.

Supplies systems consolidation as reorganization of stored traces, with prior knowledge setting what consolidates. This motivates consolidation as an edit of an existing trace's index (its key support) rather than as a new trace.

source_transplant.change:
Go-CLS consolidates offline by replaying notebook memories into the weights of a student network. Here consolidation happens within the sequence and changes no weights.
- The predictability test becomes: a stored residual rho_j would have predicted the new episode, ||rho_j - rho_t|| <= tau.
- The transfer becomes the intersection of the two episodes' sparse cortical codes. This removes the units on which the episodes differ (item identity) and keeps the units they share (rule context).
- The notebook is a bounded list of (subset key, residual, time) entries, not a Hopfield network. Retrieval returns the most specific stored key that is a subset of the query code.

From OML we take only the goal of learning a sparse code under which online updates generalize. Here that code is trained by a contrastive overlap loss, not by OML's meta-gradient.
source_transplant.object: The Go-CLS (generalization-optimized complementary learning systems) consolidation rule: a hippocampal memory is consolidated only when consolidating it aids generalization, that is, when it is predictable from structure it shares with other memories. This is combined with OML's sparse representation learned so that online updates generalize without interference, and with systems consolidation as reorganization of memory traces.

card.summary:
The model follows the complementary learning systems split. The slow cortex is a short-window encoder trained by gradient descent. It produces a predicted next-token embedding z_t and a sparse k-of-N code kappa_t of its state. The fast store H holds at most B entries. Each entry has three parts: a key K_j, which is a subset of the N code units; a residual rho_j in R^d; and a last-use time s_j.

A read collects every entry whose key is a subset of the current code. It adds to z_t the residual of the most specific such entry, meaning the one with the largest key. Ties go to the most recent entry.

A write happens only on surprise, and it takes one of three forms:
- (a) If the winning entry's key equals the current code, its residual is overwritten.
- (b) Otherwise, suppose some stored entry has a residual within tau of the new residual and shares at least m units with the current code. That entry consolidates: its key becomes the intersection of its old key and the current code.
- (c) Otherwise a new entry is inserted. If the store is full, the least recently used entry is evicted.

Rule (b) is the Go-CLS principle, that a memory consolidates only when another memory predicts it, carried out inside the sequence. Its effect is generalization by shrinking a key's support. After two demonstrations of 'x -> x+c', the key holds only the rule-context units. Any new item in that context therefore contains the key and receives the correction. An exception shown once keeps its full code and wins by specificity.

The set of keys, their sizes and the subsumption order among them are decided by the data and change during the sequence. Cost per token does not depend on n, and memory is B entries.
card.title: Subsumption Consolidation Store: in-context schemas as intersections of sparse cortical codes

toy_example.description:
A hand-set 2-D instance with the same cortex as the parent card.

Setup:
- Items 0..5 are embedded at e(i) = (i, -1), and a separator S = 6 at (0, 1).
- The cortical state is u_t = (first coordinate of the previous token, second coordinate of the current token). At S the cortex predicts a copy of the previous item.
- There are N = 7 code units. Unit j in 0..5 has row (j, -j^2/2), so at S after item x it peaks at j = x; it is an item unit. Unit 6 has row (0, 100) and fires whenever the current token is S, so it is the rule-context unit.
- Settings: k = 2, B = 4, m = 1, tau = 0.5, beta = 1.

The sequence '3 S 4 1 S 2 4 S' teaches y = x + 1:
- At the first S the store is empty, so the model predicts 3 and inserts key {3,6} with residual (1,0).
- At the second S, the key {3,6} is not a subset of {1,6}, so the model predicts 1, which is wrong. The new residual (1,0) agrees with the stored one and the codes share unit 6, so the entry consolidates to key {6}.
- At the third S, {6} is a subset of {4,6}, so the model predicts 5 for an item it never saw with the rule. The cortex alone would predict 4.

Item positions write and overwrite their own entry under key {4,5}. Six writes happen in total, one of them a consolidation. The code sets s_win = t right after the read and before the write, as in update step 4.
toy_example.python:
import json
import numpy as np
S = 6
E = np.array([[i, -1.0] for i in range(6)] + [[0.0, 1.0]])
U0 = np.array([[0.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]])
U1 = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0]])
Wo = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, -1.0]])
P = np.array([[j, -j * j / 2.0] for j in range(6)] + [[0.0, 100.0]])
k, B, m, tau, beta = 2, 4, 1, 0.5, 1.0
H = []
seq = [3, 6, 4, 1, 6, 2, 4, 6]
preds, hits, writes, cons = [], [], 0, 0
cortex_final, p_final = None, None
for t in range(len(seq)):
    prev = E[seq[t - 1]] if t > 0 else np.zeros(2)
    u = U0 @ E[seq[t]] + U1 @ prev
    z = Wo @ u
    kappa = frozenset(np.argsort(-(P @ u), kind='stable')[:k].tolist())
    J = [e for e in H if e['K'] <= kappa]
    win = max(J, key=lambda e: (len(e['K']), e['s'])) if J else None
    h = z + (win['rho'] if win is not None else 0.0)
    if win is not None:
        win['s'] = t
    logits = -beta * ((E - h) ** 2).sum(axis=1)
    if seq[t] == S:
        preds.append(int(np.argmax(logits)))
        hits.append(int(win is not None))
    if t + 1 < len(seq):
        tgt = E[seq[t + 1]]
        if np.linalg.norm(tgt - h) > tau:
            rho = tgt - z
            writes += 1
            if win is not None and win['K'] == kappa:
                win['rho'] = rho
            else:
                C = [e for e in H if np.linalg.norm(e['rho'] - rho) <= tau and len(e['K'] & kappa) >= m]
                if C:
                    c = max(C, key=lambda e: (len(e['K'] & kappa), e['s']))
                    c['K'] = c['K'] & kappa
                    c['s'] = t
                    cons += 1
                else:
                    if len(H) >= B:
                        H.pop(min(range(len(H)), key=lambda i: H[i]['s']))
                    H.append({'K': kappa, 'rho': rho, 's': t})
    else:
        cortex_final = int(np.argmax(-((E - z) ** 2).sum(axis=1)))
        p = np.exp(logits - logits.max())
        p = p / p.sum()
        p_final = round(float(p[5]), 3)
schema = sorted(int(i) for i in min(H, key=lambda e: len(e['K']))['K'])
print(json.dumps({'pred_at_sep': preds, 'hit_at_sep': hits, 'writes': writes, 'consolidations': cons, 'schema_key': schema, 'cortex_only_final': cortex_final, 'p_final_correct': p_final}))

critic.difference_if_any:
1. The 'class' is a continuous residual of a gradient-trained base predictor, and class agreement is a tau-ball test. The prediction is additive, h = z + rho.
2. The binary features are the top-k units of a learned projection P, shaped by an auxiliary contrastive overlap loss so that shared units encode rule context. In NGE/RISE the features are given.
3. The learner runs online inside each sequence, resets per sequence, and keeps a bounded store with LRU eviction.
4. It is used as a next-token-prediction layer.

The slow parameters are trained by ordinary backprop plus an auxiliary loss. The fast store is the classical rule learner itself. Neither is a new learning rule in the sense of the prefix.
critic.mapping:
Target: an incremental specific-to-general exemplar/rule learner with specificity-ordered conflict resolution. This is Salzberg's Nested Generalized Exemplars (NGE, 1991) and Domingos' RISE (1996), read in the conjunctive-feature form of Find-S / Plotkin least general generalization, with Holland default-hierarchy conflict resolution.

Symbol mapping:
- Instance features: the binary feature vector of an example is the active-unit set kappa_t = TopK_k(P u_t). A conjunctive rule's condition is a feature set K_j. 'Rule matches instance' is K_j ⊆ kappa_t.
- Class label: the class of an example is its residual rho_t = e_{x_{t+1}} - z_t. Two examples have 'the same class' iff ||rho_j - rho_t|| <= tau. Each rule carries its class rho_j.
- Classification (update 3): fire the most specific matching rule, argmax |K_j| over matching rules, with recency tie-break. This is Holland's specificity-ordered default hierarchy, or equivalently a decision list sorted by specificity, and plays the role of NGE's nesting of exceptions inside generalized exemplars.
- Training on a misclassified example (g_t = 1, rule set H):
  - (a) An exact-duplicate exemplar is relabeled.
  - (b) If a stored rule of the same class shares at least m features with the example, generalize it minimally to cover the example. For conjunctions over binary features the least general generalization is the intersection, K_c <- K_c ∩ kappa_t. This is NGE's 'nearest exemplar has the same class, so extend it', with overlap |K_j ∩ kappa_t| as the similarity, and it is Find-S's step.
  - (c) Otherwise store the example as a maximally specific new exemplar/rule, as in NGE and RISE, where rules start as instances.
  - Bounded memory with LRU eviction is an implementation choice.
- Prediction: h_t = z_t + rho_{j*}, where the base predictor z_t supplies the default when no rule fires. The 'class' is a correction vector rather than a discrete label.
critic.textbook_why: The stated source is Go-CLS: offline, predictability-gated replay of notebook memories into student-network weights. The card replaces it with an in-sequence key-intersection edit and a specificity-ordered read, with no weight change, so the source construction itself was changed. The resulting mechanism is close to the textbook Find-S / least-general-generalization plus default-hierarchy construction from symbolic concept learning, but that is not the source the card states it transplants.
critic.why:
Broken invariant: the claim is true of the card's own equations. Write rule (b) edits the address of an existing entry in place, K_c <- K_c ∩ kappa_t. The edit is gated by comparing stored content with the current residual (||rho_c - rho_t|| <= tau), and the new value is discarded. The read is an argmax over {j : K_j ⊆ kappa_t} ordered by (|K_j|, s_j). Neither step is a gated delta step or a linear functional of a fast-weight matrix.

Repairs I tried against linear_attention and its neighbours:
- Lifting to 2^N rows with a subset-marking query map. This came closest. One could even write rho_t (within tau of rho_c) into row K_c ∩ kappa_t and erase row K_c. But the target row and the gate depend on which rows of S_{t-1} are occupied and on their values. That is a key that is a nonlinear function of the state, not a delta rule. The read must also pick a single most-specific occupied row rather than sum.
- A hard-attention/Hopfield kernel memory over B slots with score |K_j|·1[K_j ⊆ kappa_t]. This captures the read as zero-temperature kernel retrieval, but not the key-editing write.
- SSM and RLS. These fail for the same reason.

So the argument against the parent's family holds, and why_unrepairable names the strongest repair with a correct failure reason. The write-order example is weak but not needed.

The card is still a known mechanism. Store maximally specific exemplars, generalize a same-class exemplar by least general generalization (intersection, for conjunctions) when a new example agrees with it, and resolve conflicts by most-specific match. That is incremental NGE/RISE in Find-S form, with Holland's default hierarchy. The card lists Find-S and classifier systems as relatives itself. Here that symbolic concept learner runs in context over learned sparse features, with residuals as classes. A known mechanism moved to a new field is not radical, so radical_enough is false.

Confidence is moderate because no single published system combines exactly these pieces (incremental LGG, overlap threshold, specificity ordering, continuous classes).

prior_art.notes: No retrieved paper describes the specific mechanism: consolidation by intersecting sparse codes of two residual-agreeing episodes, followed by specificity-ordered subset retrieval inside a bounded in-context store. So the label is not 'prior_art_tested' and not 'novel'. Closest prior work includes Holland's default-hierarchy classifier systems (W4299525426) and nonmonotonic inheritance with exceptions (W2031723716, W2407516922, W2341428601), which supply the specificity-ordered default-and-exception idea, plus Go-CLS (W4384922492), which supplies the predictability-gated consolidation principle. The results do not show empirical testing of the claimed in-context, two-shot transfer with intersection-based consolidation in a neural sequence model at comparable scale. The fast-weight and induction-head papers (W3166702123, W3166796161, W4297412003) test related in-context and associative capabilities but not this mechanism. No result shows the central claim fails, so 'known_disproven' does not apply. The card's numeric predictions are not verified by these results.

capabilities.prediction: Accuracy is at most 2/65. Permutation pairs give displacement spectra that are not a single translation. A chance repeat of a displacement can confirm a wrong translation, but that translation's image of the query matches the permutation only at chance (about 1/64).
capabilities.task:

- A random permutation of the 64 content tokens, demonstrated k = 50 times on distinct items, with an unseen query.

capabilities.prediction:
Mean held-out accuracy is at least 0.9, and within 0.05 of the accuracy on shifts {1, 2, 3}.

Reason: zero positive loss forces conj(E_v) * E_{v+1} to be constant in v. Then E_v = rho^v * E_0 with rho^16 = 1, so every shift is a translation.

Learning the relation layout.

Setup:

complexity.constants_notes: Per token the model computes K complex d-dimensional dot products, one d-vector merge and O(K) eviction bookkeeping. The O(dV) term is the output layer. With lattice or Walsh codes it drops to O(d log d + V) by an FFT or a fast Walsh transform. Per-sequence memory is K*d complex numbers for P, K integers for m and one pointer alpha, independent of n. Theta, u, beta and tau are shared across sequences and are not counted. The claims use K = 8 or 16.

sample_efficiency.mechanism: The second coherent demonstration merges into the fragment spawned by the first. The rule is then stored as one phasor, P_alpha, and applied by binding, so it reaches unseen queries. There is no gradient step at inference.

prediction.metric:
The smallest number k of demonstrations at which accuracy on an unseen query reaches at least 0.97. Accuracy is the fraction of 1000 episodes in which argmax_y p(y) equals the correct token, with ties broken uniformly.

Setup:
- Rule b = a + delta mod 64, with delta uniform in {1..63}.
- V = 65, d = 64, lattice codes with a random delimiter, K = 16, tau = 0.5, beta = 8, u = 0.
- Format a_1 b_1 ; ... ; a_k b_k ; a_{k+1}, with distinct a's and a query not among them.
prediction.statement:
Accuracy is at least 0.99 at k = 2 and at most 0.05 at k = 1.
- At k = 1 no merge has happened, so alpha is undefined, s = 0 and the prediction is uniform (about 1/65).
- At k = 2, s(correct) = 1, the other 63 content tokens score 0, and s(';') is distributed about N(0, 0.088). The mean p(correct) is therefore about e^8/(e^8 + 63 + 1.3), which is roughly 0.979.

The parent card needed k = 3.

card.core_idea: Each adjacent token pair produces a relation spectrum (an HRR circular correlation). The spectrum either merges into an existing clean-up fragment that it matches above a margin, or it opens a new fragment, evicting the lightest and oldest fragment when the store is full. The most recently confirmed fragment is bound to the current token to predict the next one.

extensions.description: During end-to-end training, the hard merge is replaced by a sigmoid of (c - tau)/temperature, which mixes merge and spawn. tau and beta can then be learned by cross-entropy. Inference uses the hard core.
extensions.name: Soft margin for training

extensions.description: Each phasor is replaced by a 2x2 unitary block per frequency, so that non-abelian rules such as dihedral reflections can be confirmed and bound.
extensions.name: Unitary block fragments

falsifiers: Shift task with V = 65, d = 64, K = 16, tau = 0.5 and k = 2: accuracy on unseen queries over 1000 episodes below 0.99, or accuracy at k = 1 above 0.05. The same holds for the XOR task with Walsh codes.

Reinstatement task with L = 20: argmax equal to query + delta_A in fewer than 0.98 of episodes. Or, in the novel-shift control, the prediction switching away from delta_B in more than 0.02 of episodes.
Capacity task with K = 8: a threshold different from R = 6 at d = 64 or at d = 128, or a threshold that moves with d. Either result would show that capacity is not set by slots and eviction.
Negative control: random-permutation accuracy on unseen queries above 2/65.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: The parent's state was R_t = sum of w_t. Here no spectrum is added into a shared state. Three choices depend on comparisons with the current store: where w_t goes (merge into j* or spawn), which fragment is evicted, and which fragment is active (alpha). On the reinstatement sequences of claim 2, the two models give opposite predictions.

known_relatives.relation: Same per-pair spectrum conj(E_{x_{t-1}}) * E_{x_t}, and the same binding readout against a tied phasor unembedding.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: Plate's clean-up memory is fixed in advance and used only for decoding. Here it is grown online from relation spectra. Its items are group elements (rules), and the item confirmed most recently is applied to new tokens by binding.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: The clustered objects are circular correlations of successive tokens in a learned phasor algebra. The prediction is not the cluster identity. It is the binding of the most recently confirmed cluster to the current token, which generalizes exactly over the abelian group realized by Theta. Once roughly d unrelated pairs are in context, the background is as large as the signal. The coherence test here is a maximum over K separate fragments, so its noise stays N(0, 1/(2d)) for any n. The stack also has no eviction, so at R = 7 in claim 3 it predicts rule 7 where this card predicts rule 6.

learning.description:
Inference has no gradient step and makes only discrete assignments. Claims 1 to 4 use hand-set lattice or Walsh phases with u = 0, beta = 8 and tau = 0.5.

Claim 5 learns only Theta. u = 0, beta = 8 and tau = 0.5 stay fixed. Theta is trained with the relation-coherence loss below, so that the hard margin test sorts relations correctly. The coherence of two spectra is c(w_i, w_j) = (1/d) Re sum_omega conj(w_{i,omega}) w_{j,omega}, and the margin is gamma = 0.2.

Training algorithm (V = 17: tokens Z_16 plus ';'; d = 16):
1. Episodes. Draw 5000 episodes once. For episode e, draw delta_e uniform in {1, 2, 3} and four distinct a_1..a_4 uniform from Z_16, and set b_i = a_i + delta_e mod 16. The tokens are x = (a_1, b_1, ;, a_2, b_2, ;, a_3, b_3, ;, a_4, b_4), which is 11 tokens and 10 spectra w_t = conj(E_{x_{t-1}}) * E_{x_t} for t = 2..11.
2. Pair sets. R_e = {2, 5, 8, 11} are the positions t where (x_{t-1}, x_t) = (a_i, b_i). Pos_e is the set of all unordered pairs (i, j), i < j, with i and j both in R_e (6 pairs). Neg_e is the set of all other unordered pairs (i, j), i < j, of positions in {2..11} (39 pairs).
3. Step. Sample a batch B of 50 episodes uniformly with replacement from the 5000. The step loss is the mean of L_e over B plus the distinctness hinge D. D runs over all unordered pairs v < v' of the V = 17 codes, including ';'.
4. Gradient. Since c(w_i, w_j) = (1/d) sum_omega cos(Theta_{x_j,omega} - Theta_{x_{j-1},omega} - Theta_{x_i,omega} + Theta_{x_{i-1},omega}) is smooth in Theta, the gradient is exact. The hard merge test, eviction, pointer and readout are not run during training, so no gradient passes through them.
5. Optimizer. Adam with learning rate 0.03 for 2000 steps. Theta is initialized i.i.d. uniform on [0, 2*pi). There are 5 seeds.

equations.name: per-episode relation-coherence loss
equations.plain: L_e = sum over (i,j) in Pos_e of (1 - c(w[i], w[j])) + sum over (i,j) in Neg_e of relu(c(w[i], w[j]) - 0.2), with c(wi, wj) = real(vdot(wi, wj))/d

equations.name: step loss with distinctness hinge
equations.plain: loss = mean(L_e for e in batch) + sum over v < v' (all V codes) of relu(real(vdot(E[v], E[v']))/d - 0.2); one Adam step on Theta

learning.few_shot_argument:
Mechanism: margin-confirmed fragment formation, followed by binding.

1. Identical spectra. If E_{f(v)} = rho * E_v, every demonstration (a, f(a)) gives w = rho exactly, for any content token a.

2. Confirmation. The first demonstration spawns the fragment rho. The second has coherence 1 >= tau with it, so it merges. The mass becomes 2, alpha points to this fragment, and P_alpha stays exactly rho, because phase(m rho + rho) = rho.

3. Unseen queries. For any query x, P_alpha * E_x = E_{f(x)}, so s(f(x)) = 1. Under lattice or Walsh codes every other content token scores exactly 0.

4. Junk stays inert. In the format a b ; a b ; ... with distinct a's, the pair spectra b->; and ;->a have coherence exactly 0 with other spectra of their own type. Against the rule spectrum and across types, coherence is distributed about N(0, 1/(2d)), with standard deviation 0.088 at d = 64. tau = 0.5 therefore lies 5.7 sigma away, so junk never merges and never becomes active.

5. Reinstatement. A fragment of mass >= 2 is evicted only when no non-active mass-1 fragment exists, so confirmed rules persist. One later demonstration of a confirmed rule merges into it and moves alpha back. One demonstration of a novel rule only spawns a fragment and leaves alpha unchanged.

6. Capacity. Each demonstration spawns 2 junk fragments. The first-demonstration fragment of rule r survives until its second demonstration only while at least 2 older mass-1 fragments are available for eviction. This holds exactly for r <= K - 2.

readout.latex: s_t(y) = \tfrac{1}{d}\,\mathrm{Re}\sum_{\omega} P_{\alpha,\omega}E_{x_t,\omega}\overline{E_{y,\omega}}\ (s_t = 0 \text{ if } \alpha \text{ undefined}),\qquad p(x_{t+1}=y) = \mathrm{softmax}_y(u_y + \beta s_t(y))
readout.name: bind active fragment to current token and score
readout.plain: s = zeros(V) if alpha is None else real((P[alpha]*E[x[t]]) @ conj(E).T)/d; p = softmax(u + beta*s)

state.meaning:
Phase table. V is the vocabulary size, counting the content tokens and a delimiter ';'. d is the number of frequencies. The code of token v is E_v = exp(i*Theta_v), taken elementwise. E_v is a unit-modulus Fourier-domain HRR vector, so the Hadamard product is circular convolution and conj is the HRR inverse.
- Hand-set lattice case: Theta_{v,omega} = 2*pi*omega*v/64 for content tokens v in {0..63}.
- Hand-set Walsh case: Theta_{v,omega} = pi*popcount(v AND omega) with d = 64. popcount counts the 1 bits of the bitwise AND.
- In both hand-set cases the delimiter row is drawn i.i.d. uniform on [0, 2*pi) from a fixed seed.
state.name: Theta

state.meaning: u (length V) is a log-prior over next tokens. beta (a scalar) is the readout inverse temperature. tau (a scalar in (0, 1)) is the margin threshold of the merge test. All claims use u = 0, beta = 8 and tau = 0.5, and these are not trained.
state.name: (u, beta, tau)

state.meaning: K_t is the current number of fragments, with 0 <= K_t <= K. K is a fixed hyperparameter, the maximum number of fragments. Row P_j is a unit-modulus complex d-vector, a relation phasor. Rows are kept in creation order, so a smaller index means an older fragment. The store is empty at t = 1 (K_1 = 0).
state.name: P
state.type: per-sequence complex array (fragment phasors of the clean-up memory)

state.meaning: m_j >= 1 is the number of relation spectra merged into fragment j, counting the one that created it. It is aligned row by row with P, and rows are added or deleted together with P.
state.name: m

state.meaning: Index into the rows of P and m of the active fragment, the fragment that most recently received a merge. It is undefined (None) until the first merge. When a row with a smaller index is deleted, alpha is decremented so that it keeps pointing to the same fragment. (alpha is used only for this pointer. The letters a and b denote content tokens in task descriptions.)
state.name: alpha

state.meaning: Relation spectrum of the pair (x_{t-1}, x_t) for t >= 2. Here x_1..x_n is the input sequence of length n, with each x_t in {0..V-1}. w_t is the HRR circular correlation of the two token codes, written in the Fourier domain.
state.name: w_t

state.meaning: Coherence of w_t with each existing fragment, the frequency-averaged real overlap. It is 1 for identical spectra and exactly 0 for distinct lattice displacements. Against random-phase spectra it is distributed about N(0, 1/(2d)).
state.name: c_t

state.meaning: Score of each candidate next token y: the overlap of E_y with the active fragment P_alpha bound to the current token's code. It lies in [-1, 1] and is 0 while alpha is undefined.
state.name: s_t

update.name: phasor embedding
update.plain: E[v] = exp(1j*Theta[v])

update.name: relation spectrum
update.plain: w = conj(E[x[t-1]]) * E[x[t]]

update.name: coherence and best fragment
update.plain: c[j] = real(vdot(P[j], w))/d for every existing fragment j; jstar = argmax(c); there is no jstar if the store is empty

update.latex: \text{if } j^* \text{ exists and } c_{t,j^*} \ge \tau:\; z = m_{j^*}P_{j^*} + w_t,\; P_{j^*,\omega} \leftarrow z_\omega/|z_\omega| \ (\text{unchanged where } z_\omega = 0),\; m_{j^*} \leftarrow m_{j^*}+1,\; \alpha \leftarrow j^*
update.name: merge (margin test passed)
update.plain: if jstar exists and c[jstar] >= tau: z = m[jstar]*P[jstar] + w; P[jstar] = where(abs(z) > 0, z/abs(z), P[jstar]); m[jstar] += 1; alpha = jstar

update.latex: \text{else: if } K_t = K:\ j^- = \arg\min_{j \ne \alpha}(m_j, j)\ (\text{lexicographic}),\ \text{delete row } j^- \text{ of } P, m;\ \text{if } \alpha \text{ defined and } \alpha > j^-:\ \alpha \leftarrow \alpha - 1.\ \text{Then append } P_{K_t+1} = w_t,\ m_{K_t+1} = 1;\ \alpha \text{ keeps pointing to the same fragment.}
update.name: spawn with eviction (margin test failed)
update.plain: else: if len(P) == K: jev = the index j != alpha with the smallest (m[j], j); delete P[jev] and m[jev]; if alpha is not None and alpha > jev: alpha -= 1. Then append P_new = w and m_new = 1. alpha still refers to the same fragment as before the spawn.

non_reduction_argument.broken_invariant:
The family's state is S_t = A_t S_{t-1} + B_t(x_t), with A_t and B_t functions of the input tokens only. S_t is therefore a position-weighted sum of per-token writes, sum_i lambda_{t,i} phi(x_{i-1}, x_i), read by a fixed function g.

In this card, update[2] to update[4] send w_t to fragment j* only if max_j c_{t,j} >= tau, which depends on the current store P. update[4] deletes a whole earlier fragment chosen by the state-dependent key (m_j, j). The active pointer alpha moves only on state-dependent merges. Neither the transition nor the write is a function of the input alone. Whether the state loses a token's contribution depends on what else was stored, as in the eviction of F7 in claim 3.
non_reduction_argument.known_family: linear_attention: H3-style diagonal no-decay linear attention with an elementwise phase normalization (the parent reduction)
non_reduction_argument.why_unrepairable:
The strongest repair is the two-layer stack: a linear-attention repeat detector with S = sum w_i w_i^H and a threshold, feeding a selective-SSM latch. It fails on two counts.

(1) To match the margin test, it must compute max_j |<P_j, w_t>| over separately kept items. A fixed-size sum yields only sum_i |<w_i, w_t>|^2, whose background grows like d per unrelated pair, so its decisions change with n while this card's do not (claim 2 at large L). Computing the maximum exactly over past pairs needs per-item storage and an O(n) scan per token, which is quadratic overall. Lifting phi to a larger state, or adding gates or decays, only reweights that sum.

(2) It has no state-dependent deletion. The (mass, age) eviction produces the exact K - 2 cutoff and the prediction delta_6 at R = 7 in claim 3. A latch driven by input-only gates cannot know whether a mass-1 fragment still exists.

Reproducing both points requires K explicit slots with comparison-routed writes and usage-based deletion. That is this mechanism, not a member of the A_t S + B_t x family. A softmax over past pairs would instead be attention.

references.why: From this paper we take the bind and unbind algebra: circular convolution and correlation, written as the Hadamard product and conj in the Fourier domain. We also take the clean-up memory, a separate associative memory that snaps noisy convolution-memory reconstructions to stored items. Here that memory becomes the core state, grown online from relation spectra.

From the Holographic Bloom Filter we take the margin-based decision rule on correlation scores and its concentration analysis: match scores sit near 1 and non-match scores concentrate near 0 with spread 1/sqrt(d). Here that rule decides whether a relation spectrum merges into a fragment or opens a new one.

source_transplant.change:
The changes are:
- The clean-up memory is not fixed in advance. It is grown during the sequence from the circular correlations of successive tokens.
- The margin test decides between merging and opening a new item. Merged items are phase-averaged and carry a mass, and a full store evicts by (mass, age).
- The item confirmed most recently is bound to the current token to give the next-token scores.
source_transplant.object: Plate's HRR clean-up memory (an item memory that snaps noisy circular-correlation reconstructions to stored items), combined with the margin-based match decision rule of the Holographic Bloom Filter.

card.summary:
Every token has a unit-phasor code E_v = exp(i Theta_v) of length d, a Fourier-domain HRR vector. Each adjacent pair (x_{t-1}, x_t) gives a relation spectrum w_t = conj(E_{x_{t-1}}) * E_{x_t}.

The parent card added all w_t into one vector. This card never adds spectra into a shared state. It keeps a clean-up memory of at most K fragments. The memory starts empty, and the data decide what it holds. Each fragment is a unit phasor P_j with an integer mass m_j.

For each new w_t the model computes its coherence with every fragment and applies a margin test, following the Holographic Bloom Filter decision rule:
- If the best coherence is at least tau, w_t merges into that fragment by phase-normalized averaging. The fragment's mass grows by one and it becomes the active fragment (pointer alpha).
- Otherwise w_t becomes a new fragment of mass 1. When the store is full, the non-active fragment with the smallest (mass, age) key is evicted first.

The readout binds the active fragment to the current token's code and scores every vocabulary item against the result.

Suppose a rule acts as a phase translation, E_{f(v)} = rho * E_v. Every demonstration then yields exactly rho. The second demonstration confirms the fragment, and from then on the rule applies to queries never seen in context. Unrelated pairs fail the margin test, stay as mass-1 fragments, are recycled, and never become active.

Additive memories cannot produce three behaviours of this card:
- One demonstration reinstates a confirmed rule, however many demonstrations of another rule came in between.
- One demonstration of a novel rule does not switch the prediction.
- In the delimited format the store holds exactly K - 2 rules. Slots and eviction set this limit, not crosstalk in d.

Cost is O(d (K + V)) per token and memory is O(K d), independent of n.
card.title: Self-Growing Holographic Clean-up Memory: in-context rules as margin-confirmed relation fragments

toy_example.description:
Lattice codes with d = V = 16 encode Z_16. K = 4, tau = 0.5, beta = 8, u = 0, and there is no delimiter. The active pointer is called act in the code.

The pair displacements, in order, are 3, 1, 3, 2, 5, 4, 5, 6, 5, 7, 5, 8, 3, 9. That is rule A (shift 3) twice, rule B (shift 5) four times, then A once, with unrelated displacements in between.

The store ends with fragments for displacements [3, 5, 8, 9] with masses [3, 4, 1, 1], and the active fragment is the A fragment. The query 2 is therefore mapped to 5, with p = e^8/(e^8 + 15), roughly 0.995. The additive displacement histogram, as stored by the parent card, has its mode at 5, which is rule B.
toy_example.python:
import numpy as np, json
d, K, tau, beta = 16, 4, 0.5, 8.0
E = np.exp(2j*np.pi*np.outer(np.arange(d), np.arange(d))/d)
seq = [0, 3, 4, 7, 9, 14, 2, 7, 13, 2, 9, 14, 6, 9, 2]
P, m, act = [], [], None
R = np.zeros(d, dtype=complex)
for t in range(1, len(seq)):
    w = np.conj(E[seq[t-1]]) * E[seq[t]]
    R = R + w
    c = [float(np.real(np.vdot(Pj, w))) / d for Pj in P]
    j = int(np.argmax(c)) if c else -1
    if j >= 0 and c[j] >= tau:
        z = m[j] * P[j] + w
        az = np.abs(z)
        P[j] = np.where(az > 0, z / np.where(az > 0, az, 1.0), P[j])
        m[j] += 1
        act = j
    else:
        if len(P) == K:
            jev = min([i for i in range(len(P)) if i != act], key=lambda i: (m[i], i))
            del P[jev]
            del m[jev]
            if act is not None and act > jev:
                act -= 1
        P.append(w)
        m.append(1)
x = seq[-1]
s = np.zeros(d) if act is None else np.real((P[act] * E[x]) @ np.conj(E).T) / d
lg = beta * s
p = np.exp(lg - lg.max())
p = p / p.sum()
disp = [int(np.argmax(np.real(np.conj(E) @ Pj))) for Pj in P]
hist = np.rint(np.real(np.conj(E) @ R) / d).astype(int)
print(json.dumps({'fragment_displacements': disp, 'masses': [int(v) for v in m], 'active': int(act), 'pred': int(np.argmax(p)), 'p_pred': round(float(p.max()), 3), 'additive_hist_mode': int(np.argmax(hist))}))

critic.difference_if_any:
What remains after the mapping:
- The clustered objects are HRR circular correlations of adjacent tokens, so each cluster is a group element: a translation under lattice codes, an XOR under Walsh codes.
- The readout binds the most recently resonated cluster to the current token instead of outputting the cluster identity. This gives exact generalization to unseen queries over the abelian group realized by Theta.
- The eviction tie-break (pin the active fragment, then take the minimum (mass, age)) produces the exact K-2 capacity in the delimited format.

These are a choice of input stream, a choice of readout and a cache-replacement detail. None is a new update form.

The Theta training in claim 5 is a standard contrastive/hinge metric-learning loss on the codes, optimized by Adam. It is not a different learning rule.
critic.mapping:
Known form: Adaptive Resonance Theory, i.e. ART-style vigilance categorization (Carpenter & Grossberg). Equivalent forms are Hartigan's sequential leader clustering and bounded DP-means. It runs on a capacity-limited slot store with LFU-then-FIFO replacement, which is cache replacement or DNC-style usage-based allocation. Its input stream is the HRR relation spectra, and an HRR unbind readout is added.

Symbol by symbol:
- ART input pattern I_t := w_t = conj(E_{x_{t-1}}) ⊙ E_{x_t}. This is the previous-token-key times value product from the parent's H3 mapping. Here it is the clustering input instead of being summed.
- Category prototypes := fragment phasors P_j.
- Choice function T_j(I) := coherence c_{t,j} = (1/d) Re<P_j, w_t>, with winner-take-all j* = argmax_j T_j.
- Vigilance rho := tau. The match test c_{t,j*} >= tau is the resonance-or-reset decision.
- Resonance learning := merge P_{j*} <- phase(m_{j*} P_{j*} + w_t). This is the count-weighted running-mean prototype update of leader clustering or sequential k-means, followed by an elementwise projection onto the unit torus.
- Mismatch reset and recruitment of an uncommitted node := spawn P_new = w_t with m = 1.
- Finite category pool with replacement := K slots, evicting argmin_{j != alpha}(m_j, j). This is LFU with a FIFO tie-break that pins the most recently used entry. It is a standard cache-replacement policy and NTM/DNC least-used allocation.
- Most recently resonating category := alpha.

Readout: s_t(y) = (1/d) Re<P_alpha ⊙ E_{x_t}, E_y>, followed by softmax(u + beta s). This binds the last resonated prototype to the current token, as in HRR binding with Plate's unbind and clean-up decoding, and scores against a tied unembedding. It is the parent's phase-translation readout with g(R_t) replaced by P_alpha.

Why the equations coincide: each per-token step of the card is the ART / leader-clustering loop applied verbatim to w_t. The steps are: score all prototypes, take the winner, apply the vigilance threshold, update the winner or recruit a new node, and replace the least-used slot.
critic.textbook_why: The cited source object is Plate's fixed, offline HRR clean-up memory combined with the Holographic Bloom Filter margin test. The card changes it substantively: the memory is grown online, items merge by mass-weighted phase averaging, a full store evicts by (mass, age), and the last merged item is bound to the current token. The modified construction coincides with a different textbook algorithm, ART / leader clustering with bounded slots, which is recorded in the reduction.
critic.why:
Escape argument, invariant check: the argument holds. update[3] and update[4] route w_t by max_j c_{t,j} >= tau, which depends on the stored P. update[4] deletes a row chosen by the state-dependent key (m_j, j), and alpha moves only on state-dependent merges. So the state is not S_t = A_t S_{t-1} + B_t(x_t) with input-only A_t and B_t. No basis change, feature lift or gate repairs the parent's H3 / diagonal linear-attention mapping.

Repairs tried:
1. The card's own two-layer stack (linear-attention repeat detector plus selective-SSM latch). The card's objection is correct: the background of the summed squared overlaps grows with n, and the stack has no state-dependent deletion.
2. Softmax attention over past spectra. A previous-token head computes w_t, then a sharp attention detects repeats and copies the last repeated spectrum. This came closest. It reproduces claims 1, 2 and 4 in quadratic time, but its capacity is unbounded, so at R = 7 it predicts rule 7 rather than delta_6 (claim 3). It is not exact.
3. Delta-rule and Hopfield memories. These still superpose writes or retrieve softly, with no threshold-gated recruitment or eviction.

The card therefore escapes the sequence-model families. The per-token loop it escapes into is itself textbook: ART vigilance categorization, or leader clustering / DP-means, with running-mean prototypes and a bounded pool under LFU/FIFO replacement. The card's own known_relatives list concedes leader clustering, DP-means and DNC allocation. What remains new is feeding that algorithm HRR relation spectra and reading out by binding the last resonated prototype. That is a known mechanism moved into in-context sequence modelling, combined with a known HRR readout. The headline behaviours follow directly from winner-take-all categories plus cache replacement: K-2 slot capacity, one-shot reinstatement, and a novel rule not switching the prediction. The escape argument holds against linear attention, but the card reduces to other_known and is not radical.

prior_art.notes: The found work covers the components but not the combined mechanism. Plate's HRR clean-up memory (W82661287) is a fixed, offline associative memory used for decoding, not one grown online from relation spectra. The Holographic Bloom Filter (2601.20921) supplies a margin-based match rule, and the HRR papers supply the bind/unbind algebra. The Dirichlet-process working memory (W7168293524) opens slots on novelty, which is the closest analogue to growing the store, but it does not use phasor relation spectra or a margin-confirmed merge. The HRR self-attention paper (ddcfdcab) tests HRR sequence modelling at long lengths, a related but different claim. No found paper tests few-shot in-context rule confirmation, mass-and-age eviction, or the K-2 capacity threshold, so the central capability claims have little or no empirical support in the results. No result shows the central claim failing, so known_disproven does not apply. The search does not establish full novelty, since the components have close prior art.

complexity.constants_notes: Per-token costs: forming Phi(w_t) costs m d^2. The same matrix serves the readout at t and the accumulation at t+1, so it is formed once per token. The Gram update costs d m^2, the evidence update d m, K ISTA steps K m^2, and the readout d m + V d. Memory: the in-context state (M_t, b_t, r_t) is m^2 + 2m numbers and does not depend on n. The learned B has m d^2 numbers and the fixed E has V d. Optionally, G[w] = Phi(w)^T Phi(w) can be precomputed for all w (V m^2 extra memory), which lowers the Gram update to O(m^2). Capability claims are for the converged lasso: when measuring, K is raised (at most 200) until the support is stable. This is a constant factor and does not change the order in n.
complexity.time_per_token: O(m d^2 + d m^2 + d V)

sample_efficiency.mechanism: Lasso support recovery on the accumulated energy (few_shot_argument), in the planted setting: E fixed with i.i.d. unit rows, atoms with i.i.d. N(0,1/d) entries, one true atom, uniform first token, and w_u = argmax_v e(v)^T B_i e(w_{u-1}). The union estimate of failure after k pairs is (m-1) Q(q sqrt(k d)), with q about c_V/sqrt(d).
