At k = 2 it is 255 Q(3.96), about 0.01. The lambda = 0 min-norm least-squares solve of identical (M_t, b_t) needs k_0.9 >= 16 = m/d.

card.core_idea: A two-level predictive coding network infers a sparse code r for each sequence over a repertoire of m token-transition operators, by minimizing the summed prediction-error energy of all past token pairs plus an L1 prior; this energy is kept exactly in an m-by-m sufficient statistic, so one repertoire rule is identified after a number of demonstrations that grows only logarithmically in m, while the same statistics without the L1 prior need about m/d.

extensions.description: The core never forgets, so after rule a has been shown k_a times, switching to rule b needs more than k_a demonstrations of b. A decay gamma < 1 on (M, b) speeds switching. This makes accumulation a decaying linear recurrence, and it is not part of the claims.

equations.plain: M = gamma*M + Phi.T@Phi; b = gamma*b + Phi.T@E[w_t]

extensions.name: Forgetting for rule switches

extensions.description: Each pair is weighted by pi_t = 1/(1 + ||eps_t||^2/sigma^2), which gives iteratively reweighted robustness to off-rule pairs.
extensions.name: Precision-weighted errors

extensions.description: Nesterov momentum in the rule-layer relaxation reduces the K needed for large m.
extensions.name: FISTA acceleration

falsifiers: In the planted setting with m = 256, d = 16, V = 256: if the lambda = 0 min-norm least-squares solve of the same (M_t, b_t) reaches 0.9 query accuracy with k <= 2 pairs, the claim that the L1 prior is the source of few-shot identification is refuted.

In the planted setting with d = 16 and V = 256: if k_0.9 of the lambda > 0 model exceeds 2 at m in {64, 256} or exceeds 3 at m in {1024, 4096}, or grows by more than 1 pair from m = 64 to m = 4096, the support-recovery explanation (k growing like ln m / ln V) is wrong.

Consider sequences where the KKT check computed from (M_t, b_t) certifies the planted support. If converged ISTA returns a different support in more than 1% of them, or the readout then misses the rule's next token in more than 1% of queries, the claim that the relaxation solves the stated lasso is refuted.

If the local rule, trained online with fixed random E on the planted corpus defined in mechanism.learning (m0 = 32 planted operators, 10^4 sequences of length 32, d = 16, V = 256), leaves more than 10% of planted operators with best-match cosine similarity < 0.9 among the learned atoms, the claim that the repertoire can be learned locally is refuted.

If accuracy at 4 demonstrations falls by more than 1 percentage point as the query moves from n = 10^2 to n = 10^5 in rule-consistent sequences, the claim that the energy is carried without loss is refuted.

If the core exceeds 0.15 recall on the capacity-limit task (P = 32 random bindings, m = 64, d = 32, V = 256), something other than repertoire selection drives its behaviour, and the theory does not describe the model.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: The state is indexed by rule space (m x m), not by key/value space. The readout is not a linear query of S_t. It is the fixed point of an L1-regularized energy (a lasso). That fixed point does non-separable explaining-away and zeros wrong atoms, which is the claimed source of logarithmic-in-m sample complexity. The lambda = 0 ablation (falsifier 1) tests this.
known_relatives.name: Linear attention (Transformers are RNNs) and SSMs
known_relatives.relation: M_t and b_t are running sums of the form S_t = S_{t-1} + B_t x_t, so the accumulation step is a linear-attention-style recurrence.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: TTT writes a d x d weight with SGD per token. Here only an m-dimensional code over frozen operators is inferred, to the exact optimum and under a sparse prior, with sample cost logarithmic in m instead of about d pairs. The price is that the model cannot learn bindings outside its repertoire.
known_relatives.name: TTT layers and fast weights
known_relatives.relation: Both optimize a prediction loss inside the context.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: The mixing code does not come from a per-token gate. It is inferred from the accumulated errors of all past pairs, is shared across the sequence, and is made sparse by an energy prior, not by top-k routing.
known_relatives.name: Mixture of experts
known_relatives.relation: The B_j act like experts mixed by r.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: Here the coded object is the set of all transitions of a sequence. It is carried exactly in rule-space statistics, with d new measurements per token and warm-started per-token inference.
known_relatives.name: Sparse coding / ISTA (Olshausen-Field dictionary learning)
known_relatives.relation: Same energy, inference dynamics and local dictionary rule.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: The attractor card completes one stored pattern with a cubic coupling tensor. The Koopman card fits a free dense operator by RLS, which needs about d demonstrations. This card solves a convex lasso over learned operators using an m x m statistic.
known_relatives.name: Rule-Repertoire Attractor (card-d1d383d5) and Koopman Power Readout (card-537e161c) in this run
known_relatives.relation: Both infer a transition rule in context from pair evidence.

learning.description: Learning is offline and local and uses the predictive-coding (Olshausen-Field) dictionary rule. Only B is learned. E stays fixed, so no backpropagation is needed. The procedure is online over sequences: sequences are processed one at a time, with one update of every atom per sequence. Sequences with n < 2 contain no pair (M = 0) and are skipped. For each training sequence w_1..w_n, (M_n, b_n) is accumulated and ISTA is run to convergence (up to 200 steps, until the support is stable) to give r_hat. Each atom then takes one step along the negative gradient of F_n with respect to B_j and is renormalized. That gradient uses only quantities local to the synapse: the atom's activity r_hat_j, the errors eps_u and the presynaptic embeddings e(w_{u-1}). Training corpus used for the claims and falsifiers (the planted corpus): m0 = 32 planted operators B*_1..B*_m0 with i.i.d. N(0,1/d) entries. N_seq = 10^4 sequences of length n = 32. Each sequence draws one planted index j uniformly, draws w_1 uniformly from the V tokens, and sets w_u = argmax_v e(v)^T B*_j e(w_{u-1}). The learned B has m = m0 atoms, initialized with i.i.d. N(0,1/d) entries and normalized. lambda during training equals the lambda used at test time.

equations.latex: \Delta B_j = \eta_B\, \hat r_j \sum_{u=2}^{n} \epsilon_u\, e(w_{u-1})^\top,\quad \epsilon_u = e(w_u) - \Phi(w_{u-1})\hat r,\quad \hat r = \arg\min_r F_n(r)
equations.name: local operator update for one training sequence w_1..w_n
equations.plain: Skip the sequence if n < 2. r_hat = converged ISTA on (M_n, b_n). For u = 2..n: eps_u = E[w_u] - Phi(w_{u-1}) @ r_hat. For each j: B[j] += eta_B * r_hat[j] * sum_{u=2..n} outer(eps_u, E[w_{u-1}]); then B[j] *= sqrt(d)/||B[j]||_F.

learning.few_shot_argument: Mechanism: lasso support recovery at the top predictive-coding level. Notation: u indexes pair positions, k is the number of demonstration pairs, S is the support of the true code r* and sigma its signs, Q is the standard normal tail, and c_V is the expected maximum of V i.i.d. standard normals (c_256 is about 2.8; asymptotically sqrt(2 ln V)). After k pairs, F_t is exactly the lasso with a stacked kd x m design, and (M_t, b_t) hold it without loss. (1) Deterministic condition, computable from (M_t, b_t) alone, with no assumption on E or B. Suppose M_SS is positive definite, r_S = M_SS^{-1}(b_S - lambda sigma) has signs sigma, and |b_j - M_jS r_S| < lambda for every j not in S. Then the KKT conditions make (r_S, 0) the unique lasso minimizer. Converged ISTA returns it, and the readout uses only rules in S. (2) When this holds with high probability: the planted setting, with E fixed random, atoms with i.i.d. N(0,1/d) entries, one true atom i, and greedy rule tokens. Each pair adds q to b_i, where q is the mean of max_v e(v)^T B_i e(w). Since e(v)^T B_i e(w) is N(0,1/d), q is about c_V/sqrt(d): 0.7 at d = 16 and 0.5 at d = 32 for V = 256. To each wrong b_j a pair adds an exactly N(0,1/d) term, since B_j e is N(0, I/d) and independent of the unit vector e(w_u). With S = {i}, the KKT check reduces to the true atom beating every wrong one. Ignoring explaining-away, which only helps, the union estimate of failure is (m-1) Q(q sqrt(k d)) = (m-1) Q(c_V sqrt(k)). The required k therefore grows like 2 ln m / c_V^2, which is about ln m / ln V. (3) Role of L1: the threshold zeros the wrong atoms, so the readout is the true rule's prediction. With lambda = 0 and kd < m, the min-norm code is about (d/m) Phi^T y. The true atom gets weight about (d/m) k q. Every wrong atom gets about (d/m) N(0, k/d), and their summed squared weight is about k d/m. The correct token then scores about (d/m) k q^2 = k c_V^2/m. Each distractor gets a N(0, k/m) score, so the distractor maximum is about c_V sqrt(k/m). The correct token wins only if k > m/c_V^2. For d > c_V^2 (about 7.8) this exceeds m/d, so in the whole underdetermined range kd < m least squares fails, and it needs at least about m/d pairs. (4) Reuse: nothing is forgotten, b_i grows linearly in rule-consistent pairs, and the relative threshold lambda/M_ii shrinks like 1/k.

readout.latex: p(w_{t+1} = v \mid w_{\le t}) = \mathrm{softmax}_v\big( E\, \Phi(w_t)\, r_t / \tau \big)
readout.name: top-down prediction and next-token distribution
readout.plain: y_hat = Phi(w_t) @ r_t (length d); logits = E @ y_hat / tau (length V); p = softmax(logits). At t = 1, r_1 = 0 and p is uniform.

state.meaning: Token embedding table. V is the vocabulary size and d the embedding width. Rows e(w) = E[w,:] are drawn once, i.i.d. uniform on the unit sphere of R^d, and then frozen. Row e(w) is the bottom-level representation of token w and also serves as the unembedding.
state.name: E

state.meaning: Repertoire of m transition operators (dictionary atoms). B_j = B[j] maps the current token embedding to a predicted next-token embedding under rule j. Each atom is renormalized to Frobenius norm sqrt(d) after every learning step.
state.name: B

state.meaning: lambda is the L1 weight of the rule-layer prior. tau is the readout temperature. K is the number of warm-started ISTA steps per token (default 3). eta_B is the learning rate of the offline operator update (default 0.05). lambda and tau are chosen on held-out sequences.
state.name: theta
state.type: 4-tuple of hyperparameters: (lambda: positive real, tau: positive real, K: positive integer, eta_B: positive real)

state.meaning: Rule-space Gram (precision) matrix: the sum of Phi_u^T Phi_u over pair positions u = 2..t, with M_1 = 0. It is the quadratic part of the cumulative energy.
state.name: M_t

state.meaning: Rule-space evidence: the sum of Phi_u^T e(w_u) over pair positions u = 2..t, with b_1 = 0. It is the linear part of the cumulative energy.
state.name: b_t

state.meaning: Top-level activity: the sparse rule code of the sequence after position t, which approximates the minimizer of the cumulative energy. It is warm-started from r_{t-1}, with r_1 = 0.
state.name: r_t

update.latex: \Phi_t = \Phi(w_{t-1}) = [B_1 e(w_{t-1}), \dots, B_m e(w_{t-1})] \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times m}, \quad t = 2, \dots, n
update.name: bottom-up basis of the previous token
update.plain: Tokens are w_1..w_n, and u or t index positions. At position t >= 2 the pair (w_{t-1}, w_t) arrives. Phi_t is the d x m matrix whose column j is B[j] @ E[w_{t-1}], i.e. rule j's prediction of the next embedding. Forming it costs m d^2. It is the same matrix the readout at position t-1 already formed, so it can be reused.

update.name: energy accumulation (precision)
update.plain: M = M + Phi_t.T @ Phi_t, starting from M = 0

update.latex: b_t = b_{t-1} + \Phi_t^\top e(w_t),\ b_1 = 0;\quad F_t(r) = \tfrac12 \sum_{u=2}^{t} \|e(w_u) - \Phi_u r\|^2 + \lambda\|r\|_1 = \tfrac12 r^\top M_t r - b_t^\top r + \lambda\|r\|_1 + \text{const}
update.name: energy accumulation (evidence)
update.plain: b = b + Phi_t.T @ E[w_t], starting from b = 0. The cumulative energy is F_t(r) = 1/2 r^T M_t r - b_t^T r + lambda*||r||_1 + const.

update.latex: L_t = \max_i \sum_j |(M_t)_{ij}|;\ \text{if } L_t = 0:\ r_t = r_{t-1};\ \text{else } r \leftarrow r_{t-1},\ \text{repeat } K:\ r \leftarrow \mathcal{S}_{\lambda/L_t}\big(r + (b_t - M_t r)/L_t\big),\ r_t = r;\quad \mathcal{S}_c(x) = \mathrm{sign}(x)\max(|x|-c,0)
update.name: predictive-coding relaxation of the rule layer (warm-started ISTA)
update.plain: L = max row-abs-sum of M. If L == 0 (always the case at t = 1, before any pair), keep r_t = r_{t-1}. Otherwise set r = r_prev and repeat K times: r = soft(r + (b - M @ r)/L, lambda/L), with soft(x,c) = sign(x)*max(|x|-c,0). By Gershgorin, L >= the largest eigenvalue of M, so 1/L is a valid ISTA step. Note that b - M r = sum_u Phi_u^T eps_u with eps_u = E[w_u] - Phi_u r, i.e. the projected bottom-up errors.

references.why: Deep predictive coding networks infer sparse codes by minimizing prediction error plus L1 with proximal gradient (ISTA/FISTA) steps. The rule-layer relaxation is taken from this.
Initializing predictive coding neurons from the previous equilibrium preserves progress and cuts inference steps. Here this becomes warm-starting r_t from r_{t-1}.
Shows that the local predictive-coding rule on transition-predicting inputs discovers structured representations. This motivates learning B with the same local error rule.
A hierarchy in which slower levels predict faster ones. The slow sequence-level rule code predicting fast token transitions follows this arrangement.

source_transplant.change: The bottom layer predicts the next token's embedding from the current token's embedding through m transition operators. It does not code a static input. The top-layer code is shared by all positions of a sequence, and its energy is summed over all past token pairs. That sum is kept exactly in rule-space sufficient statistics (M_t, b_t), so inference runs incrementally per token with warm starts. A softmax readout of the top-down prediction turns the network into a next-token model.
source_transplant.object: The predictive-coding energy of a two-layer sparse generative model (sum of squared bottom-level prediction errors plus an L1 prior on top-level activity), minimized by warm-started proximal-gradient (ISTA) inference, with the local dictionary update Delta B_j proportional to r_j * eps * x^T

card.summary: The bottom level predicts the embedding of the next token as a mixture of m linear transition operators applied to the current token's embedding. The top level holds one slow variable for the whole sequence, a sparse rule code r. Each token pair adds its prediction-error energy to a running quadratic form (M_t, b_t) over rule space. The top level then relaxes by warm-started proximal-gradient (ISTA) steps. These steps are the predictive-coding inference dynamics, because b_t - M_t r is the sum of all bottom-up prediction errors projected onto the atoms. The next-token distribution is a softmax over the top-down prediction. Operators are learned offline by the local predictive-coding dictionary rule on a defined training corpus. Embeddings are fixed and random. In-context learning is therefore exact sparse model selection, not weight writing. KKT conditions computable from (M_t, b_t) decide whether the lasso picks the right rule. In a planted random setting these conditions fail with probability about (m-1) Q(q sqrt(k d)) (union estimate) after k demonstrations. Per-token cost does not depend on n: it is O(m d^2 + d m^2 + d V). The in-context state is O(m^2). The core can only select and mix rules from its repertoire. It cannot store arbitrary new bindings.
card.title: Sparse Rule-Code Predictive Coding: in-context learning as lasso inference over a learned repertoire of transition operators

toy_example.description: V = 4 tokens with one-hot embeddings (d = 4). The repertoire has m = 3 operators: identity, shift +1 mod 4 and shift +2 mod 4. The sequence 0, 1, 2 demonstrates shift +1. After each pair, (M, b) is accumulated and r is relaxed by warm-started ISTA (lambda = 0.5, step 1/L, skipped if L = 0). The next token is then predicted with tau = 0.25. After one pair, M = I and r = [0, 0.5, 0], so the model predicts 2 with p = 1/(1+3e^-2). After two pairs, M = 2I and r = [0, 0.75, 0], so it predicts 3 with p = 1/(1+3e^-3).
toy_example.python:
import json
import numpy as np
V, m, lam, tau, K = 4, 3, 0.5, 0.25, 50
E = np.eye(V)
shifts = [0, 1, 2]
def Phi(w):
    return np.stack([E[(w + s) % V] for s in shifts], axis=1)
def soft(x, th):
    return np.sign(x) * np.maximum(np.abs(x) - th, 0.0)
def infer(M, b, r):
    L = np.abs(M).sum(axis=1).max()
    if L == 0:
        return r
    eta = 1.0 / L
    for _ in range(K):
        r = soft(r + eta * (b - M @ r), eta * lam)
    return r
def readout(w, r):
    z = E @ (Phi(w) @ r) / tau
    p = np.exp(z - z.max())
    p = p / p.sum()
    return int(np.argmax(p)), float(round(float(p.max()), 4))
seq = [0, 1, 2]
M = np.zeros((m, m))
b = np.zeros(m)
r = np.zeros(m)
out = {}
for t in range(1, len(seq)):
    P = Phi(seq[t - 1])
    M = M + P.T @ P
    b = b + P.T @ E[seq[t]]
    r = infer(M, b, r)
    pred, p = readout(seq[t], r)
    out['r_after_%d' % t] = [float(round(float(v), 4)) for v in r]
    out['pred_after_%d' % t] = pred
    out['p_after_%d' % t] = p
print(json.dumps(out))

critic.difference_if_any: LEARNING_RULE: The operators B_j are learned by the local Olshausen-Field dictionary rule Delta B_j proportional to r_hat_j * sum_u eps_u e(w_{u-1})^T, with renormalization, at the converged lasso code and with E frozen. There is no backpropagation through the readout, whereas Mesa layers and test-time-regression layers are trained end to end by backprop. Beyond the learning rule, two further differences remain. First, the in-context regularizer is L1 over coordinates in a learned operator dictionary instead of L2 over a free d x d map, which is what yields support recovery with sample cost logarithmic in m instead of about m/d. Second, the readout is an iterative proximal solve (non-separable explaining-away), not a closed-form linear query. Both are a different regularizer and solver inside the known accumulate-statistics-then-solve-regression template. They are not a new state update.
critic.mapping: Known form: the Mesa layer (von Oswald et al. 2023, 'Uncovering mesa-optimization in transformers'), also called in-context least squares or test-time regression. It accumulates key-key and key-value statistics with a linear-attention recurrence, then reads out the solution of a regularized regression on them: S_kk,t = S_kk,t-1 + k_t k_t^T, S_kv,t = S_kv,t-1 + k_t v_t^T, W_t = argmin_W sum_u ||v_u - W k_u||^2 + R(W), y_t = W_t q_t. Card symbol map: (1) The regression parameter W corresponds to the fast transition map W_t = sum_j r_j B_j, which is constrained to span{B_j} and parameterized by r in R^m. Then Phi(w) r = (sum_j r_j B_j) e(w), so the card's prediction is a linear map W_t applied to e(w). (2) The design rows (keys) are Phi_u = Phi(w_{u-1}), a d x m block, i.e. d scalar measurements of r per pair. (3) The values are v_u = e(w_u). (4) S_kk corresponds to M_t = sum Phi_u^T Phi_u and S_kv to b_t = sum Phi_u^T e(w_u). These are exactly linear-attention / SSM accumulations S_t = S_{t-1} + B_t x_t with matrix-valued keys, and the card concedes this in known_relatives. (5) The query is Phi(w_t), and the readout is y_t = Phi(w_t) r_t followed by the softmax unembedding E. (6) The regularizer R is lambda ||r||_1, solved by warm-started ISTA, where the Mesa layer uses ridge with a closed-form or CG solve. With lambda -> 0 (or ridge) the card is literally a Mesa layer over m-dimensional dictionary coordinates: r_t = M_t^{+} b_t, y = Phi(w_t) M_t^{+} b_t. The equations therefore coincide except for the choice of regularizer in the readout optimization. A secondary view gives a soft MoE with frozen linear experts B_j and one sequence-level mixing vector r. Here r comes from a lasso on accumulated error statistics, not from a per-token gate.
critic.textbook_why: The core is Olshausen-Field sparse coding / lasso: L1-regularized least squares, ISTA inference, and the local gradient dictionary update r_j * eps * x^T. Its dictionary has the bilinear operator form Phi(x) = [B_j x] already known from bilinear sparse coding (Grimes and Rao). Summing the energy over token pairs with a shared code is just a stacked lasso design, and keeping (M, b) is the standard incremental sufficient statistic of online lasso / dictionary learning. The card substitutes token-embedding pairs for the field's own inputs and adds a softmax readout, without changing the update, coupling or learning rule.
critic.why: The per-token state update is pure linear-attention / SSM accumulation of a Gram matrix and a cross-correlation vector, and the card admits this. The readout is the argmin of a regularized least-squares problem on those statistics, which is exactly the Mesa-layer / test-time-regression template, so the only change is swapping ridge for lasso over a learned dictionary of transition operators. Lasso support recovery with (m-1)Q(.) union bounds and KKT certificates is textbook high-dimensional statistics, and sparse coding with ISTA and the local dictionary rule is textbook predictive coding. Combining them gives a structured, regularized in-context regressor that a researcher familiar with mesa-optimization and sparse coding would anticipate. It is a known mechanism moved into sequence modelling, with a capacity restricted to a repertoire, not a surprising new core mechanism.

prior_art.notes: No found paper implements the card's mechanism: in-context identification of one rule by warm-started L1 inference over a learned repertoire of m transition operators, with (M_t, b_t) sufficient statistics. The closest relevant items are the lasso reference (W2564702731) and meta-learned support recovery (W3130248626), which show that support recovery can be sample-efficient but do not study transition-operator repertoires or sequence rule identification. Asymptotic in-context learning theory for linear attention (W4412122873) is a related theoretical result. The card's central capability claims, including k_0.9 <= 2 at m = 256 and the logarithmic-in-m sample scaling, lack empirical testing in these results. Predictive-coding sparse inference (2101.06848) is the closest mechanism match but addresses static inputs, not in-context sequence rules. The lambda = 0 contrast and the capacity-limit claims are not tested by any listed work. The toy example in the card checks out by hand: r after one pair is [0, 0.5, 0] and p is about 0.711, and after two pairs r is [0, 0.75, 0] and p is about 0.87.

capabilities.prediction: Values are rounded to 3 decimals. One exemplar: P(same subordinate) = 0.525, P(same basic, other subordinate) = 0.250, P(same superordinate, other basic) = 0.092, P(other superordinate) = 0.000. Three same-subordinate exemplars: 1.000, 0.064, 0.004. Three basic-spanning exemplars: P(basic) = 1.000, P(superordinate) = 0.060. The Gromov products computed from Poincare distances match ln3 * LCA depth to 1e-9, so unrounded probabilities match the closed form at the exact depths to within the same order.
capabilities.task: Xu-Tenenbaum-style word learning on the anchor-star embedding described above: superordinate depth 1, basic 2, subordinate 3, exemplars 4, G = ln3 * LCA depth, delta = 1, lambda = 0.5, h = 0. Three conditions: one exemplar; three distinct exemplars of one subordinate kind; three exemplars from three subordinates of one basic class.

capabilities.prediction: P(other exemplar of the positive's subordinate kind) = (3^1.5 - 3)/(9 - 3) = 0.366. P(any member of the negative's subordinate kind, or of any other subordinate in the basic class) = 0.000.
capabilities.task: Negative evidence on the same embedding: one positive exemplar plus one negative example from a sibling subordinate kind, so h = 2 ln3.

capabilities.prediction: Mean P on held-out members >= 0.85 and mean P on non-members <= 0.15. On at least 90% of concepts, the 1-example condition orders P(same parent) > P(same grandparent) > P(outside the grandparent).
capabilities.task: Learned embedding: WordNet nouns under mammal.n.01 (about 1180 nouns), embedded in a 10-d Poincare ball by Riemannian SGD on transitive-closure is-a pairs. delta and lambda are fit on 100 training concepts. The 300 held-out concepts are synsets with at least 4 leaf descendants, at all depths. Each episode gives 3 distinct leaf examples sampled from the concept, then queries 10 held-out members and 10 non-members.

capabilities.prediction: Every query probability is identical (difference < 1e-12) to the value obtained when the same word's events are presented alone, because each word's state is its own 4-number entry: 4000 numbers in total. Representational limit, checked on all 5000 queries: for each word, P is a nondecreasing function of z = G(y, a_w) alone, with zero violations. No extent outside the family H_r around one anchor can be expressed.
capabilities.task: Many words in one context: 1000 novel words, each with up to 5 interleaved positive or negative examples and 5 queries, about 2 x 10^4 tokens, on the anchor-star embedding.

capabilities.prediction: With no negatives, g drops to the common superordinate, so P(wolf) = 1.000 and accuracy on wolf negatives is 0.000. With one wolf negative, h >= g, so the readout falls back to 1[z >= g] and still accepts wolves. Disjunctions are outside the core.
capabilities.task: Scope limit: disjunctive concepts that are not a shadow, for example 'pet' = {dogs, cats} excluding wolves. Positives are dogs and cats, and queries are wolves (a sibling basic class under the same superordinate).

complexity.constants_notes: n is the context length. U <= n/3 is the number of concept words with an entry in T. Each write or query computes one Gromov product: three squared norms of d-vectors (about 6d flops), two atanh and one acosh. A query adds 3 exponentials and expected O(1) hash lookups. For large c, use the stable form P = (e^{c(m-g)} - e^{c(h-g)}) / (1 - e^{c(h-g)}) to avoid overflow. Parameters: V_C*d for E plus 2 scalars. The in-context state is 4 numbers per concept word. n does not enter the per-token cost, and no stored example is scanned.

sample_efficiency.mechanism: Size principle over Gromov shadows. The min over positives sets g, the count k sets the sharpness c = delta*k - lambda, and the closed-form posterior turns two examples from different subordinate kinds into certain basic-level generalization.

prediction.metric: Minimum number of positive examples needed for P >= 0.99 on every held-out member of a basic-level class. The anchor-star embedding places every token y by the hyperbolic law of cosines so that G(y,a) = ln3 * depth(LCA(y,a)) in a 4-level taxonomy, with exemplars at depth 4. delta = 1 and lambda = 0.5. The examples are drawn from distinct subordinate kinds of that class.
prediction.statement: Two examples from two different subordinate kinds give g = 2 ln3, the basic level. Every basic-level member then has z >= g and P = 1.000 exactly. One example gives only P = 0.250 to a basic-level member and 0.525 to a same-subordinate member.

card.core_idea: A novel word shown with a few example tokens is generalized by averaging over a continuum of nested 'Gromov shadows' H_r = {y : (y|a)_0 >= r} of a learned Poincare embedding, where (y|a)_0 is the Gromov product based at the center 0 of the ball and the shadow sizes shrink as e^{-delta r}; k positive examples then give the closed-form posterior P(y) = (e^{cm} - e^{ch}) / (e^{cg} - e^{ch}) with c = delta*k - lambda, computed from a four-number statistic per word, so the answer depends on how many examples were seen and not only on which ones.

extensions.description: In regions of the embedding that are not tree-like (large delta_H), re-anchor to the positive example with the largest rho after each write and recompute g over a small stored list of positives. This reduces the error and the order dependence that come from a single fixed anchor.
extensions.name: Anchor refinement

extensions.description: Keep negatives that arrive before a word's first positive in a short per-word list and apply them when the anchor is set. This removes the one order dependence that holds even on an exact tree.
extensions.name: Early negatives buffer

extensions.description: Keep up to two anchors per word and compute the posterior over unions of two shadows, to handle concepts like 'pet' that the core cannot express.
extensions.name: Disjunctive concepts

extensions.description: A small tagger maps natural-language spans ('these are daxes: ...', 'is this a dax?') to the (w, op, x) events that the core consumes.
extensions.name: Learned event parser

falsifiers: Exactness on the anchor-star embedding. The theory is refuted if any Gromov product computed from Poincare distances differs from ln3 * LCA depth by more than 1e-9 (the toy checks this for its five tokens and prints G_exact_ok), or if any query probability, rounded to 3 decimals as in the reference code, differs by more than 0.001 from the values listed in capabilities 1 and 2 or in the toy example.

Euclidean ablation on the WordNet mammal task: replace the Poincare ball by a Euclidean 10-d embedding trained on the same pairs, and compute the Gromov product with Euclidean distances and base point 0. The prediction is a member/non-member mean-P gap at least 0.15 smaller than the hyperbolic gap. If the Euclidean gap is within 0.05 of the hyperbolic gap, the claim that hyperbolic geometry supplies the hypothesis family is refuted.

Size-law check on WordNet mammal.n.01. Let b be the mean number of children over non-leaf synsets in that subtree, counted in WordNet. Let s be the least-squares slope of G(x,y), computed on E, against depth(LCA(x,y)) in WordNet, over 10^5 uniformly sampled pairs of distinct leaves. One level deeper in Gromov product divides the shadow by b, so the predicted exponent is delta* = ln(b)/s (on the toy geometry, b = 3 and s = ln3 give delta* = 1). The boundary-measure size law is refuted if the delta fitted on training episodes lies outside [delta*/2, 2 delta*].

Count dependence: on WordNet, presenting one leaf example 3 times should lower the mean P on non-member siblings of its parent by at least 0.1 relative to presenting it once. If there is no significant drop over 300 concepts, the learned delta*k term carries no information and the few-shot argument fails.

Near-exchangeability on WordNet: over the 300 held-out concepts, the mean absolute change in query P when the 3 positive examples are presented in a random different order (so that a different example is the anchor) should be at most 0.05. A larger mean change means E is too far from tree-like for the single-anchor family.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: No tree and no labels are built in context. The hierarchy is in a learned embedding. The answer is a graded posterior that changes with the number of examples, and a Boolean prefix or containment test cannot depend on that count.
known_relatives.name: Online tree path-labeling (Dewey / Tropashko nested intervals), the parent card's reduction
known_relatives.relation: Both answer hierarchical membership queries over symbols seen in context.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: The hypothesis space is not an explicit taxonomy. It is the continuum of Gromov sublevel sets of a learned hyperbolic embedding, with sizes given by the exponential boundary-measure law e^{-delta r}. The posterior is an integral with a closed form, computed from an O(1) statistic per word with O(d) work per token. The discrete-node version gives different numbers: 0.477 instead of 0.366 in the toy example.
known_relatives.name: Bayesian word learning with the size principle (Xu and Tenenbaum)
known_relatives.relation: Same inference principle: strong sampling with hypothesis-size likelihood over nested extents.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: Those models fix the class regions offline, per trained class. Here the extent of a novel class is inferred in context from a handful of examples, as a posterior over region depth, with no nearest-prototype rule.
known_relatives.name: Hyperbolic prototype / entailment-cone classifiers (2209.05842, Poincare embeddings)
known_relatives.relation: Same geometric substrate: hierarchy is encoded in negatively curved space and membership is decided geometrically.

known_relatives.claimed_difference: The stored value is a sufficient statistic, not a returned answer. The readout integrates over all consistent extents with a size-weighted likelihood. Find-S, 1[z >= g], is only the limit c -> infinity of the readout.
known_relatives.name: Exact-match cache / hard attention; Find-S most-specific-hypothesis learner
known_relatives.relation: The word-keyed table is retrieved by exact match. Taken alone, g is the most specific consistent hypothesis.

learning.description: The learned parts of the core are the hyperbolic embedding E and the two scalars theta = (delta, lambda). E is pretrained on hierarchy-bearing data, such as is-a pairs or co-occurrence of labels with no given hierarchy, following 2101.04997. The pretraining uses the stable geodesic (Riemannian) update of 1805.10487, so that Gromov products encode common-ancestor depth. theta is then fit, with E fixed or jointly, by minimizing the cross-entropy of the yes/no readout on training episodes and differentiating through the closed form. Nothing is trained in context. The context only updates the sufficient statistic (a, g, h, k) of each word.

equations.name: episode loss for theta (and optionally E)
equations.plain: loss = -sum over training queries of [s*log(P) + (1-s)*log(1-P)], with s = 1 if the query token belongs to the concept and P from the closed-form readout

equations.name: geodesic pretraining step for E (1805.10487 style)
equations.plain: E[x] = exp_map(E[x], -eta * ((1-|E[x]|^2)^2/4) * grad_l(E[x])), where l is the pretraining loss, eta the step size, and exp_map moves along the Poincare geodesic

learning.few_shot_argument: The named mechanism is the size principle on a geometric hypothesis family. (1) The learned embedding supplies, for every anchor, a continuum of nested candidate extents H_r, so the hierarchy does not have to be shown in context. (2) Hyperbolic volume growth makes the size of H_r decay exponentially, as e^{-delta r}. Under strong sampling, each additional positive example that falls inside a deep extent multiplies the posterior odds of depth r against a shallower depth r' by e^{delta (r - r')}. (3) The positives fix g, the deepest consistent extent, through a min over Gromov products. One example from each of two subordinate kinds therefore raises g to the depth of their common ancestor, and every member of that class gets P = 1. Repeating one example keeps g but raises c, so generalization beyond the example falls off as (e^{cz}-1)/(e^{cg}-1). A rule shown k times is thus reused with a confidence that is a known function of k and of three Gromov products. In the toy example, a sibling breed gets 0.366 after one dalmatian and 0.060 after three. On tree-like embeddings this confidence does not depend on the order of the examples after the first positive (see T).

readout.latex: H_r = \{y: G(y,a_w)\ge r\},\ |H_r| = e^{-\delta r},\ \pi(r)=\lambda e^{-\lambda r}\ \Rightarrow\ p(r\mid \text{data}) \propto e^{c r}\,\mathbb{1}[h_w \le r \le g_w],\quad c = \delta k_w - \lambda
readout.name: posterior over the extent depth (size principle on Gromov shadows)
readout.plain: The hypotheses are the nested sets H_r. Each positive x has likelihood 1[x in H_r] * e^{delta r} (strong sampling), so the k positives together require r <= g. A negative requires r > G(neg, a), so r > h. The posterior density on [h, g] is proportional to exp(c*r) with c = delta*k - lambda.

readout.latex: z = G(y,a_w),\ m=\max(h_w,\min(z,g_w));\ P = \begin{cases} \frac{e^{cm}-e^{ch_w}}{e^{cg_w}-e^{ch_w}} & g_w>h_w,\ c\ne 0\\ \frac{m-h_w}{g_w-h_w} & g_w>h_w,\ c=0 \\ \mathbb{1}[z\ge g_w] & g_w\le h_w \end{cases}
readout.name: membership probability (closed form)
readout.plain: z = G(y, a); m = max(h, min(z, g)); if g > h: P = (exp(c*m) - exp(c*h)) / (exp(c*g) - exp(c*h)) (or (m-h)/(g-h) when c == 0); else P = 1 if z >= g else 0 (point mass at the tightest positive extent). Clip P to [0,1]. y is in H_r iff r <= z, so P is the posterior mass of r <= z.

readout.latex: p(v) = \begin{cases} \epsilon/|V| + (1-\epsilon)\,[P\,\mathbb{1}(v=\text{yes}) + (1-P)\,\mathbb{1}(v=\text{no})] & \text{buf}=(w,?,y),\ w\in W,\ y\in C \\ 1/|V| & \text{otherwise} \end{cases},\quad P=\tfrac12 \text{ if } w\notin T
readout.name: next-token distribution (predicts x_{t+1} at every position)
readout.plain: If buf == (w, '?', y) with w in W and y in C: P comes from the closed form if w in T, else P = 0.5; p = full(|V|, eps/|V|); p[yes] += (1-eps)*P; p[no] += (1-eps)*(1-P). At every other position: p = full(|V|, 1/|V|).

state.meaning: E[x] lies in the open unit ball of R^d, for each of the V_C content tokens x in C. It is pretrained so that hierarchy is encoded in hyperbolic geometry: the Gromov product (x|y)_0, based at the center 0 of the ball, approximates the depth of the common ancestor of x and y. E is frozen during a context.
state.name: E
state.type: learned parameter block: Poincare-ball embedding of content tokens

state.meaning: delta > 0 is the exponent of the shadow-size law |H_r| = e^{-delta r}, the boundary measure of the Gromov shadow at depth r. lambda >= 0 is the rate of the exponential prior over the extent depth r. Both are fit by maximum likelihood on training episodes.
state.name: theta

state.meaning: There is one entry per concept word that has received at least one positive example. U is the number of such words; U <= n/3, where n is the context length (each write uses 3 tokens). a_w in C is the anchor, the first positive example. g_w >= 0 is the minimum over positive examples x of G(x, a_w), the deepest extent that contains all positives. h_w >= 0 is the maximum over negative examples x of G(x, a_w), initially 0; extents must be deeper than h_w. k_w >= 1 is the number of positive examples, counting repeats. Order: the anchor makes the state order-dependent in general. Two exact statements hold. (i) A negative that arrives before the word's first positive is dropped. (ii) If the Gromov products of E are those of a tree (0-hyperbolic), then g_w, the clipped value m = max(h_w, min(G(y,a_w), g_w)) and the branch g_w > h_w do not depend on which positive is the anchor, so P is exchangeable in all events after the first positive. On a delta_H-hyperbolic embedding (delta_H is the four-point hyperbolicity constant of the Gromov products of E), changing the anchor to another positive moves these truncated products by O(delta_H).
state.name: T
state.type: hash table: concept word w -> (a_w, g_w, h_w, k_w)

state.meaning: The last three tokens (x_{t-2}, x_{t-1}, x_t) of a context x_1..x_n of length n over vocabulary V = W ∪ C ∪ R. W is the set of novel concept-word tokens. C is the set of content tokens, each with an embedding. R = {'+', '-', '?', 'yes', 'no', BOS} are reserved tokens. Positions before the start are padded with BOS, so buf is defined at every t >= 1.
state.name: buf

state.meaning: Smoothing mass 0 < eps < 1, spread uniformly over the |V| tokens so that every readout is a proper distribution. The default is 1e-3.
state.name: eps

update.name: Gromov product in the Poincare ball, based at the center 0
update.plain: The base point is 0, the center of the unit ball. rho(x) = 2*atanh(norm(E[x])) is the hyperbolic distance from 0 to E[x]; dist(x,y) = acosh(1 + 2*|E[x]-E[y]|^2 / ((1-|E[x]|^2)*(1-|E[y]|^2))); G(x,y) = (rho(x) + rho(y) - dist(x,y)) / 2

update.latex: (w,\mathrm{op},x) = (x_{t-2},x_{t-1},x_t);\; \text{act only if } w\in W,\ \mathrm{op}\in\{+,-,?\},\ x\in C;\ \text{otherwise no state change}
update.name: parse (once per position t, after x_t enters buf)
update.plain: w, op, x = buf; if w not in W or op not in {'+','-','?'} or x not in C: no state change. op == '+' -> positive write; op == '-' -> negative write; op == '?' -> readout only, no write.

update.latex: w\notin T:\ T[w] \leftarrow (x,\, G(x,x),\, 0,\, 1);\quad w\in T:\ g_w \leftarrow \min(g_w,\, G(x,a_w)),\ k_w \leftarrow k_w+1
update.name: positive write
update.plain: if w not in T: T[w] = [x, G(x,x), 0.0, 1]   (G(x,x) = rho(x)); else: a = T[w].a; T[w].g = min(T[w].g, G(x,a)); T[w].k += 1

update.latex: w\in T:\ h_w \leftarrow \max(h_w,\, G(x,a_w));\quad w\notin T:\ \text{no change}
update.name: negative write
update.plain: if w in T: T[w].h = max(T[w].h, G(x, T[w].a)); else: ignore (a negative needs an anchor; this is the one order dependence that holds even on a tree)

non_reduction_argument.broken_invariant: The reduction depends on two properties of the parent. Its in-context state is a table of labels, each a deterministic injective function of the node's root path in a tree assembled from in-context facts. Its readout is a Boolean prefix (interval-containment) test on two labels, unaffected by how often facts repeat. This card breaks both. (1) No tree or path label is formed in context. The hierarchy is the learned metric of E, and the context writes only (a, g, h, k) per novel word, through update[2] and update[3]. (2) readout[1] returns P = (e^{cm} - e^{ch}) / (e^{cg} - e^{ch}) with c = delta*k - lambda. This is a real-valued posterior that depends on the example count k and on continuous Gromov products. In the toy example the same pair (dax, poodle) gets 0.366 after one dalmatian and 0.06 after three identical dalmatians. Repeating an identical fact cannot change any path label or any prefix test.
non_reduction_argument.known_family: other_known: online tree path-labeling for ancestor queries (Dewey labels / Tropashko nested-interval 2x2 integer matrix encoding) with a prefix or containment test
non_reduction_argument.why_unrepairable: A labeling scheme returns a function of two labels with values in {0,1}. My readout is graded, and for fixed labels it varies with k, so no relabeling, change of generator basis or richer label alphabet reproduces it. The strongest repair would give the critic the tree underlying the embedding, label it with Dewey paths, and add Xu-Tenenbaum Bayesian averaging over the discrete ancestors of the anchor with sizes e^{-delta depth}. The repair still fails, for two reasons. (a) It needs an explicit tree, but the core has only a learned embedding whose Gromov products are not integer depths. (b) Even on the toy's exact geometry, the discrete average over node depths {0, ln3, ln9} with weights e^{c r} gives P(poodle | one dalmatian) = (1 + sqrt3)/(1 + sqrt3 + 3) = 0.477, while my continuum integral gives 0.366. Matching the card would require the repair to integrate over a continuum of extents bounded by real Gromov products, and that integral is the core of this card, not a labeling scheme. I do not claim novelty for the in-context accumulator itself (min, max, count). What is new is the posterior readout over learned hyperbolic shadow sets, whose sizes follow the exponential boundary law.

references.why: Hyperbolic label embeddings learned jointly when the label hierarchy is not given. I take from it the idea that hierarchy can live implicitly in a learned Poincare embedding, which is the role of E here; no tree is supplied or built in context.

Hyperbolic class prototypes with membership decided geometrically. I replace the fixed per-class region with a posterior over a nested family of regions (Gromov shadows) inferred in context for a novel class.
The stable geodesic update on hyperbolic space, used as the pretraining step for E.

source_transplant.change: Class regions are not fitted per class. For a novel word, the candidate extents are the sublevel sets H_r = {y : (y|a)_0 >= r} of the Gromov product (based at the ball center 0) around an anchor a. Their sizes follow the hyperbolic exponential boundary-measure law e^{-delta r}. Membership is a Bayesian size-principle posterior over r with a closed form, driven by an in-context sufficient statistic (anchor, minimum positive product, maximum negative product, count).
source_transplant.object: Learned Poincare-ball label embedding whose geometry encodes an unknown class hierarchy (2101.04997), with hyperbolic regions as class extents (2209.05842), trained by geodesic updates (1805.10487).

card.summary: This is a specialized in-context concept learner, not a general language model. The context introduces novel words (dax, wug, ...) through positive examples 'dax + dalmatian', negative examples 'dax - poodle' and queries 'dax ? beagle'. Each query gets a graded yes probability. No tree is built in context. The hierarchy lives only in a pretrained Poincare-ball embedding E of the content tokens. The relative depth of two tokens is read as their Gromov product (x|y)_0, with base point 0, the center of the ball. In a tree this is the depth of the lowest common ancestor; in a delta_H-hyperbolic space it is that depth up to O(delta_H). For a word with anchor a (its first positive example), the candidate extents form a one-parameter nested family H_r = {y : (y|a)_0 >= r}, r >= 0. The size of each set is modeled as its boundary-at-infinity measure, e^{-delta r}, where delta is a learned exponent. Under strong sampling, each positive example inside H_r has likelihood e^{delta r}. With an exponential prior lambda e^{-lambda r}, the posterior on the consistent interval [h, g] is proportional to e^{(delta k - lambda) r}. Here g is the smallest anchor Gromov product among the positives and h is the largest among the negatives. The probability that a query y belongs to the concept is the posterior mass of r <= (y|a)_0, which has a closed form. One example generalizes broadly. Repeating the same example sharpens the extent toward that example, which is the size principle or 'suspicious coincidence'. Examples from two subordinate kinds move g up to their common ancestor and give P = 1 to the whole basic-level class. Each token costs O(d), and each word keeps four numbers.
card.title: Gromov-Shadow Size Principle: few-shot concept extents as closed-form Bayesian posteriors over nested sublevel sets of a learned hyperbolic embedding

toy_example.description: Five content tokens are placed in the Poincare disk with the hyperbolic law of cosines, so that their Gromov products with the anchor 'dalmatian' (radius 2 ln3) are exact: poodle, terrier and beagle at ln3 (same basic class 'dog'), and cat at 0. delta = 1 and lambda = 0.5. Word dax: after one dalmatian, the sibling breed poodle gets 0.366 and cat gets 0. After three dalmatians (k = 3), poodle drops to 0.06, which is the size principle. Word fep: dalmatian, poodle and terrier lower g to ln3, so beagle gets 1.0 and cat gets 0. Word wug: a dalmatian positive plus a poodle negative gives h = ln3, so dalmatian gets 1.0 and beagle gets 0. G_exact_ok checks that every Gromov product with the anchor, computed from Poincare distances, matches its exact value to 1e-9.

critic.difference_if_any:
1. The scalar similarity is supplied by a specific substrate: the Gromov product based at 0 of a pretrained Poincare embedding.
2. The region-size law e^{-delta r} is motivated by hyperbolic shadow measure (the Sullivan shadow-lemma scaling), with delta fit as a free exponent.
3. A single first-positive anchor makes the learner order dependent off exact trees.
4. delta and lambda are meta-fit by cross-entropy on episodes, which is ordinary hyperparameter fitting of a known Bayesian model, not a new learning rule.
critic.mapping:
Known form: Bayesian concept learning with the size principle over a continuous nested family of consequential regions. Sources are Shepard (1987), Tenenbaum (1999, the 'healthy levels' interval concepts), Tenenbaum & Griffiths (2001), and Xu & Tenenbaum (2007). The family here is one-sided threshold regions on a scalar similarity. The card's state is the Find-S plus count sufficient statistic of that learner.

- Card z = G(y, a_w) becomes the scalar similarity coordinate s(y) of the query to the stored exemplar. The card's own capability 4 concedes that P is a nondecreasing function of z alone.
- Card H_r = {y : z >= r} becomes the nested consequential region 'similarity at least r', which is a one-parameter nested hypothesis family.
- Card |H_r| = e^{-delta r} becomes the assumed hypothesis size |h_r|. Card strong-sampling likelihood 1[x in H_r] e^{delta r} becomes the size-principle likelihood (1/|h|)^k.
- Card prior lambda e^{-lambda r} becomes the standard exponential (Erlang-type) prior on region size used by Shepard and by Tenenbaum-Griffiths.
- Card g_w = min over positives of G(x, a) becomes the most specific consistent hypothesis (the Find-S boundary). Card h_w = max over negatives becomes the most general boundary excluded by the negatives. Card k_w becomes the sample count n in (1/|h|)^n.
- Card P = integral of the posterior over r <= m, giving (e^{cm} - e^{ch}) / (e^{cg} - e^{ch}) with c = delta k - lambda, becomes the Tenenbaum-Griffiths generalization function p(y in C | X) = sum over h containing y of p(h | X), evaluated for a continuous one-dimensional nested family. That is one elementary integral of an exponential.
- Card update[2] and update[3] (min, max, increment) become the streaming maintenance of that sufficient statistic. The card's argument concedes this accumulator is not new.
- The parse window and the eps-smoothed yes/no token are a sequence-model wrapper.

The equations coincide term by term. Posterior proportional to prior times likelihood gives lambda e^{-lambda r} e^{delta k r} on [h, g]. Integrating over the regions that contain y gives the card's closed form.
critic.textbook_why: The cited source objects are hyperbolic label embeddings and fixed hyperbolic class regions (2101.04997, 2209.05842). The card changes them: per-class fitted regions are replaced by an in-context posterior over nested Gromov sublevel sets. The added piece is itself the textbook Shepard/Tenenbaum size-principle construction, so the card composes two known constructions rather than transplanting one unchanged.
critic.why:
The broken_invariant holds for the parent's family. Readout[1] is real-valued and depends on k, so no Dewey or nested-interval labeling with a Boolean prefix test reproduces it. The parent's repair (relabeling, generator change, richer labels) fails as the card says.

The argument does not survive the neighboring family it names itself. Its strongest stated repair is discrete Xu-Tenenbaum averaging, and it refutes that only by pointing out that the hypothesis set is a continuum (0.366 vs 0.477). Continuous nested hypothesis spaces with size-principle likelihoods and exponential size priors are the textbook form. Shepard's universal generalization law and the Tenenbaum-Griffiths and Tenenbaum interval models are exactly that integral. The closed form is one line of algebra. I checked 0.366: g = 2 ln3, h = 0, z = ln3, c = 0.5 gives (sqrt3 - 1)/2.

The repair that came closest, and succeeds, is that Bayesian size-principle learner run on the scalar z = G(y, a) as its similarity coordinate. Everything else is known:
- the min/max/count statistic (Find-S plus count, conceded by the card);
- Gromov shadows and their exponential measure (standard hyperbolic geometry);
- the learned hyperbolic embedding (Nickel-Kiela style).

The result is a composition of known pieces, a cognitive-science Bayesian generalizer fed by a hyperbolic feature. It is not a new sequence mechanism, and it should not surprise a researcher who knows these families.

prior_art.notes: None of the 35 results addresses the central mechanism: a Bayesian size-principle posterior over nested Gromov shadows of a learned Poincaré embedding, computed from a per-word sufficient statistic (anchor, g, h, k). No result mentions the size principle, Bayesian word learning, or Gromov-product extents, so the mechanism is labeled novel. The closest results are hyperbolic embedding and classification work: W2934497416 (hyperbolic image embeddings, including few-shot settings), W3015597782 (entailment-cone hierarchical classification), W2617943363 (hyperbolic graph embeddings), and W2803294777 (hyperbolic neural network layers). These supply the geometric substrate but use fixed per-class regions and no in-context posterior over extent depth. The theory's listed references (2101.04997, 2209.05842, 1805.10487) and Xu–Tenenbaum do not appear in the results, so they were not used as evidence. The card's own falsifiers (Euclidean ablation, size-law check, count dependence, order sensitivity) are untested in the literature found here. Labels are judged only on the results supplied.
